The covid-19 pandemic may have also had an indirect effect on cases lately via the rise of remote learning and prolonged screen time, they add. “This case highlights the importance of considering EAI in children presenting with reticulated rashes, particularly in the context of increasing electronic device use,” the doctors concluded. Personally, I just hope having a cat on your lap or chest isn’t hot enough to cause toasted skin, because otherwise I could be in trouble down the line.

item.title: ‘The Last of Us’ Season 3 Is Now Likely to Be the Show’s End
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.50
There was always a question of how much Last of Us we would be getting. Before even a single episode of the show aired, co-creator Craig Mazin was being asked about how many seasons were planned and whether it could go above and beyond the story of the video games. Later, he even floated the idea of a season four, though season two’s structure seemed to suggest a potential end. And now, one of the people who would definitely know has weighed in. Speaking to Deadline after the Emmys, HBO CEO Casey Bloys said that The Last of Us season three is coming at some point in 2027 and that “I think [showrunner] Craig [Mazin] has planned it as the final season.” Which, of course, is not a definitive statement, but it’s worth noting that Bloys was not as certain of Mazin’s plans as recently as earlier this year. Plus, if Mazin’s boss is under the impression season three is the end, it’s probably the end. If that is indeed the case, it makes sense on several levels. Season two of The Last of Us adapted the first half of The Last of Us Part II video game and season three is set to do the second half. That game, and the show, split its story between two characters, Ellie (Bella Ramsey) in this season and Abby (Kaitlyn Dever) in the upcoming season. That’s where the game series ends, at least for now. And with game and series creator Neil Druckmann no longer working on the show, adapting that second half of his game seems like a nice way to keep him involved in spirit. There’s also the simple fact that season two of The Last of Us didn’t light up the world in the way season one did. In large part, that’s probably due to the fact that season one starred one of the biggest movie stars out there, Pedro Pascal, and season two killed him off in an early episode. But Pascal probably wouldn’t have even done The Last of Us at all had that not been built into the DNA of the story. So he giveth and taketh away. Nevertheless, The Last of Us Part II video game is a hugely satisfying conclusion to the series (which is rumored to continue with a new game at some point), so if Mazin can capture that with season three, it’s better to go out on top. The last thing any of us want is five seasons of wheel-spinning. Three and out feels right. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: Scientists Studied 185,896 Miles of Roman Roads—and That’s Still the ‘Tip of the Iceberg’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.35
Last year, archaeologist Tom Brughmans and colleagues released itiner-e—the largest map of the Roman road system, covering 186,411 miles (300,000 kilometers). Since then, the researchers have been picking apart their database for new insights into these famous roads. Turns out, a lot of what we assume about Roman roads may be wrong. To Gizmodo, Brughmans explained that the latest findings, published today in Nature Communications, bust several popular myths about Roman roads. First, despite the popular saying, not all roads lead to Rome, and networks were more effectively distributed throughout the Roman Empire. Second, Roman roads weren’t as exceptionally straight as previously thought. Third, the idea that Roman roads have persisted for so long that we’re still walking on them might be an overstatement. The overall takeaway is that, because the Roman road grid was so extensive—not even itiner-e covers everything, Brughmans noted—generalized assumptions will probably fall short of describing these ancient networks. “I found it hugely frustrating that we simultaneously seemed to know so much and so little about Roman roads,” said Brughmans, of Aarhus University in Denmark. “But most frustrating is that these easily dismissible assumptions prevented scholars from asking the really interesting questions underpinning them.” An innovation According to Brughmans, Roman roads represented the “first continental-scale transport network in human history.” This enabled the transmission of people, animals, disease, goods, and ideas, the researchers wrote. The system represented a mix of newly built roads and upgrades to existing ones; the roads supported the Roman Empire’s conquest of new regions in addition to a vast trading network. The latter included smaller transactions in local communities for buying and selling necessities like produce. “The system was crucial to keep a 1 million population alive in the capital city, Rome, which was highly dependent on the import of grain all the way from Alexandria in Egypt,” Brughmans explained. “The roads reveal so much more than Roman emperors’ politics and military campaigns: they shaped the lives of the ‘silent majority.’” That said, despite scholars’ long-time interest in Roman roads, our understanding of them has largely depended on qualitative studies based on snippets of direct and indirect evidence, according to the paper. The goal of the latest study, therefore, was to conduct a formal quantitative assessment of Roman roads. Needless to say, the team, having put together itiner-e, was in an excellent position to pursue this project. The debunk The latest analysis began with three common assumptions: the centrality of Rome with regard to the network, the roads’ topological nature, and their continuity to the present day. Exploring these questions led to other inquiries, Brughmans explained. For instance, if the roads didn’t just lead to Rome, where did they go, and why? How did local landscapes affect the course of roads? How did the roads change over the past 2,000 years? As for the first question, the team found that, while Rome did serve as a center for Mediterranean shipping, the overall network was more broadly distributed throughout the empire, especially around provincial capitals. This probably came in handy for provincial administration and tax collection. Meanwhile, Constantinople, which became the capital in the fourth century, was actually more of a “central” location for the empire, “way more so than Rome,” Brughmans added. The idea of straight Roman roads comes from examples like Via Appia, and Romans were certainly exceptional engineers. However, roads were straight only if the local terrain allowed for it, according to the paper. The connection between Roman and modern roads wasn’t as strong as previously believed. Some older roads did survive, and of those some stayed the same while others were renovated following the Industrial Revolution. Others simply disappeared over time. Not all roads… That said, the team noted in the paper that it used the “best available,” not necessarily complete, dataset of Roman roads, although the researchers made sure to run robustness checks on their analyses. Another important caveat is that the Roman road system itself came from earlier routes and evolved with the empire—as well as the societies that followed the Romans. “Our research reveals that this is just the tip of the iceberg: the Roman road system is way more extensive than even our work reveals,” Brughmans said. “The multi-scalar nature of our results fascinates me. The continental-scale patterning that emerges from millions of local histories. It is baffling to realize that infrastructure built two thousand years ago still affects peoples’ interactions in the present.”

item.title: The US Put Weapons in Space. What Could Possibly Go Wrong?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.88
Oh good, space has weapons now. The U.S. has publicly acknowledged for the first time that it has weapons in orbit, a decidedly less sci-fi development than it might sound. The admission comes as the Space Force gears up for a future in which satellites and other systems in orbit could face increasingly serious threats—and the decision to say it out loud may itself be part of the strategy. On Monday, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink confirmed that the U.S. deployed weapons to space to be prepared against existing threats. “The United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said during a speech at the 2026 Air and Space Cyber Conference. The unusually candid statement comes as a surprise, with the U.S. military previously remaining vague when it comes to sharing information regarding its defense capabilities. While the purpose of the sudden admission remains unclear, the statement has already prompted a response from China warning against orbital warfare. Space wars In the past few years, U.S. officials have increasingly talked about offensive space capabilities and space-based interceptors. The recent admission, however, was far more explicit and seemingly more deliberate than any previous statement. Although the details of the on-orbit space weapons were not clear, Meink doubled down on his statement when asked about it later. “That phrase was very well thought out,” Meink said, according to SpaceNews. “So whatever I said before is what I say again.” Meink’s statement is an apparent transition from decades of proposals and official advocacy to an explicit public acknowledgment that the U.S. has operational weapons in orbit. Last year, President Donald Trump signed an executive order emphasizing the Space Force’s role not just in defense but as an active attacking and space-control force. In July, the Space Force deployed an electromagnetic warfare device designed to “detect, deny, disrupt, and degrade adversary capabilities” to create a so-called silence zone. As part of its Tactically Responsive Space (TacRS) program, the Space Force also pitted two satellites against each other in a simulated orbital threat scenario. Orbital threats The U.S. has become increasingly concerned about the growing space capabilities of nations like Russia and China, with officials warning of systems designed to disrupt, disable, or destroy satellites and other orbital assets. The surprising admission to having weapons of its own has prompted a response from the country’s rivals. “We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space,” China’s foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news briefing, according to AFP. Russia also called for space to be kept weapon-free. “We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarization of space,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday. While talks of the militarization of space are nothing new, the U.S. has generally kept its arsenal under wraps. That’s why the recent move to publicly admit to having space weapons comes as a surprise. “I don’t think any US government official has ever said that before,” Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation’s chief director of space security and stability, told Defense One. “The US also now has to accept the Chinese and Russians doing/saying the same. I don’t think that this is going to be in the interest of US national security.” To be clear, the U.S. does not appear to be violating international agreements by developing conventional weapons for use in space (assuming these are conventional weapons). The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, but it does not ban all weapons in space.

item.title: Scientists Found Chocolate’s Biggest Climate Problem—and It Isn’t Heat or Drought
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.81
Chocolate is one of the most beloved foods in the world. To watch the rich delight disappear from candy shop shelves, trick-or-treat bags, and secret back-of-the-pantry stashes would be a travesty. But chocolate has a greater significance, too. Cocoa is a global commodity that nearly 6 million smallholder farmers depend on, and climate change is upending their livelihoods. Chocolate lovers are feeling the impact on their wallets. The cost of raw cocoa tripled in 2024, pushing chocolate brands to raise their prices, reduce the size of their products, or opt for reformulated products. A study published Monday in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences reveals an overlooked threat to cocoa harvests. The findings suggest that heavy rainfall—not extreme temperatures or drought—is the biggest constraint on cocoa yields across major producing regions. The researchers hope that quantifying this “underappreciated risk” will help farmers better prepare for its impact. “Heavy rainfall is potentially more actionable because it is an event that can be forecast,” Anna Lea Albright, who led the research as a postdoctoral fellow at the Harvard University Center for the Environment, told Gizmodo in an email. “If you know that a period of very heavy rain is expected during flowering or early pod development, there are actions that farmers can do to reduce the damage, particularly around drainage and disease management.” Too much of a good thing In an article published last year, the authors of this new study explained that nearly all cocoa comes from the humid tropics, where the seasonal shift of a band of clouds known as the Intertropical Convergence Zone drives rainfall patterns. Warm temperatures and plentiful rainfall alternate with short dry seasons, and while cocoa trees are well-adapted to this regular variability, they are highly sensitive to extremes. Scientists have long recognized heat and drought as threats to cocoa yields, but after analyzing district-level cocoa production records from Ghana alongside daily rainfall and temperature data, Albright and her colleagues found that heavy rain is actually the strongest climate risk to this crop. “Heavy rainfall can hurt cocoa in several ways,” Albright explained. “Very wet conditions can interfere with flowering and the development of young pods, and they can also create conditions that are favorable for fungal diseases.” “But the timing is really important,” she continued. “Cocoa is not equally sensitive to rainfall throughout the year. Heavy rain during flowering or early pod development can be much more damaging than the same amount of rain at another time.” Shifting rainfall patterns Long-term, human-driven climate change is substantially altering the timing and intensity of rainfall in the world’s cocoa-growing regions. For every 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit (1 degree Celsius) of global warming, the atmosphere can hold about 7% more moisture. “You can think of it like a bucket that’s getting bigger: holding more water, so that when it does rain, more comes down at once,” Albright explained. “It loads the dice towards heavier rainfall.” For example, in West Africa—which produces about 70% of the world’s cocoa—the heaviest wet-season rainfall events have become more intense over the past couple of decades. The new study shows that in Ghana, the most damaging rains occur during the April-to-June wet season, when cocoa trees flower and young pods begin to form. Then, during the November-to-February dry season, lack of rain hurts crops as their pods continue to develop. Albright’s team observed a similar trend in Ecuador and Indonesia, finding that cocoa crops suffered more during years with heavier wet-season rains. Near-term, natural climate swings like El Niño also have a significant influence over rainfall patterns in the tropics, though its impact varies across the region. In West Africa, El Niño tends to reduce the risk of heavier rainfall while increasing the risk of dry-season drought. But in Ecuador, El Niño typically brings wetter conditions during the wet season. Because the rains that hurt cocoa are tied to larger climate patterns, bad years may be predictable, according to Albright and her colleagues. Right now, a “super” El Niño—potentially the strongest on record—is taking shape. The ability to anticipate this event and track its development could give cocoa farmers time to prepare for its impact. Long-term changes associated with global warming are more difficult to predict, however. Current climate models struggle to accurately represent the current climatology rainfall over West Africa, so projecting it under various warming scenarios is challenging. Albright hopes to continue working with partners in West Africa and Ecuador to understand exactly how heavy rain impacts cocoa trees. This will not only help farmers proactively protect their yields but also provide more insight into how cocoa will respond to a warming world. “If extreme rainfall becomes more frequent or more intense, can farmers adapt quickly enough?” Albright said. “That is particularly difficult for cocoa because these are perennial trees. You cannot just change what you plant next year. Decisions about cocoa production are decisions that can last for decades.”

item.title: Doctors Scanned This Man’s Chest and Found a Sewing Needle in His Heart
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.73
A 35-year-old man’s bloody urine turned out to have an explanation no one could have seen coming: sewing needles jammed into his body. Doctors in China described the unusual injury in a case report earlier this month. The man, who was intellectually disabled, had multiple needles inside his body, all likely self-inserted. The doctors were able to remove the one closest to his heart, and the man recovered. “Cardiac foreign bodies associated with presumed self insertion behaviors can be clinically occult and diagnostically challenging, particularly when a definitive history is difficult to obtain,” the authors wrote in their paper, published last week in BMC Cardiovascular Disorders. A needle surprise According to the report, the man visited doctors two weeks into having urinary pain and blood in his urine. Though he seemed fine otherwise, an initial imaging test revealed a shadow near his heart. Additional CT scans then uncovered the presence of multiple “needle-like metallic foreign bodies” throughout his body, including his abdominal wall, pelvis, bladder, and penis. One needle, about 1.4 inches long (36 millimeters), had pierced the pericardium, the fluid-filled sac that protects the heart; it was inside the left ventricle cavity and was found to be moving in sync with the heart chamber. The man was legally under the care of his father, who gave the doctors written informed consent to discuss the case. Neither the patient nor his family could confirm where the needles had come from, the doctors wrote. Two years earlier, the man visited another hospital, where doctors removed two needle-like objects from his abdomen; however, the medical records from this visit were not available. Despite the missing information, the doctors say the man had likely inserted all these needles himself. Though rare, people with intellectual disabilities are known to be at higher risk of engaging in this type of behavior, which can also include swallowing foreign objects. The man’s fate Though the man had many needles inside his body, some were in locations that carried a high risk of serious complications if doctors tried to surgically remove them. Ultimately, the team only decided to remove the most life-threatening needle near the heart, while planning to keep a close eye on the others for possible removal in the future. The surgery went well without any major problems, with the doctors removing an intact and black metallic sewing needle. Remarkably, they noted, the man’s chest wall showed no signs of an entry wound or scars, while the needle itself was corroded, both of which suggest that it had been inside the man’s heart cavity for quite a long time. The man’s heart function did drop significantly after the surgery, likely as a result of the needle’s damage to his body as well as the strain of the surgery. However, he did eventually improve and was discharged safely from the hospital. At a nine-month follow-up visit, the man appeared to be clinically stable. The doctors say these sorts of cases tend to be very complex, both due to the fact that patients with cognitive impairment might not be able to communicate their medical history well and the fact that such injuries aren’t necessarily easy to outwardly spot. Detecting these cases tends to require a “multimodal imaging strategy,” the doctors wrote. Needle heart cases in particular are also very rare. A 2024 review uncovered only 34 other cases in the medical literature dating back to the 1960s of people deliberately inserting sewing needles in their heart.

item.title: Apple Home’s AI Security Camera Features Are Opt-In, if You Can Afford Them
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.68
Apple has finally launched its big Siri AI upgrade for its entire software ecosystem, and for Apple Home users, that means big, AI-powered changes for how their security cameras might work. Happily, the company isn’t raising prices on the existing subscriptions that enable these features and thereby forcing customers who don’t want them to pay up anyway. But for those who do want to open their wallets, it’ll get expensive, fast. The new Apple Intelligence-powered security camera capabilities will only work for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible devices—recent examples include Aqara’s Camera Hub G350 and Doorbell Camera G400—and not those that only support live streaming through Apple Home, like those offered by Arlo. Happily, the features are opt-in, so those who want them will need to explicitly turn them on, either via a splash screen that may appear in the Home app after you update your 2nd-gen-or-later Apple TV 4K and/or HomePods to tvOS 27 or HomePod Software Version 27 (it didn’t, for me), or in the app’s Home Settings menu. After you update, you’ll get a new Apple Intelligence option in the Home Settings that contains a “Summarize Videos” toggle. Flip that on—then visit a sub-menu to pick which cameras you want it to work for—and you’ll get features like natural language search of footage and descriptive notification summaries that tell you what happened when a camera detected something. These descriptions are a lot more specific than before. I haven’t tested extensively yet, but a screenshotted summary from a story from The Verge about the update shows one description: “A cat walked by and walked through the yard. Birds walked around the yard. Chickens walked around the yard.” I don’t think I care about how many birds visited my yard, but I definitely like the idea of being able to search videos to find out if and when a package was delivered. The sting, if you’re interested in the AI security camera features, is in the pricing. You’ll need to pay for at least a $10-per-month, 2TB iCloud+ plan, which only covers a single camera. The price quickly skyrockets if you want to add more cameras. Apple charges $30 per month for a two-camera, 6TB iCloud+ plan and $60 for a 12TB subscription that includes up to five cameras. That’s a lot when compared to, say, the Google Home Premium Advanced plan, which is just $20 a month for similar features and carries no limit to the number of cameras it covers. It’s nice that Apple isn’t just cramming its AI features into its lower-tier plans and raising prices, the way Google did at first for its Google Home Premium plans. But unless you need all the extra iCloud storage and iCloud+ features like Private Relay and Hide My Email, those prices are hard pills to swallow. Still, rolling them into existing subscriptions and pricing tiers as optional features seems smart, considering the generative AI propensity for misinterpreting events or confidently presenting false information. I know I don’t want to specifically pay for a feature that might lie to me. All of this is subject to change. As Apple notes in a support page on its site, “Supported camera counts and other iCloud+ plan features may change over time.” The company doesn’t say whether the counts will go up or down, but based on the undefined limits in a separate Apple Intelligence Usage Terms page, it feels like the company is hedging against the potential for rising costs of generative AI affecting how much it’s willing to offer. iOS 27 and its related operating systems are all available now. To update your HomePods to HomePod Software Version 27, make sure your iPhone or iPad is already on iOS 27/iPadOS 27, then open the Apple Home app, tap a given HomePod, and look for an “Update” button at the top of the screen. For the Apple TV 4K, go to Settings > System > Software Updates and click “Update Software.”

item.title: The Himalayas Are Melting Faster Than Ever. Scientists Worry Nepal’s Floods Are Just the Beginning
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.35
Over 5,130 people are still missing and at least 1,386 more are confirmed dead in Nepal since a collapsing glacier high atop Langtang Lirung in the Himalayas cascaded into devastating flash floods on August 26, 2026—washing away entire towns and flooding hydroelectric power plants. With hundreds more missing and dozens dead across the border in China and relief crews scrambling to locate an estimated 900 utility workers trapped in Nepal’s wrecked hydroelectric tunnels, a new report warns that the Himalayas’ icy peaks are just beginning their deadly thaw. The roughly 1439 cubic miles (6,000 cubic kilometers) of glacial ice capping Asia’s towering mountain range is now melting 65% faster than it was a decade ago, according to a private industry report conducted with technical assistance from the Indian government. Sustainable development consultancy Systemiq collaborated with India’s Govind Ballabh Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment and other groups focused on the mountains to produce its assessment. The report warns that the entire region is facing a tipping point of “peak water” by mid-century, a phase of increasingly cataclysmic floods before nearly dry Himalayan peaks cut off fresh water to rivers, reservoirs, and agriculture across large swaths of south Asia. “The Himalayas are the Third Pole,” as economist Nicholas Stern, chair of the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment and a member of the UK House of Lords, explained to the BBC. “Unlike the Arctic or Antarctic, this pole has hundreds of millions of people living beneath it.” Slippery slopes If anything, Stern’s analysis vastly undersells the scope of the potential consequences. For one thing, Systemiq’s new report notes that rivers sustained by the Himalayas’ historic hydrological cycle of seasonal glacial growth and melt are ultimately responsible for the food and water security of about 2 billion people. “On current trajectories, the Hindu Kush Himalaya could lose up to 80% of its present glacier volume by 2100,” according to the report, echoing increasingly more dire estimates from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development. (Like the Indian government, ICIMOD contributed technical information for Systemiq’s report.) Perhaps the most alarming aspect of these findings, however, is the room for mass-casualty surprises. Only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalayas—and the Karakoram mountain range to its northwest bordering Pakistan, China and India—are monitored by scientists in any sort of detail. Similar concerns plague China’s neighboring Tien Shan mountain range. An unknown tally of unstable glacial lakes are quietly swelling, in other words, with no early warning systems in place for their almost inevitable breach, some on the border between two regional nuclear powers who don’t especially get along. But even with these large unknown variables, what’s known about the meltwater pooling into these makeshift natural dams of loose rock is concerning enough. “India now has close to 200 glacial lakes identified as high risk and almost a quarter being ‘very high risk,’ leaving millions exposed downstream,” Systemiq’s report found. Tipping points India is already feeling the deadly impact of this threat. Although Himalayan land constitutes only about 18% of Indian territory, the region now accounts for as much as 35% of the country’s natural disasters, based on Systemiq’s analysis, which was also conducted in coordination with the Integrated Mountain Initiative (IMI). One notably lethal flash flood in India’s northeast busted dams, buried traffic in mudslides, and killed at least 70 people when the glacial lake South Lhonak ruptured in 2023. But beyond the immediate spectacle of such damage, the report notes that the protracted economic fallout will be no less extreme: Himalayan water supports about 20% of India’s annual GDP, providing hydropower and irrigating wheat, rice, and tea crops, among other basic needs. “The Himalayas are one connected system,” the researchers noted, “but its benefits and its risks are distributed far beyond the mountains themselves, with ripple effects felt in South Asia, and potentially the entire world through supply chain disruptions, climate migrations or geopolitical risk.”

item.title: The New ‘Other Mommy’ Trailer Turns a Ball Pit Into an Ocean of Horror
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.21
The first trailer for Other Mommy was totally unnerving, giving us a peek at Jessica Chastain’s dual role as a regular human mother—and a creature who exactly resembles a regular human mother, except for her tendency toward very creepy behavior. This new trailer, which leans into the film’s behind-the-scenes connections to Obsession and Backrooms, doubles down on the parental freak show. Two words: bubble bath. Two more words: ball pit. Watch, and be glad you’re not a little kid realizing for the first time that adults aren’t always who they say they are. Unlike 2026 horror sensations Obsession and Backrooms, the James Wan-produced Other Mommy has literary origins; it’s based on the book Incidents Around the House by Josh Malerman, who also wrote Bird Box. Rob Savage, whose previous horror credits include Host and The Boogeyman, directs the Oscar-winning Chastain, with Arabella Olivia Clark (The Housemaid) playing the girl who realizes her mom’s doppelganger isn’t so “nice” after all. In fact, she has deeply malevolent intentions, and she’s not afraid to crash a kiddie play zone to try and get what she wants. The rest of the cast includes Jay Duplass, Dichen Lachman (Severance), Arian Moayed, and Karen Allen (the Indiana Jones films). Other Mommy arrives in theaters October 9. Will you be checking out this tale of smotherly love? Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: Scientists Warn This Year’s El Niño Could Create Brand New Extreme Weather Patterns
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.98
Something weird happened during the El Niño event of 2023 and 2024. Climate scientists with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado, noticed that the recurring global climate event somehow did not bring the expected wetter seasons to the United States’ southern tier, nor a dry season to its northern regions. But this El Niño’s powerful effects were still felt elsewhere—including punishing droughts in the Amazon, the likes of which Brazil had not seen in 120 years. The explanation, as NCAR’s researchers determined the next year, was that global warming’s slow roasting of tropical Indian and Atlantic Ocean waters had offset El Niño’s effects across North America, disrupting a once reliable pair of climate patterns known as a “teleconnection.” Now, scientists are worried that the current state of climate change is poised to make this year’s extreme El Niño conditions even more unpredictable, according to Bar-Ilan University climate scientist Eran Vos, who spoke to the journal Nature about the issue this month. “We know less about the teleconnections of the new atmosphere,” Vos told Nature, adding that perverse synergies between global warming effects, like rising sea surface temperature, and El Niño’s behavior will make it not only harder to forecast, but consequently harder to prepare for. A chaos theory Speaking to Science News, ecosystem scientist Sergio de Miguel at the University of Lleida and the Joint Research Unit CTFC-Agrotecnio in Spain, likened the phenomena of teleconnections in 2023 to “a kind of complex butterfly effect” where events “in one place have many derivatives very far away.” The recurring regularity of these paired events can last weeks or even years, and they include patterns like the El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) which has become much discussed as ENSO is the climate teleconnection whose warming helps produce El Niño. Vos and his colleagues have combed through historic meteorological records, hoping to track our warming climate’s countervailing impact on El Niño events. They found that warming patterns created by El Niño across southern Asia and northeast Africa between the years 1960 and 1990 have since bizarrely inverted, leading to colder temperatures in those regions during more modern bouts of El Niño. Elsewhere, in Western Europe, cold snaps tied to El Niño during those same decades have now flipped, consistently correlating to warmer seasons during modern El Niño events. “You change the patterns and the weather reacts,” as Vos told Nature. Uncharted waters But climate change isn’t the only factor leading to a more intense and unpredictable El Niño this year. The 2026 El Niño itself is the first since the late 1990s to be generated by warm ocean temperatures in the eastern Pacific as opposed to the central Pacific. There’s not a lot of precedent from the past three decades of warming years, in other words, to predict how it might behave or how climate teleconnections might alter. Clara Deser, a senior scientist at NCAR, and her coauthors on that study into the odd 2023-24 El Niño season spelled it out this way, “historical precedent may no longer be a reliable guide to ENSO teleconnections as anthropogenic warming patterns intensify.” The sea surface temperatures themselves create uncharted waters, with the atmosphere itself changing too. As Deser told The New York Times this May, “We are now in a different base line climate.”

item.title: TP-Link’s New 4K Video Doorbell Sounds Like an All-Seeing, Subscription-Free Dream
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.97
TP-Link smart home brand Tapo has announced the Doorbell Pro D260, a 4K video doorbell that takes a local-first approach that requires no subscription for features that often call for a monthly fee. It’s available starting Sept. 30 for $220, which is on the pricey end but could be worth it for those who cherish cloud independence. The D260 emerges as the priciest, but also most feature-rich video doorbell that the company offers. Its 4K resolution is twice that of Tapo’s other offerings, and its 180-degree field of view is an improvement over the 160-degrees captured by the $75 Tapo D210. (The D130 matches the D260’s field of view.) Also, it supports both hardwired and battery power, with up to 180 days on a charge—Tapo’s other such cameras can do one or the other, but not both. The company claims the Doorbell Pro D260 can capture sharp details from up to 30 feet away, although I’d be dubious about what that means without seeing it firsthand. The D260 uses dual PIR and radar for detection, whereas other Tapo models only use PIR, which could improve motion detection. Like the company’s other doorbell cameras, the Doorbell Pro D260 uses on-device processing for person, package, vehicle, and animal detection, and supports up to a 512GB microSD card, though it doesn’t come with one. Facial recognition also runs on-device, too. Some companies, like Ring or Google, will charge for features like those, and much of the processing and storage happens in the cloud. Others, like Reolink, offer a local-first option that’s cheaper than Tapo’s camera, but comes with a lower video resolution. You can hardwire the D260, but it also offers up to 180 days of battery life, according to Tapo. It uses both 2.4GHz and 5GHz Wi-Fi to connect—5GHz is somewhat rare on video doorbells and smart home cameras in general, and could mean the camera’s live feed loads faster and looks clearer than on those restricted to the 2.4GHz band. The Doorbell Pro D260 is also compatible with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Samsung SmartThings, the latter of which the current crop on Tapo’s website won’t work with. It has no Matter support, though, so anyone outside of those ecosystems is out of luck. You’ll find a lot of other pretty typical video doorbell niceties here, like full-color night vision, HDR recording, and two-way audio that lets you talk to the person on the other side of your door before you open it. Tapo doesn’t mention AI-supported video search, although you’re not necessarily missing much there. Whether the Doorbell Pro D260 is worth considering depends on your smart home platform of choice and how you prioritize keeping things out of the cloud. 4K resolution sounds nice and is rare among video doorbells, but I’ve found that a higher resolution doesn’t always mean crisp, clear footage. Just look at the comparisons between the SwitchBot Smart Video Doorbell and the Google Nest Doorbell Cam, both 2K cameras that produce vastly different-looking footage.

item.title: This open-source Android keyboard finally fixed what Gboard gets wrong
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 6.06
Android's default keyboard, Gboard, ships with clever predictions and slick design, but it also ships with a permanent connection to Google's servers. HeliBoard, a free and open-source alternative, actually makes a pretty good case for a replacement. What's HeliBoard? A privacy-first descendant of Android's original keyboard HeliBoard is a free and open-source virtual keyboard for Android, maintained as a fork of OpenBoard, which in turn traces back to the keyboard implementation baked into the Android Open Source Project. That's felt from the get-go, as it feels pretty AOSP-y. OpenBoard launched at the end of 2019 and was actively developed until late 2022, when work on it stopped. HeliBoard, built by a developer known as Helium314, picked up where it left off and has continued shipping updates since, with new releases still landing regularly through GitHub and F-Droid. The project is licensed under GPL-3.0, meaning its full source code is publicly auditable, and it requires Android 5.0 or newer to run. The keyboard's defining trait is that it has no Google dependencies and never connects to the internet, which is why privacy-focused communities often recommend it as a Gboard substitute. There's no account to sign into and no telemetry phoning home in the background. Functionally, it covers most of what people expect from a modern keyboard: per-language dictionaries that users can supply themselves, customizable themes with adjustable colors and background images, support for custom layouts, a split-keyboard mode and one-handed mode for larger phones, clipboard history, a floating keyboard option, and backup-and-restore for settings. It also supports a wide range of scripts, including Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew, Hindi, Arabic, and Korean, though it does not currently handle Chinese or Japanese input. Glide typing is available too, but only through a separate, closed-source gesture-recognition library, since that particular piece of technology isn't something the open-source project has replicated on its own. How is it better? On-device processing instead of a constant data pipeline The core difference between HeliBoard and Gboard comes down to where typing data goes. Gboard leans on cloud infrastructure for several of its marquee features: predictive text, dictionary syncing across devices, grammar correction, and voice typing all route through Google's servers to some degree. That's convenient, but it also means keystrokes and voice input are, in some form, leaving the device. HeliBoard was built to do the opposite. Every suggestion, correction, and dictionary lookup happens locally, with nothing transmitted off the phone. That design shows up most clearly in HeliBoard's "force incognito mode," which temporarily disables word learning, autocorrect, auto-capitalization, clipboard history, and delete-key swipe actions in one toggle, useful for typing in sensitive apps without leaving a trace in the keyboard's memory. There are no ads and no account prompts anywhere in the app, which is a notable departure from most keyboard apps distributed through the Play Store. And as it turns out, HeliBoard also offers a level of granular customization that Gboard doesn't match. Settings for keyboard height, text size, font, and padding are all independently adjustable, letting users fine-tune the typing surface to their exact preference rather than choosing from a handful of preset themes. Recent updates have added support for newer Unicode emoji sets, separate scaling options for foldable phones, and touchpad-style cursor control by sliding across the space bar, suggesting the project is still actively iterating rather than sitting still. Should I use it? A strong fit for some, a dealbreaker for others HeliBoard is an easy recommendation for anyone who already gravitates toward open-source tools and wants a keyboard that doesn't require trusting a cloud service with everything typed on it. The trade-offs are worth knowing up front, though. Because glide typing depends on a closed-source library rather than HeliBoard's own code, privacy purists may want to leave that feature switched off, even though it's optional. The lack of Chinese and Japanese input support is a hard limitation for anyone who needs those languages, and prediction quality overall may feel a step behind Gboard's cloud-backed, neural network-driven suggestions simply because everything is computed on-device rather than on Google's infrastructure. There's also a distribution wrinkle: HeliBoard isn't available on the Play Store, so installing it means going through F-Droid or downloading an APK directly from GitHub, an extra step that will feel unfamiliar to users who've never sideloaded an app before. For anyone comfortable with that process, though, HeliBoard is worth a trial run. Installing it through F-Droid, backing up an existing keyboard's settings beforehand, and spending a few days testing glide typing and prediction accuracy should be enough to tell whether the trade-off between convenience and control is the right one. A private keyboard with real trade-offs HeliBoard won't out-predict Gboard, and it skips Chinese and Japanese entirely. But for anyone willing to sideload an app in exchange for a keyboard that keeps every keystroke on-device, it's one of the few genuine alternatives worth using.

item.title: Your Ethernet adapter is negotiating itself down to 2003 speeds—here's how to fix it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.95
Switching to Ethernet was simultaneously the best and the cheapest network upgrade I've ever gotten. Simply ditching Wi-Fi for a cable is fantastic, and in most cases, it improves your connection tremendously. But what if one Ethernet-related setting actually makes your PC feel slow? That can happen, and after some digging, I found the culprit. Speed & Duplex decides how fast your Ethernet link actually runs Auto Negotiation is doing more than you might think If you've never heard of Speed & Duplex, I won't blame you, but this is actually a pretty important setting. It controls how your Ethernet adapter talks to the device at the other end of the cable. Most of the time, that'll be your router. The "speed" part of the name determines whether that link runs at, say, 100Mbps, 1Gbps, or 2.5Gbps. Duplex, on the other hand, decides whether data can travel in both directions at the same time. It shouldn't surprise you that modern Ethernet usually uses full duplex. The reason I said that if you've never heard of this setting, I won't blame you, is that it's pretty niche. Under normal circumstances, you shouldn't have to choose any of this yourself, and that's because of Auto Negotiation, which lets your PC's network adapter and the router/switch compare what they both support and agree on the best compatible link speed and duplex mode. It's not much unlike what USB cables and ports do. To check this setting for yourself in Windows, go to the Device Manager, then expand network adapters. Right-click your Ethernet adapter, and choose Properties > Advanced. Then, dig for Speed & Duplex or a similarly named setting, and select Auto Negotiation. 99% of the time, Auto Negotiation is exactly what you want. This usually isn't the case of needing to tweak something manually, and forcing your connection to 1Gbps or 2.5Gbps doesn't make it faster if the connection (the entire connection, hardware and all) isn't prepared to handle it. Worse yet, doing so can actually mess things up instead of helping. The interesting thing is what happens when Auto Negotiation doesn't land on the speed you expected, and that's why this setting is worth checking. That'll be your first sign to dig deeper. A 2.5GbE PC can still end up crawling along You don't want to describe your connection as "crawling," right? So, what does Auto Negotiation have to do with your connection feeling slow? Quite a lot, because the speed it negotiates is the one your Ethernet connection actually runs at, so if something goes wrong along that whole line, your internet might feel incredibly sluggish. First, some numbers. A 2.5GbE connection tops out at 312.5MB/s, and 1Gbps has a raw ceiling of 125MB/s. Meanwhile, 100Mbps crawls along at around 12.5MB/s before overhead. So, if something in the link causes your network adapter to negotiate down to 100Mbps, you're missing out on so much internet speed you might as well hop in a time machine back to 2003. Such a slowdown is going to reverberate throughout your entire connection, unfortunately. Large downloads, streams, gaming—all of that stuff is majorly affected when suddenly the internet speeds you were meant to have just aren't there. Even with a fast PC, most tasks will crawl along at a snail's pace. There's a fix, of course. Don't fix it by forcing the biggest number That doesn't actually help Given what we now know about Speed & Duplex, your first instinct might be to go in there and force the highest number you possibly can, but I'm here to tell you not to do it. Auto Negotiation exists specifically for the purpose of two devices agreeing on a configuration that actually works on both ends. If you end up picking something that works on one end but not the other, it's not like one of the devices can force the other to just somehow learn how to negotiate at a higher speed. Doing this means that at best, you gain a big fat zero, zilch, nothing. At worst, the link can become unstable or fail to come up properly. So, if Auto Negotiation has landed you at 100Mbps even though you expected gigabit Ethernet or better, it means it's time to investigate instead of forcing it to do what you'd like to see. Check what speed was actually negotiated Link speed and internet speed are not one and the same Forcing it isn't the answer, then what is? You just need to check what Auto Negotiation actually gives you. In Windows, you'll find this under Settings > Network & internet > Ethernet if you look for link speed. You can also check your adapter's status in the Control Panel. If you have a gigabit or 2.5GbE connection but Windows reports a slower link, well, there you go. One thing to note: Don't confuse that number with your actual internet speed. Link speed only talks about the connection between your PC and the next device on your local network, which is most commonly a router. Your ISP determines how fast you can actually reach the internet, so that factors into the equation, too. If Auto Negotiation is disappointing, check the cable The setting may just be shining a light on the real problem On rare occasions, Auto Negotiation may indeed be the problem, in which case you can always force the link to follow a certain speed—but this will only work if all the devices involved, including the cable itself, can support that speed and are working properly. If not, you just got a pretty important hint as to where to look for the troublemaker. The first thing I'd check is the Ethernet cable itself. Unplug it and reseat both ends. Then, swap it out for a different cable that you know works perfectly well, and make sure it's Cat5e or better. There's a good reason cables can mess with this at times. Gigabit Ethernet needs all four twisted pairs inside the cable, while 100BASE-TX can get by with only two. A damaged pair can leave you with a connection that technically works, but doesn't perform the way you'd think. A fast PC is only as fast as its slowest link Any PC, aging or otherwise, is only as fast as its slowest link. If something is bottlenecking your connection, Speed & Duplex may expose it. Tweak the setting as needed, but if you're uncertain about the hardware's capabilities, you might have to start there first.

item.title: Windows 11 is running hidden tasks that drain your laptop battery—here's how to stop them
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.55
Your laptop had a full charge at the start of the day, but by noon, you're reaching for the outlet to refill the battery. The battery percentage kept dropping even though you didn’t stream anything or run a demanding task. That’s because Windows 11 isn’t sitting idle while you work. In the background, a quiet parade of apps, services, and sync routines run constantly in the background — none of which you ever asked for. The good news is that you can stop most of them. Some of the tasks are necessary for Windows to run properly. But several features and apps don’t need to run constantly. Here are the main culprits to look for if your Windows 11 laptop isn’t lasting as long as you want. Background apps Check battery usage before touching anything else Windows 11 allows apps to run in the background by default. Some have a legitimate reason and need to sync even when you’re not using them. However, the app you open once a week or a game launcher doesn’t deserve the same treatment. Battery Usage is the best place to improve your laptop’s battery efficiency. Windows 11 tracks which apps consumed the most power over the last 24 hours and seven days. This is accessible under Settings -> System -> Power and battery -> Battery usage. Instead of disabling background activity across the board, select the apps that consistently consume significant power and that you don’t need running constantly. To do this, you can go to Settings -> Apps -> Installed Apps, open each app’s settings, and set Background app permissions to Never. Startup apps Cut down what launches with Windows. When you boot Windows and sign in, the operating system launches certain apps, and those silently continue running in the background throughout the session. Furthermore, apps often add themselves to startup after an update or installation. Open Task Manager -> Startup apps tab, and you will see the programs that are configured to launch when Windows starts, along with information about their impact. You can right-click to disable anything you don’t need at boot. This action doesn’t uninstall the app or prevent you from opening it manually whenever you need it. Windows Search Your drive is crawled more than it needs to be Windows Search constantly crawls your files so the results appear instantly, making it easier to find something. Indexing happens in the background, so Windows doesn't have to scan your drive every time you search for something. There’s a fix for this — you can control which locations Windows indexes instead of turning it off entirely. Head to Settings -> Privacy and security -> Searching Windows to review the indexing options available on your PC. Limiting unnecessary locations and items that don’t need to be searchable can reduce the work Windows Search does in the background. Cloud sync Not everything needs to be synced. All the time Cloud storage apps are useful, but they do plenty of work in the background. OneDrive is the most common example on Windows 11. Your laptop may be doing more than you realize if you’re syncing a large folder, uploading or downloading a file. It uses additional system resources and network activity. If you don’t require real-time sync, you can pause cloud syncing instead of disabling it when you’re trying to squeeze more battery life out of your laptop. Syncing can be paused for 2, 8, or 24 hours by right-clicking the OneDrive icon in the system tray. If you want a permanent fix, head to OneDrive Settings -> Sync and backup -> Manage backup and then select the specific folders to sync rather than everything. Google and Dropbox also have similar sync options in their own settings menu. Widgets and notifications These stay active even when you ignore them The Windows widgets panel fetches live news, weather, and stock data even when you never open it. There’s no reason to keep it running if it’s not a part of your daily workflow. You can disable widgets from Settings -> Personalization -> Taskbar. Meanwhile, apps keep checking for new messages, updates, and other activity to send notifications you may not need. Each unnecessary notification is a small wake cycle for your PC. You can turn them off under Settings -> System -> Notifications. These are small changes, but they can eliminate another background activity you don’t need. Get more battery life from your Windows 11 laptop None of these changes are permanent. So, you can reverse them if something stops behaving the way you expect. You can also use Windows 11’s built-in energy recommendations under Settings -> System -> Power and battery -> Energy recommendations. Here, you can find screen and sleep settings that are worth checking before making any drastic changes. A few small adjustments won’t magically turn an aging laptop into an all-day machine, but together they can extend your laptop's battery life.

item.title: 7 pioneering Linux applications that never needed replacing
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.55
Linux has changed dramatically since the early days of the kernel. Desktops have gone from X11 environments with primitive window managers to polished graphical shells. Containers, cloud computing, virtualization, and immutable operating systems have transformed how people deploy Linux. Even the hardware running Linux today would have seemed extraordinary to many of its earliest users. Yet some applications have barely budged from their place in the Linux ecosystem. You can install a modern Linux distro in 2026 and still find yourself using software whose origins stretch back decades. Some of these programs are older than most Linux distros themselves. Others became popular during Linux’s formative years and simply refused to disappear: Vim The editor that started a feud Vim was developed in 1991 as an improved version of the classic vi editor. It eventually became one of the defining applications of the Unix and Linux world. Its staying power comes from an editing model that remains extremely efficient once learned. Vim lets users manipulate text almost entirely from the keyboard, making it particularly useful on remote machines where a graphical editor is unavailable. There is also a cultural reason Vim has remained so visible. The long-running Vim versus Emacs argument is one of the oldest rivalries in computing, with generations of users debating which editor deserves their loyalty. I have seen plenty of that debate over the years, but Vim has another advantage in internet culture: the infamous "How do I quit Vim?" problem. For decades, jokes about getting trapped inside Vim have turned into memes, tutorials, stickers, and even running gags among developers. The joke works because the problem is real, and a newcomer can open Vim, start typing, press a few unfamiliar keys, and suddenly have no idea how to get back to the shell. That combination of a genuinely different editing model and decades of community folklore has kept Vim remarkably visible even as newer editors have become easier for beginners to approach. Vim has also expanded well beyond the limitations of the original vi. Plugins, scripting, language integrations, syntax highlighting, and modern terminal capabilities have turned it into a remarkably capable development environment while preserving the core workflow that made it popular. OpenSSH Remote administration became a Linux superpower OpenSSH emerged in the late 1990s and became one of the most important pieces of software in Unix and Linux administration. SSH solved a fundamental problem of controlling remote servers securely. That need has only grown as servers moved into data centers, cloud platforms, and geographically distributed environments. OpenSSH is now used for much more than opening a remote shell. It supports secure file transfers, authentication, tunneling, port forwarding, automation, and connections used by development tools. A Linux installation can be stripped down to the essentials and still provide a secure administrative interface through SSH. That makes OpenSSH less like an ordinary application and more like a piece of the operating system’s infrastructure. rsync File synchronization that never became obsolete rsync was released in 1996 to solve a problem that remains familiar to Linux users. It provides an efficient way to synchronize files between two locations without repeatedly transferring data that has not changed. Rather than copying an entire directory every time, rsync compares the source and destination and transfers only the data required to bring them into sync. That made it useful for backups, migrations, website deployments, mirroring, and server administration. It also made the program exceptionally attractive to system administrators because it can be incorporated into shell scripts and automated workflows. Cloud storage has changed how many people think about backups and file synchronization, but it has not eliminated the need for direct filesystem operations. rsync remains particularly useful when you control both ends of the transfer and need predictable behavior. It understands permissions, timestamps, symbolic links, directory structures, and other Unix filesystem characteristics. Samba Linux learned to coexist with Windows networks Samba began in 1992 as an effort to implement Microsoft’s SMB networking protocol on Unix systems. That project became enormously important because Linux and Windows systems frequently need to coexist. A Linux server might provide shared storage to Windows workstations, participate in authentication infrastructure, or expose files using protocols familiar to Microsoft’s operating systems. As Microsoft introduced newer versions of SMB, Samba continued adding support for those changes, so Linux systems could keep participating in Windows-based networks. Its support eventually expanded from basic file and printer sharing to domain authentication, Windows domain membership, and Active Directory domain-controller functionality. The project therefore did not need to replace its original purpose, which allowed Samba to remain a practical part of Linux networking more than three decades after its initial release. GIMP An image editor that refused to disappear The Gimp appeared in 1995 and became one of the most prominent graphical applications in the Linux ecosystem. GIMP gave Linux users a serious local image editor at a time when proprietary graphics software dominated professional creative work. It supports image manipulation, retouching, compositing, format conversion, scripting, and plugins. The software industry has changed considerably since then. Subscription-based creative suites and browser-based applications are now common, while powerful image editing is available on almost every major platform. GIMP still has an important advantage for Linux users in that it remains a capable native application that can be installed locally and used without subscribing to a proprietary ecosystem. ImageMagick The command line still knows how to process pictures ImageMagick dates back to the early 1990s and became one of the most versatile command-line image-processing tools available on Linux and Unix systems. Its greatest strength is automation. A graphical editor is excellent when a person needs to make creative decisions about an individual image. ImageMagick becomes extremely useful when the same operation needs to happen hundreds or thousands of times. A script can resize an entire directory, convert images between formats, crop files, manipulate metadata, generate thumbnails, or perform more complicated transformations without requiring someone to sit in front of a graphical interface. That makes ImageMagick valuable to developers, publishers, system administrators, and anyone building automated media-processing workflows. Evolution The Linux email client that became a full productivity suite Evolution has been part of the Linux desktop for more than two decades. Originally developed for the GNOME desktop, it started as an email and personal information management application and grew into a broader groupware client. It handles email, calendars, contacts, tasks, and other information that users might otherwise manage through several separate applications. It also supports common enterprise email and collaboration systems, which helped make it useful beyond the typical home Linux desktop. Evolution's history is particularly interesting because email clients have gone through several major shifts since it appeared. Webmail became dominant, smartphones changed how people handled messages and calendars, and cloud services moved much of the underlying infrastructure away from desktop computers. Yet there are still Linux users who prefer having their email, calendar, contacts, and tasks in a native desktop application. Evolution continues to fill that role. It also demonstrates why some older Linux applications survive even when their category becomes less fashionable. Evolution does not need to compete with every web mail service. It simply needs to remain a capable desktop client for people who want one. That has been enough to keep it around through multiple generations of Linux desktops. These applications survived because their problems did The most interesting thing about these applications is not their age. It is the fact that modern Linux users can still encounter the same fundamental problems their creators were trying to solve. Technology has changed around these applications without eliminating the jobs they perform. Some have also benefited from an enormous ecosystem built around them. That does not mean every one of these programs is the best choice for every user. A new editor may be easier to learn, but the replacement has to provide enough additional value to justify changing a workflow that already works. A program written thirty years ago does not have to look modern to remain useful. It simply has to continue solving a problem that people still have.

item.title: Waze's best feature is also its most annoying—here are the settings I changed to tame it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.05
One of the best things about Waze is also one of the worst. The app lets users report hazards, which are then shared with every other Waze user on the same stretch of road. These alerts can be really useful, but they can quickly get incredibly annoying. Waze's constant warnings were driving me mad I didn't want to know about every car on the shoulder Some of the community-submitted Waze alerts are genuinely helpful. Where I live, there are a lot of old roads, many of which have horrific potholes. Some are so deep they could damage my car if I'm not careful to avoid them. Waze giving me an audible warning about a pothole ahead is genuinely useful. Since the locations are user-submitted, almost all the worst potholes in my area generate alerts, making them far easier to avoid and saving me from expensive repairs. Unfortunately, Waze doesn't stop at pothole alerts. It also alerts you to many other road features, from speed bumps and sharp curves to complex intersections and multi-lane merges. Beyond road features, Waze alerts you to crashes, traffic, vehicles on the shoulder, bad weather, blocked lanes, and even animals in the road. The constant barrage of alerts can soon get annoying. This is especially true when you're listening to your perfectly curated road trip playlist or trying to follow the complex plot of an audiobook, and it keeps getting interrupted by yet another alert telling you that there's a car on the shoulder. Waze says it limits alerts, but there are often still too many The intent is to reduce distractions Waze gives a lot of alerts, but it could actually be even worse. In some situations, Waze may actively reduce the number of alerts you get. According to the Waze support pages, the alerts that you receive will depend on your current driving location. You may get more alerts "where you need to pay more attention to the road, such as when you are approaching an accident-prone segment, where there is a hazard on the road, a significant speed decrease and more." The support page goes on to state that "in order to minimize drivers' distraction, we limit the amount of alerts a driver may see on a single route." It also explains that alerts are prioritized based on different factors such as how familiar you are with the road and how many alerts affect your route. The upshot is that you may not get alerted about everything. Despite these features, the default Waze settings are still far too annoying for my liking. I get so many alerts about cars parked on the shoulder, which I'm not particularly worried about. Thankfully, there's a simple fix that means I don't need to switch back to Google Maps. You can take control of how Waze alerts are delivered Replace audible alerts with visual ones The good news is that Waze gives you some level of control over how you receive these types of alerts. You can opt to disable the hazard alerts completely, receive audible and map alerts, or have them appear only on the map. Choosing the latter option can make driving using Waze far less annoying while still letting you see the important information. To change these settings, open Waze, tap the menu icon, and select Settings. Under Driving preferences, tap Alerts and reports. Select Reports to see a full list of all the available types of reports. To change whether an alert is spoken or shown on the map, tap a report type, such as Vehicle on shoulder. Toggle Show on Map and Alert while Driving on or off to suit your needs. Some sections, such as Road features, contain multiple types of alerts, and you can configure each of these individually. Your settings apply globally; if you change how a report is delivered, it will apply to all subsequent journeys, not merely the one you're currently making. If you want to bring audible alerts back, you'll need to go back into the settings and re-enable them. Waze is now far less annoying to use I get the alerts I want without those that I don't The control Waze gives you is reasonably granular, but not completely. You can adjust a large number of report types, but some alerts fall under a wider category, so you can't disable them individually. For example, pothole alerts fall under Other hazards, so I have to leave this category enabled in order to get them. I was able to disable the Vehicle on shoulder alerts, however, and these were the ones that annoyed me the most. I still see them on the map, but my music doesn't get interrupted by audio ducking every time I pass a car that's pulled over safely on the side of the road. With so many reports available, it can take a little time to get the settings exactly how you want them. It's worth the effort; driving with Waze is now a far less annoying experience. Make Waze your own Not every journey is the same, and some of the Waze alerts may not be ideal for the routes you drive most often. Adjusting the report settings ensures you only get the alerts you want, without distractions from information you don't need. if you're still not sure whether to use Waze or Google Maps, it's worth taking a look at the key differences.

item.title: 5 features hiding behind your car's USB port
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.04
My car came with more USB ports than I thought I would need, and it's understandable to ignore any that don't charge your phone. But you can do a lot more with your ports than just charge a battery. Once you have a cable that works and isn’t useless, you can use those same ports to do a lot more to your car. You can update your car with a flash drive Wireless updates fail way too often An Over-the-Air (OTA) bypass through USB is just manually updating your car's infotainment software with a flash drive instead of Wi-Fi or 5G. That matters because wireless OTA updates fail all the time. There are plenty of reasons, like bad cell reception, network throttling, subscription paywalls, or the automaker just being slow to push it out. Wireless updates over a shaky connection are pretty risky. If the firmware patch gets interrupted mid-transmission, you can corrupt files and brick the head unit. Delivering the files directly by USB kills the network dependency and gives you a clean, block-level flash. To do it, just go to the manufacturer's portal or support site. There's usually a ZIP download. Once it's formatted, extract the update files straight to the root folder, so the bootloader can find the config files. With the drive ready, plug it into the data USB port in the car. Avoid the rear or console ports; those are charge-only. Keep the vehicle running or in accessory mode and turn off any automatic engine shutoff. In your car settings, pick the update prompt and let it run. Music sounds a lot better through a flash drive Bluetooth cuts out the parts that make music sound good Streaming uncompressed audio from a USB drive just means playing lossless files straight through your car's media player. Bluetooth is convenient, but it uses lossy codecs to squeeze audio into a tiny wireless bandwidth pipe. That compression throws away real musical detail. You'll notice it if you're actually paying attention. USB is a wired connection, so the digital bitstream goes to the head unit bit for bit. You don't need to worry about wireless compression or processing latency. That means factory systems and good aftermarket setups can actually hit their full potential. To actually use this, you need the lossless files. You can rip CDs to WAV files or buy 24-bit studio master downloads from high-res platforms. Then organize the files into nested folders, artist name up top, album subfolders inside. Make sure you have good tags like title, artist, album art, genre, and then let the car's background indexer build everything up and load it from your USB. A cheap dongle will turn your car into a hotspot You can keep everyone online without melting your phone A USB hotspot maker is basically a tiny 4G/LTE or 5G modem dongle. Once it's plugged in, it creates its own Wi-Fi network inside the cabin. That lets passengers run phones, tablets, handheld consoles, laptops, and smart car accessories all at once. Since the dongle handles all the data routing, your phone doesn't get cooked. The setup is pretty simple. Buy an unlocked 4G/5G USB Wi-Fi dongle and drop in a SIM from a carrier with a cheap data-only plan. Plug it into an active primary or accessory USB port in your center console or dash. When you switch the ignition to accessory mode or start the engine, the dongle powers up, boots its OS, and starts broadcasting its SSID. On your device, find that SSID and enter the default password printed on the label or scan the setup QR code. Then open a browser and enter the dongle's gateway IP. From there, you can set custom APN carrier settings, change WPA2 keys, add firewall rules, or view real-time data usage. A dashcam is cheap insurance It only takes a few minutes to stick one on your glass A USB-powered dashcam is a standalone camera that plugs into a cabin USB port and records. Mine cost about $46 and works as well as the $200 one I got before. The whole point is cheap insurance and a little extra security with almost no installation. All you have to do is mount the camera on your windshield or rear glass with the adhesive bracket so it has a clear view. Then route the thin USB cable to a USB port. I like to use tape and glue to keep it from looking messy. It also keeps it from snagging when people come in and out. Do not plug it into the data USB port. Just use the USBs that give power; that's all you need. Your camera will start loop recording as soon as it gets power, which is great for accidents. A good camera will start recording the minute there is a bump or loud noise. A little display keeps your speed at eye level It solves the problem of not seeing your gauges A USB digital speedometer is a small dashboard display that calculates your speed using a GPS receiver inside it. It gets all its power from USB. The whole point is to show your speed at eye level so you don't have to keep glancing down. I have an SUV, but the gauges are blocked because I like my seat particularly high. So the cover that protects the gauges from sunlight makes them harder to see. I'm sure I'm not the only one. Run the USB cable to any port you've got, and you'll find the speedometer works like a charm. Not all cars come with this many USBs Not everything here will apply to every car or every driver. While an SUV comes with plenty in the front and back, a regular sedan will usually have only a couple under the dash. So it's better to only use what you need. In my case, I would never drive a car without some form of dashcam, so make sure to get one if you don't have one. WOLFBOX X3 PRO Dash Cam - Front Camera Resolution - 1440p - Field of View - 106 Degrees You get both a front and back dash cam with this WOLFBOX combo, letting you be able to protect yourself from all angles.

item.title: Home Assistant phone and watch notifications just got a major upgrade
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.01
Phone and watch notifications are one of the most effective ways to share information from Home Assistant. A recent update to the Home Assistant Companion app quietly made these notifications even more powerful. Home Assistant now supports Live Activities on iOS Notifications can update over time instead of disappearing If you're an Android user, this isn't particularly exciting news. Home Assistant has supported Live Updates on Android 16 or later since February 2026. For iPhone users, however, this is a brand-new feature. Live Activities show ongoing, changing information on iOS devices without having to display notification after notification. The Live Activity stays visible on the iPhone Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island on supported devices, with the information it contains able to update over time. You need to run the 2026.9.0 release or later of the Home Assistant Companion app, Home Assistant Core 2026.7.0 or later, and at least iOS 17.2 on your iPhone. You can then use Home Assistant to send Live Activity notifications to your iPhone. You can display progress bars and live countdowns Some processing can happen on device Turning a Home Assistant notification into a Live Activity (or Live Updates on Android) is as simple as adding live_update: true and a tag to the data payload of the notification. The Companion app will then display the notification as a Live Activity rather than a standard notification. You can update the Live Activity simply by sending another notification with the same tag and live_update: true. This replaces the current Live Activity rather than creating a new one. Home Assistant recommends avoiding sending constant updates, since iOS may throttle or even drop push delivery if updates are too frequent, although throttling doesn't apply if you're using local push. You can also let your iPhone handle some of the updates itself. You can use chronometer to add a timer to the Live Activity, and the iPhone will process it, so you don't need to send updates every second. There are plenty of useful ways to use these Live Activity notifications. You can display the progress of your robot vacuum, including the room it's currently cleaning. You can track the progress of your 3D printer and see how long is left on the print, or monitor how long a door has been left open. I'm using a Live Activity notification to track how long I sit at my desk. It uses an mmWave presence sensor to detect when I'm in my home office chair, and the Live Activity shows the elapsed time since I sat down and clears once I get out of the chair. It's a great motivation to get up and walk around when I can see that I've been sitting down for hours at a time with a quick glance at my phone. Live Activities can automatically appear on your Apple Watch See your smart home status on your wrist If you have an Apple Watch, you can also see Home Assistant Live Activities on your wrist. Your watch can automatically mirror the Live Activity from your iPhone. The Live Activity will appear at the top of the Smart Stack that you can access by swiping up or rotating the Digital Crown. This means that you can check the status of a Home Assistant Live Activity just by looking at your wrist, without having to fish out your iPhone. If you're keeping track of how long your washing machine has been running, for example, then a quick glance can show you how long it's been running or how long is left. If you don't want these Live Activities to appear on your Apple Watch, you can disable them through the Watch app on your iPhone. Go to General -> Auto-Launch -> Live Activities Settings, and scroll down and tap Home Assistant. Toggle Mirror Live Activity from iPhone off. Live Activities aren't suitable for everything They're great under the right circumstances This update doesn't mean that you'll never use standard phone notifications again. Live Activities can be useful, but they're not always the best option. If you want to get immediate information about something that has changed, such as a window opening, motion being detected, or your water leak sensor detecting a leak, then a standard notification is a better choice. A critical alert can be even better if the information is urgent enough that you need to be notified even when your phone is muted or in a Focus mode. There are also some practical limitations. If your sensor updates every 30 milliseconds and constantly changes values, sending every update as a Live Activity notification will soon cause notifications to be throttled or dropped. Activities that only run for a few seconds are also unsuited, since you may not even notice them on your phone before they're gone.
