In the right circumstances, however, using Live Activities can be an even more useful way to display information from Home Assistant. It's well worth experimenting to see what you can do with them. Live Activities are a significant upgrade The real benefit of this change isn't that you get more stylish or better-looking notifications. It's that you can now make ongoing information from your smart home easily visible somewhere that you're regularly looking, whether that's your phone's screen or your smartwatch. It makes tracking this updating information even easier to do.

item.title: Please stop using the HDMI cable that came with your monitor
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.55
Most people buying a high-end monitor spend real time researching panel technology, refresh rates, and color accuracy, then plug it into the cable that came in the box without a second thought. That cable is usually a budget part from a generation or two ago, rated for a fraction of the bandwidth the display actually needs. That's the problem. You have to stop pretending that the cable is part of the whole package; it's more like a bonus when you pick the right monitor for your PC. The cable in the box is holding your monitor back Your free cable can't handle the signal People drop serious money on a monitor with high refresh rates, native 4K or 8K, deep color, and then plug it in with the cable that came in the box. That stock cable is usually a cheap one that helps offset the cost for the seller. It's generally gonna be an old Standard or High Speed HDMI cable that would be terrible for any 4k screen. Those kinds of cables can't carry the data a modern high-performance panel needs. So the GPU can't bring up a full-bandwidth link or reliably read the detailed timing parameters, and the whole thing just falls back to whatever it can manage. You end up stuck at 1080p or 60 Hz, which is fine for an older cheap monitor but not for the expensive ones you're buying today. You are literally being held back because of the limitations of your cable. Digital video isn't just some clean stream of ones and zeros floating through the wire, even though that's what most people assume. The cables themselves move it, and the quality of that cable and how it was made matters a lot. Cheap bundled cables cut corners hard on construction and materials to save money. You have to be careful because some could have tinned copper braiding, or maybe the maker skipped the secondary braid or used low-grade foil that tears during manufacturing. You have to match your cord to your monitor, but it's very rare that the cable in the box actually matches what your monitor needs. In this case, you're going to need to look for a cable yourself and add that cost at the end of it. However, they're pretty cheap compared to any monitor, so it's worth the price. If you're feeling cheap, just remember there's not a single panel that can do better than the cable you use, no matter how good the hardware or backlighting is. Pick a cable that actually fits your setup Certified cables keep your picture clean You want something officially certified for the resolution and refresh rate you're actually running. Premium High Speed HDMI guarantees 18 Gbps, which handles uncompressed 4K at 60 Hz with HDR. Ultra High Speed HDMI goes through Category 3 testing and delivers the full 48 Gbps, enough for 4K at 120 Hz or 8K at 60 Hz. The certified HDMI cables also tend to use gold-plated connectors. If you don't know any better, that sounds extravagant, but they're meant to resist oxidation and keep contact resistance low. That's what stops the random blackouts you get from cheap nickel plating breaking down. They normally have solid oxygen-free copper conductors, foamed insulation, and shielding built from twisted-pair foil wraps with a tinned copper braid over the top. All of that holds the cable at a strict 100-ohm impedance. Certification also means the cable was tested at an Authorized Test Center. That matters more than people think, since high-frequency digital noise can mess with your Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, and those tests cover it. To check if you got a real one, look for the QR certification label on the box and scan it with the authentication app. It confirms that the exact cable length was independently tested and registered. And buy a length that fits your setup, usually one to two meters. Go too long and you get signal attenuation. Go too short and you're straining your display connectors. Cable management actually matters for signal integrity too, not just looks. These signals run at tens of gigabits per second, and they're sensitive to the physical shape of the cable. So make sure you treat your cable well. Digital cables still have real limits Cheap cables break instead of getting blurry The argument against expensive cables isn't wrong, either. Digital video doesn't degrade the way analog did, where a bad cable gave you a dimmer, grainy picture. If the display decodes the bitstream, the image is perfect. If you mess with the cable or cheap out on a bad one, you'll run into problems. You'll get impedance spikes that blow past tolerance and send signal reflections back toward the source. Meanwhile, the flimsy foil shielding tears and degrades, letting in electromagnetic interference and crosstalk between pairs. Also, cheap connector contacts oxidize over time, thanks to the lack of gold, which raises resistance right at the port. Stack all that up, and you'll see it on screen. It shows up as stuff breaking instead of a blurry image. You need a new cable I will agree that bits are bits; there's no getting around that, but it's an incomplete thought. A digital signal either decodes or it doesn't, but whether it decodes depends on so many factors. A cheap bundled cable might hold together at 1080p and give you no reason to question it until you try to run 4K at 120 Hz with HDR enabled. Certified cables aren't expensive relative to the hardware they're connected to, and you'll be happy to spend the extra money when you see the quality. Highwings HDMI 2.1 cable - Length(s) - 2m - Brand - Highwings This Highwings HDMI 2.1 cable is an excellent example of a reasonably priced Ultra High Speed HDMI cable. One thing to note is that only the two-meter version of the cable seems officially certified. - Externally Powered - No

item.title: You're running PC benchmarks wrong, this is the easier and better way to do it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.21
Once you've spent $2,000 on a new graphics card or a high-end CPU, your first instinct is probably to download a suite of benchmarking tools. You want to see the numbers, compare your score with other systems, and make sure you got what you paid for. So you download 3DMark, Cinebench, and a few other tools, run them one after another, and end up with a collection of scores. Then you close everything and go back to using your computer. The problem is that a benchmark score only tells you something useful when you know what question it is answering. Running every synthetic test you can find can consume hours without telling you whether your PC actually performs well for the things you do. Start with the workload Test what you actually use Synthetic benchmarks are useful because they provide controlled workloads for comparing hardware. A CPU benchmark can help compare processors, while a GPU benchmark can reveal differences between graphics cards. The problem begins when the synthetic score becomes the goal rather than the measurement. If gaming is the reason you bought a faster GPU, your games are the most relevant test. If you compile software every day, compilation time tells you more about your CPU and storage than a generic benchmark score. If you render video or 3D scenes, measure those workloads directly. The test should follow the question you are trying to answer. A graphics card that produces an excellent synthetic score can still deliver disappointing results in a particular game if the CPU, game engine, memory, or settings become the limiting factor. Likewise, a CPU that performs extremely well in a heavily threaded benchmark may provide a smaller improvement in an application with a different workload. Build a baseline Measure the system before making changes Before installing new hardware or changing an important system setting, record how the current configuration performs. For gaming, record frame rates and frame-time behavior in the same game, at the same resolution and graphics settings. For productivity workloads, record how long the same project takes to compile, render, encode, or export. Also record temperatures and clock speeds when thermal behavior could affect performance. For example: CPU: Intel Core i9-14900K GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 Memory: 32 GB OS: Fedora Workload: Blender render Run 1: 08:42 Run 2: 08:39 Run 3: 08:41 Peak CPU temperature: 78°C Sustained CPU clock: 4.2 GHz After the upgrade, repeat the same workload under comparable conditions. Now you have a meaningful before-and-after comparison instead of two unrelated benchmark scores. Keep the rest of the configuration as consistent as possible when evaluating a specific component. Changing the CPU, motherboard, memory, storage, and operating system at the same time makes the final performance difference difficult to attribute. A single benchmark run can be affected by background activity, temperature, power management, or other temporary conditions. Running the same test two or three times gives you a better idea of the system’s normal behavior. Consider these results: 10,421 10,438 10,397 10,429 10,415 There is little reason to treat 10,438 as the definitive score. The results are tightly grouped and establish a fairly consistent range. Now consider: 10,421 9,812 10,437 The middle result deserves investigation because it is considerably lower than the other two. Something may have interrupted the workload, affected the hardware’s clocks, or changed its thermal or power behavior. You do not need dozens of runs. A few consistent results are usually enough for everyday testing, and an average can provide a useful summary when the measurements are comparable. Monitor the hardware Find out why performance changes A benchmark score tells you what happened but monitoring can help explain why. For CPU workloads, watch temperature, utilization, clock frequency, and power consumption. For GPUs, monitor utilization, temperature, clock speed, memory usage, and power. On Linux, tools such as lm-sensors can provide useful information depending on your hardware. On Windows, you can use the HWiNFO sensor. This becomes particularly important when a result is lower than expected. Suppose a CPU benchmark produces a surprisingly low score. Monitoring may show that the processor reaches its thermal limit and subsequently reduces its clock speed. The benchmark has identified a performance problem, while the monitoring data has identified a likely cause. The same principle applies to GPUs. High temperatures, power limits, or unstable clocks can affect sustained performance, particularly in laptops and small-form-factor systems where cooling capacity is limited. You can also use monitoring to evaluate upgrades that do not produce a higher benchmark score. A new cooler might leave performance almost unchanged while substantially reducing temperatures and fan noise. That can still be a successful upgrade. Test your real applications Measure time, frame times, and completion The most useful benchmark is often the workload you already perform. If you compile software, time a full build using the same source tree and build configuration. If you render video, export the same project with the same settings. If you work with 3D applications, render the same scene. For gaming, use the same game, resolution, graphics settings, and test sequence. Gaming deserves particular attention because average FPS does not describe the entire experience. Frame-time data can reveal short periods of severe stuttering that an average FPS figure hides. Looking at 1% lows can also help identify inconsistent performance. The same principle applies to storage. An NVMe SSD might advertise sequential read speeds around 7 GB/s, but that figure tells you little about how quickly your applications start or how a workload involving thousands of small files will perform. Real workloads connect the measurement directly to the experience you are trying to improve. Keep testing conditions consistent Control the variables that matter Before comparing two results, make sure the important conditions are similar. Use the same application or benchmark version, workload, BIOS settings, power profile, resolution, and graphics settings where relevant. Background applications can also interfere with measurements, so close anything that could consume significant CPU, GPU, memory, or storage resources. When testing sustained performance, allow the hardware to reach a comparable thermal state. Environmental conditions matter too. A processor tested in a cool room can behave differently from the same processor in a much warmer environment. A laptop connected to AC power can also behave differently from one running on battery. You do not need laboratory conditions for useful PC benchmarking. You simply need to know which variables could affect the result and keep them reasonably consistent. A simpler benchmarking process Start with the question you want to answer, establish a baseline, choose a relevant workload, monitor the hardware, repeat the test, and compare the results. That is enough for most everyday PC benchmarking. You can still use Cinebench, 3DMark, Geekbench, Blender, fio, stress-ng, or game benchmarks when they provide useful information. The important part is knowing what the measurement tells you. Once you focus on repeatable results from workloads you actually care about, benchmarking becomes faster, easier to reproduce, and much more useful.

item.title: This free app generated subtitles for an entire folder of videos without uploading a thing
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.04
I have a lot of video files scattered between my Plex library and shared folders full of family videos. Some have subtitles, plenty don't, and I wanted an easy way to transcribe them without uploading personal footage to a third-party cloud service. While looking for something that could handle the job locally, I came across Whisperer on GitHub. I was really just looking for a transcription tool, but Whisperer turned out to be much more useful than I anticipated. It can generate standard subtitle files and process an entire folder of videos in one batch, which makes a lot more sense for someone like me with a large library. It definitely beats going through files one at a time. I could point it at a folder, let it do the work locally, and end up with subtitle files that I could use in Plex and other media players. I tested Whisperer on three very different types of videos Before using it on a larger library, I wanted to see where it struggled Before pointing Whisperer at a much larger collection, I wanted to give it a small test with videos that weren't all equally easy to transcribe. I used a NASA interview with clean speech, The Memphis Belle from the Library of Congress with older archival audio, and a personal demo video of me creating a sunburst finish on a guitar body. That gave me a decent mix of source material without turning the test into a huge project. The NASA interview looked like the easy one, The Memphis Belle was the tougher archival test, and the guitar video was closer to the kind of personal footage I actually wanted subtitles for. If Whisperer could handle all three reasonably well, I'd feel better about using it on much larger video folders. Whisperer handled the whole folder without sending my videos anywhere Setup was simple, and the batch process did most of the work Privacy was one of the main reasons I started looking for a local transcription tool in the first place. I didn't want to upload personal videos to a third-party service just to get subtitles. Whisperer keeps the processing on your own PC, so the video files stay where they are while the app creates the subtitle files locally. The setup was pretty straightforward. I used the default settings, added the folder containing my three test videos, and let Whisperer build the queue. From there, I could see all three files waiting to be processed before starting the batch. The app also lets you adjust things like the transcription engine, language, and output format. Once I clicked Start Transcribing, Whisperer worked through the folder one video file at a time. My three videos added up to about 90 minutes of footage, and the full batch finished in roughly 36 minutes on my PC. While it was running, I could watch the progress, see the live transcript as it was generated, and keep an eye on how quickly each file was being processed. When it finished, each video had its own SRT subtitle file sitting alongside the original. I didn't have to upload each file, wait for a cloud service, download the result, and repeat the process for the next one. The subtitle files worked outside Whisperer Plex picked them up without much fuss Whisperer saves the finished subtitles as standard SRT files, which is important because they aren't tied to the app that created them. Whisperer also named the SRT files correctly for Plex, so once they were sitting next to the matching videos, Plex recognized them as external subtitles. I didn't have to rename anything, re-encode the videos, or create new copies just to get the captions working. That also means the subtitles aren't limited to Plex. SRT is a common subtitle format, so the same files also work with VLC and plenty of other players that support external subtitles. For me, that makes Whisperer more useful than a Plex-specific tool. I can generate the subtitles once and keep them with the video, regardless of where I decide to play it later. The subtitles were good enough that I'd keep using them They weren't perfect, but the mistakes were minor The finished subtitles weren't flawless. I saw a few small errors where Whisperer confused similar-sounding words, such as using "an" instead of "and." There were a handful of similar mistakes, but nothing that made the subtitles hard to follow or changed the meaning of what was being said. For what I wanted, that was good enough. I'm not trying to create broadcast-ready captions. I wanted usable subtitles for videos that didn't have any, especially personal footage and older files that I'm unlikely to find captions for elsewhere. Based on this test, Whisperer gets close enough that I'd keep using it on the rest of my collection. This is one app I'll keep using Whisperer worked well enough that I'm going to keep it around. It made quick work of a folder full of very different videos, and the subtitle files dropped straight into the players I already use. I noticed a few small transcription mistakes, but not enough to make me want to go back and fix them by hand. For older footage and personal videos that don't already have subtitles, that's enough for me.

item.title: I turned my giant Excel formula into something I can actually understand
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.42
We all know someone who loves building a ridiculously complicated Excel formula and proudly announcing that it works. I used to be that person. I've been writing Excel formulas for decades, and I loved the satisfaction of making a single formula handle a problem that once seemed impossible. The trouble was, those formulas could become a lot less impressive when I came back to them later. Then along came the LET function. My long Excel formula worked fine—until I had to read it It felt like cracking the Enigma code Take this Excel table as an example. It contains nine columns, four of which feed into the performance score out of 100 for whichever salesperson I select in cell B1. The score combines three measures: 50 points for how much of their sales target they've achieved, 30 points for their profit margin, and 20 points for their average customer rating. Here's the formula I'd enter into cell B2: =MIN(SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1)/MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), 1)*50+(SUMIFS(tblSales[Profit], tblSales[Salesperson], B1)/SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1))*30+(AVERAGEIFS(tblSales[Customer Rating], tblSales[Salesperson], B1)/5)*20 There's nothing actually wrong with this formula. Excel understands it perfectly well, and it returns the score I expect. The problem is that if I need to change part of it, explain it to someone else, or come back to it a year later, it can take longer to pick apart than it took to build in the first place. I need to spot that one SUMIFS calculates revenue, that MAXIFS retrieves the sales target, that another SUMIFS calculates profit, and that AVERAGEIFS produces the customer rating. There's also some repetition hiding in there. I'm calculating total revenue twice: once to work out how much of the target the salesperson has achieved, and again to calculate their profit margin. This makes the formula longer and gives me another piece of logic to maintain if I ever need to change it. What I really want to see when I look at the formula is the logic behind it: revenue, target, profit, rating, target score, profit margin, and rating score. I don't want to have to translate a wall of functions, references, and parentheses into those concepts every time I return to the formula. LET lets me give each calculation a name The formula suddenly starts talking my language This is where the LET function—available in Excel for Microsoft 365, Excel 2024 and 2021, and Excel for the web—comes in. I can give each intermediate result a meaningful name, then use those names later in the formula. First, I'll tell Excel that I want to use the name revenue for my first calculation. The name comes first, followed by a comma, then the calculation that produces its value: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), Next, I'll add the salesperson's target: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), target, MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), I'll do the same thing for profit and the average customer rating: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), target, MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), profit, SUMIFS(tblSales[Profit], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), rating, AVERAGEIFS(tblSales[Customer Rating], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), At this point, I've replaced four chunks of complicated-looking calculations with four names that tell me exactly what each result represents. More importantly, I can now use those names to build the next part of the calculation. The targetScore is the salesperson's revenue divided by their target, capped at 100%. The profitMargin is profit divided by revenue, and the ratingScore is the rating converted from a five-point scale: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), target, MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), profit, SUMIFS(tblSales[Profit], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), rating, AVERAGEIFS(tblSales[Customer Rating], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), targetScore, MIN(revenue/target,1), profitMargin, profit/revenue, ratingScore, rating/5, Finally, I'll combine those three scores using their respective weightings: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), target, MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), profit, SUMIFS(tblSales[Profit], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), rating, AVERAGEIFS(tblSales[Customer Rating], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), targetScore, MIN(revenue/target,1), profitMargin, profit/revenue, ratingScore, rating/5, (targetScore*50)+(profitMargin*30)+(ratingScore*20) ) The underlying calculations haven't changed. I'm still using SUMIFS to calculate revenue and profit, MAXIFS to retrieve the salesperson's sales target, and AVERAGEIFS to calculate the average customer rating. I've simply named those results to reflect what they mean: revenue, target, profit, and rating. These named variables are now clearly listed in the formula, so I can quickly scan them and see the building blocks of the calculation at a glance. I can then use those names to create targetScore, profitMargin, and ratingScore before combining them into the final score calculation. Also, revenue is now calculated only once and then reused in both targetScore and profitMargin. And if I decide to change one of those calculations or its weighting later, I can find the relevant named component much more easily than I could in the original formula. This is the part of LET that appeals to me most. I'm still asking Excel to do the same work, but the formula is easier to understand, and the logic is more visible. Where do helper formulas fit into the equation? It depends on the intermediate calculations I'm a big fan of helper formulas, whether they're added as columns to an existing dataset or gathered together in a separate table. The screenshot above shows the trade-off. The helper table makes every intermediate calculation easy to see and reuse, but it also adds a sizable chunk of spreadsheet structure for a calculation that ultimately produces a single value. I'd choose helper formulas over LET if I wanted to use those intermediate calculations elsewhere, such as in a separate analysis, a chart, or a PivotTable. But the trade-off is that they add extra machinery. Every additional calculation creates another moving part in the workbook, and the more moving parts you have, the more opportunities there are for errors. So when deciding whether to use LET or helper formulas, I generally follow this rule of thumb: if an intermediate calculation is useful on its own, give it a helper formula. If it's simply supporting one final result, LET can keep it contained in a single formula while keeping the logic clear. Yes, I could hide or group the helper calculations, but that adds another layer of spreadsheet structure to navigate and maintain. With LET, I can keep the supporting calculations inside the formula, leave the existing structure intact, and present the final result without adding calculations that most people will never need to see. My formulas don't have to be a mystery anymore Thanks to functions like LET, I no longer have to create long, unreadable formulas that only make sense to me at the time. I can still make Excel do complicated things, but I can also make the logic behind those calculations much easier to understand. And if I want to add even more context, I can tuck in plain-language notes using the N() function trick.

item.title: Rokid wants anyone to build AI agents for its smart glasses
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.53
What you need to know - Rokid's AIUI Studio is a browser-based platform that lets anyone build spatial AI apps for Rokid Glasses, with no coding experience or dev kit required. - Developers can describe an idea, while the AI-native workflow helps turn it into a working app. - The built-in smart glasses simulator lets developers create and test projects before getting physical hardware involved. Rokid is making it easier to build apps for its AI glasses, and you won't need a coding background or even to own a pair of the glasses. The company has launched AIUI Studio globally at IFA Berlin 2026, giving developers a browser-based platform for creating and publishing spatial AI applications. Much of the development process takes place via an AI-native workflow in AIUI Studio. You can say what you want to build in plain language, and the platform can take that idea and build an app without the traditional coding skills. It also offers a simulation of Rokid’s smart glasses, enabling developers to work on their projects without having to purchase the hardware. There’s still a reason to get the real hardware involved eventually, though. Rokid’s developer documentation advises testing agents in its Interactive Inview simulator before performing a final check on the actual glasses. For developers who want to have more control, Rokid pairs its AIUI Skills Library framework with AIUI Code assistance. The company says this helps creators make better use of the glasses’ hardware while also optimizing apps for less latency, less memory use, and less power consumption. The move is the latest as Rokid’s developer ecosystem continues to grow. The company says it now has some 35,000 registered developers and more than 500 agents available through its Agent Store. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android AIUI Studio is now available worldwide. If Rokid can take advantage of that growing developer base to create a steady stream of useful agents, its glasses might just become a platform that people actively build around. item.title: iQOO 16 display leaks were true: Samsung's 2K 165Hz panel is official
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.40
What you need to know - The iQOO 16 is set to debut as the first smartphone with a 2K resolution OLED display running at a 165Hz refresh rate. - Co-developed with Samsung Display on a dedicated production line, the panel marks the Android debut of Samsung's latest M16 luminescent material and LEAD 2.0 architecture. - The screen reaches 2,800 nits global peak brightness (10,000 nits local peak), features 508 PPI, and delivers sub-pixel-level calibration for color accuracy. Rumor has it that the iQOO 16 will be released soon, and iQOO has now confirmed one of the upgrades that could make this gaming-focused flagship stand out from the crowd. The next phone from the company is said to be the first to sport a 2K OLED panel with a 165Hz refresh rate from Samsung, which iQOO is calling a smartphone first. The announcement also confirms earlier reports that the iQOO 16 would sport Samsung’s newer M16 OLED technology. The company says the phone will be the first Android smartphone to use the material, along with its new 2K LEAD 2.0 technology. For context, we saw the original LEAD OLED panel debut with the iQOO 15. LEAD 2.0 has been developed in partnership with Samsung, built on a dedicated production line just for iQOO’s flagship. The two companies also designed a custom high-refresh-rate display IC and a dedicated production line for the phone. The panel is rated at 2,800 nits for global brightness and 10,000 nits for local brightness. It also offers 508 ppi, wide P3 color coverage, DC dimming, and better brightness and color uniformity than the iQOO 15. iQOO also claims sub-pixel-level calibration leads to extremely tight color accuracy. There is also a less obvious upgrade here: Samsung recently said the new display uses roughly 31 percent less power at 150 nits than a similarly sized 1.5K panel. That’s particularly useful, as improving both resolution and refresh rate often comes with a battery cost. The target is clearly gaming. The display features 500Hz multi-touch sampling and 5,000Hz instantaneous sampling rate, while iQOO’s Q-Flex technology focuses on reducing input lag. There’s also 3,300Hz PWM dimming and many eye-comfort features. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The iQOO 16 is expected to launch in China sometime near the end of September. If the rest of the hardware is up to the mark as this display, the top gaming flagships out there will have a serious new competitor on their hands. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: Android makes switching password managers much easier
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.14
What you need to know - You can now move passwords and passkeys directly between supported apps on Android without exporting sensitive data to an unencrypted file. - Your new password manager hands the process to Android, which detects compatible managers installed on your phone and coordinates the transfer. - Once authorized, Android moves the credentials between apps without requiring manual file handling. Android has always made it a pain to switch password managers. Moving passwords usually involved exporting your data into an unencrypted text file, and passkeys were pretty much stuck in place. Android is tackling both of those issues with a new transfer experience that makes moving your credentials much more secure and simple. In a blog post, Google said the new system lets you transfer passwords and passkeys directly between password managers, without first having to download a file. That eliminates one of the biggest security hassles of the old process, which was that sensitive credentials were sitting unprotected on your device for a while. Furthermore, passkeys weren’t transferable, so you had to manually recreate them across websites and apps. The process is built to be mostly out of your way. Start in your new password manager and select the option to import or copy credentials from another provider. The app then hands the job to Android, which knows which compatible password managers you have already installed on your phone and shows you where the data can come from. You are then sent back to the password manager you already use to select, review, and approve the transfer. Once approved, the passwords and passkeys move between the apps in just a few seconds. The feature is already available with Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Dashlane notes that CXP is compatible with devices running Android 10 or newer with the latest Play Services update. Bitwarden needs Android 14+ with Play services 26.21+. It is not merely a matter of convenience. Passkeys are more secure than passwords and resistant to phishing. Adoption has been stalled in part due to user concerns around vendor lock-in. CXP removes that barrier. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Bitwarden says the creation of passkeys peaked this summer at over 500% compared to early 2024, with nearly half of all passkeys created in the past three months alone. Google says more partners are on the way. If you’ve been waiting to change password managers because of the hassle, that excuse just went out the window. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: These popular Samsung phones just received their final software update
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.91
What you need to know - Samsung has officially ended software support for the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 after five years. - Both foldables received four years of OS upgrades and five years of security updates, as Samsung originally promised. - Samsung has removed both phones from its security update page, meaning they won't receive regular security patches anymore. Samsung's foldable phones that launched in the summer of 2021 have officially reached the end of their software support cycle. Most Samsung flagship smartphones today, including the Galaxy S26 Ultra and even 2024's Galaxy S24 Ultra, come with seven years of software support. But Samsung hasn't always offered updates for this long. Older flagships came with shorter support promises, and now the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 have officially reached the end of theirs. As spotted by Android Authority, the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 have received their final software updates. At launch, Samsung promised four years of OS upgrades and five years of security updates for both foldables, and the company has now fulfilled that promise. Samsung has also removed both devices from its security updates page. This means Samsung won't be releasing any further regular software or security updates for these devices. The oldest foldables officially supported by the company are now the Galaxy Z Fold 4 and Galaxy Z Flip 4. Even those devices have moved to a quarterly update schedule, unlike newer Samsung phones that continue to receive monthly updates. So, if you're still using a Galaxy Z Fold 3 or Galaxy Z Flip 3, your phone won't receive any new regular security patches from Samsung going forward. That means any new security vulnerabilities discovered from here on may remain unpatched on these devices. If you're still holding onto one of these foldables, this might finally be the time to start thinking about an upgrade. Samsung recently introduced a completely new form factor with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, while its latest foldables also come with a much longer software support promise. If you've managed to keep your Fold 3 or Flip 3 running for five years, one of Samsung's newer foldables should last you considerably longer. item.title: Steam Frame costs $1,059, but Android games could give it an edge
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.87
What you need to know - Steam Frame starts at $1,059 for 256GB, while the 1TB model jumps to $1,299. - Android games are supported, giving the headset access to existing Android APKs without requiring completely separate ports. - Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 + 16GB RAM powers the headset, with SteamOS handling native games and compatibility layers. Valve has finally put a price tag on the Steam Frame, its new wireless VR headset that aims to blur the line between a standalone gaming device and a PC accessory. The catch? It won’t be as simple as clicking “buy” to get one. The Steam Frame starts at $1,059 for 256GB, with the 1TB model costing $1,299. Each headset has tracked controllers, and Valve is bundling Half-Life: Alyx with the device, the company announced. It can play supported games locally or stream more demanding titles from a PC. It’ll also support Android games, with developers using the same Android APKs they already use to bring mobile titles to the Meta Quest. This could give the Frame access to a much larger game library without developers needing to build entirely separate versions for Valve’s headset. The Frame also supports wireless PC streaming with the 6GHz dongle that Valve bundles in. Under the hood, the Frame is packed with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and 16GB of RAM, with native software and compatibility layers handled by SteamOS. The storage options are also worth a closer look. You can upgrade from 256GB to 1TB for $240, but the Frame also has a microSD slot. So if your main game stream is from a PC, there may be little reason to pay extra for the bigger model. Valve had originally said it wanted the Steam Frame to cost less than the $999 Index, but the final starting price puts it $60 above that benchmark. Rising memory and component costs have complicated the pricing strategy of Valve’s hardware, as seen with the Steam Machine. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Availability will also be controlled by a reservation system, with sign-ups running until September 17 and purchase invitations starting September 18. The Steam Frame is clearly not aimed at the budget VR crowd at $1,059. Valve is betting its Steam library, Android support, wireless PC streaming, and standalone abilities will justify the premium. item.title: MediaTek's first 2nm flagship chip is here — meet the new Dimensity 9600 Pro
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.78
What you need to know - MediaTek's Dimensity 9600 Pro is the company's first 2nm flagship chipset, promising better performance and efficiency. - The new 2+3+3 All Big Core CPU delivers up to 17% faster single-core performance while using significantly less power. - MediaTek's upgraded NPU supports on-device AI models with up to 30 billion parameters while improving AI power efficiency. MediaTek has officially taken the wraps off its latest flagship smartphone chipset, called the Dimensity 9600 Pro. And it's the company's first flagship chip built on a 2nm process. The new flagship smartphone season is almost upon us, and chipset makers have started unveiling their next generation of processors. Qualcomm is set to announce its next flagship Snapdragon chipsets later this month, but MediaTek has beaten it to the punch by unveiling its first 2nm chipset. Called the Dimensity 9600 Pro, MediaTek says its new chipset combines flagship performance and power efficiency with advanced agentic AI experiences. The chip features a 2+3+3 All Big Core CPU design, which MediaTek says delivers an impressive 61% reduction in multi-core power consumption. The architecture consists of two C2 Ultra cores clocked at up to 4.55GHz, three C2 Pro cores running at up to 4.35GHz, and another three C2 Pro cores clocked at up to 3.1GHz. MediaTek says single-core performance has improved by up to 17%, while multi-core performance is up to 15% higher than the previous generation, all while consuming less power. Of course, there's also a big focus on agentic AI experiences. MediaTek says the chipset's new dual-NPU architecture and Agentic AI Engine are designed to power the next generation of on-device AI. Its second-generation Super Efficient NPU reportedly reduces AI power consumption by up to 40%, while delivering 51% higher LLM prefill performance and 55% higher token generation per watt. The Dimensity 9600 Pro can also support AI models with up to 30 billion parameters directly on the device, which should allow more complex AI tasks to run without constantly relying on the cloud. There's also a larger 34.5MB cache, alongside support for LPDDR6 memory and UFS 5.0 storage for the first time. MediaTek says its new Scheduling Engine can intelligently allocate computing power and memory resources between hardware and software, allowing multiple apps to continue running smoothly in the background while using fewer resources. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Gaming is getting a significant upgrade as well. The new G2-Ultra NX GPU delivers up to 27% higher peak performance while consuming 24% less power. MediaTek says the GPU can deliver what it calls console-grade gaming on-device at up to 185fps. For cameras, there's a new Imagiq 1290 ISP, which MediaTek says will enable more advanced computational photography and content creation features on upcoming smartphones. There aren't any smartphones powered by the Dimensity 9600 Pro just yet, but we shouldn't have to wait long before the first devices arrive. Apple's 2nm A20 Pro has already launched inside the iPhone 18 Pro series, while Qualcomm is expected to reveal its answer at Snapdragon Summit later this month. item.title: A mysterious Google Wear OS fitness tracker just appeared at the FCC
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.35
What you need to know - A mysterious Google-made wearable has appeared at the FCC with clues suggesting it could run Wear OS. - The device reportedly skips Wi-Fi and relies on Bluetooth LE, suggesting it may be a fitness tracker. - GPS support and a metal frame are also listed, while ADB testing suggests some form of Wear OS software. - The device could sit between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch, potentially filling the gap left by Fitbit Charge. A mysterious new Wear OS fitness tracker has been spotted at the FCC, and there are a few clues suggesting it could be an upcoming Google Pixel or Fitbit-branded device. Google has been enjoying success with both the Pixel Watch lineup and the recently launched Fitbit Air, and it looks like the company could be preparing to expand its fitness tracking lineup even further. As spotted by 9to5Google, a mysterious new Google-made device has now appeared in an FCC listing. The device, described as a "Wireless Device," carries the model number G8BL6 and is manufactured by Goertek, a company that has previously manufactured several generations of Pixel Buds. Interestingly, the FCC listing suggests there's no Wi-Fi connectivity onboard. Instead, the device appears to rely entirely on Bluetooth LE. There are also clues suggesting the device could run some form of Wear OS, as the EUT operation test setup specifically mentions ADB testing. In terms of other connectivity, the mysterious device reportedly supports GPS or GNSS and features a metal frame that will also act as its antenna. The lack of Wi-Fi is particularly interesting, since most traditional Wear OS smartwatches have supported Wi-Fi. That could suggest we're looking at a different type of wearable altogether, potentially a more traditional fitness tracker rather than another Pixel Watch. And there might already be another clue. During the Pixel 11 launch, Google briefly showed an unannounced fitness tracker with a small display in one of its teasers, and there's a chance this FCC listing could be related to that device. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android If so, the new wearable could potentially sit somewhere between the Fitbit Air and Google's more expensive Pixel Watch lineup. It's also worth remembering that Fitbit hasn't updated its Charge lineup since 2023, so this device could fit quite nicely into that missing middle ground. item.title: Meta’s Phoenix mixed reality headset is finally starting to look real
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.06
What you need to know - Meta’s Project Phoenix is finally coming into focus after more than a year of rumors about a lightweight, high-end mixed-reality headset. - Phoenix looks more like smart glasses than a traditional VR headset, using nose pads and temple-mounted sensors. - An external compute puck appears to be part of the design. Whispers about Meta working on a lightweight, high-end mixed reality headset codenamed Project Phoenix have floated around the tech sphere for over a year. Now, we finally get our first real look at what Mark Zuckerberg's hardware team has been cooking up, and it seems Meta accidentally left the key under the mat. The images were revealed through Meta’s HorizonOS Prescription Lens package, which first appeared in August as a mostly blank system package, as noticed by UploadVR. An update in September showed detailed pictures of how prescription lens inserts attach to the Phoenix and how users scan a QR code to set them up. Interestingly, the hardware looks less like a traditional VR headset and more like chunky glasses. Phoenix uses nose pads instead of the bulky face interface of the Quest 3 and other XR headsets, with sensors along the temples. There’s also a cable coming from the left temple, seemingly confirming previous reports that Phoenix will use an external compute puck. It's a design that could change the way people think about wearing a mixed reality headset. If you’ve been using more traditional XR headsets, you’ll probably find it comforting to realize potential benefits here, like less weight on your face, but the compromise moves elsewhere: you’ll need to deal with a separate computing unit and a cable. For Meta, the greater challenge might be getting that extra hardware to feel invisible enough that Phoenix still feels like something you can casually wear, rather than another device you have to gear up for. There's another interesting clue here. The leaked setup stuff seems to be based on prescription inserts and controller-free interaction. Meta hasn’t officially announced Phoenix yet, but Meta Connect 2026 starts September 23 and has a session dedicated to controller-free interaction on its agenda. If Phoenix shows up there, we might finally learn whether Meta’s push toward lighter mixed reality headsets is a real shift in headset design, or just a clever way to move the weight somewhere else. item.description:

What you need to know - Rumors claim Samsung is developing a new pair of smart glasses, and has tapped Samsung Display for an in-lens color display. - The glasses would allegedly focus on displaying "text, notifications, icons, and more" on an extremely thin panel. - Samsung has its Intelligent Eyewear, which is supposedly coming out this fall, but those are mostly voice-focused with Google's Gemini and a camera. Samsung has barely dipped a toe into the world of smart glasses, and there's already a rumor that it wants to go bigger next time. This report from The Elec (Korean) claims Samsung might've started developing smart glasses with a color display (via 9to5Google). The publication cites its "industry sources" in saying Samsung has tapped Samsung Display to "create microdisplays" for a future pair of AI smart glasses. These rumors claim Samsung has a lot on its plate to prepare this product. Specifically, the post claims Samsung has a "technical challenge" to overcome: its FOV (field of view). The company is purportedly chasing a wide FOV for these glasses to accommodate the information users would see. What's more, Samsung is leaning on its Display side to create "ultra-small panels" of ~0.2 inches or smaller for the lenses. Samsung is allegedly focusing on displaying "text, notifications, icons, and navigation arrows" (machine-translated). It's still incredibly early to know for sure how Samsung's first color display smart glasses will arrive. However, the publication suggests the glasses could see a launch in the second half of 2027 or "early" in 2028. Got lenses? Samsung's getting serious. I don't think its Intelligent Eyewear are a bad start, though. It's starting simple. Useful, even. Everything is based on your voice. You still have a camera to take photos, and Gemini is there to help with hands-free assistance. To put a color display—a proper screen—would definitely take things up a notch. To me, I think this rumor is probably a little more eye-catching. We can't help but think about the Ray-Ban Display glasses from Meta. In fact, that's probably the kind of competition Samsung wants to get itself involved in. These glasses also feature the neural band. It makes it easier to control the display and content on your lenses with hand gestures. There's plenty of time still to see how Samsung manages this. Right now, we have (kind of) Samsung's "Intelligent Eyewear." These glasses are in partnership with Google, alongside designs from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. These are Samsung's first smart glasses, but they lean more on the user's voice. Users can communicate with Gemini for navigation, order pickups, and photos. The glasses feature a camera and a microphone to get all of this done. Google reiterated its Samsung partnership during this summer's Unpacked. These glasses aren't out yet. During the original announcement this past spring, Samsung said we shouldn't expect to see them until "later this fall." item.title: I found something better than the Bose QC Ultra Gen II: meet Noble's FoKus Amadeus
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.12
There's extensive choice if you want to get a pair of decent earbuds. Bose, Sennheiser, and Sony continue to be heavy-hitters in this category (I use my Bose QuietComfort Ultra Gen II while traveling), and phone brands also a good job with their earbuds — Google's Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro deliver a vibrant sound with plenty of useful features. But if you want the best sound quality, you'll need to turn your attention to Noble Audio. The boutique brand is known for its IEMs, and it has ventured into wireless earbuds in recent years. I've heard plenty of great things about the brand, so I was excited to get my hands on the FoKus Amadeus. Retailing for $320 on Amazon, the Amadeus is in the similar price bracket as the Bose QC Ultra Gen II and Sony WF-1000XM6, but what you're getting here is markedly different. For starters, the design of the FoKus Amadeus is unlike any other earbuds around. Mainstream brands play it pretty safe with their designs, and they're not meant to stand out — that isn't the case here. With a bright red design and a custom shell that's bigger than most earbuds, these are guaranteed to grab attention. Like the Amadeus name, the red design is an homage to Mozart’s signature tailcoat, says Noble. Build quality is great, and while the size of the shell means the earbuds jut out, I didn't see any issues with comfort. Each bud weighs 7g, and that's in line with other products in this category. The only omission is ingress protection, so I wouldn't suggest using these at the gym. Just like the buds, the case itself is bigger, but the square design makes it easy to take anywhere. Coming to connectivity, the Amadeus gets Bluetooth 5.4 via Qualcomm’s QCC3091 modem, and there's SBC, AAC, LDAC, and AptX Adaptive. The buds connect to two devices at once, and I had no problems pairing with my Pixel 11 Pro XL, Find X9 Ultra, and iPad Pro M4. There's good ANC as well, and the buds did a great job tuning out the ambient sounds in my surroundings. Obviously, sound quality is where the Amadeus excels. The sound signature from the 8.3mm dynamic driver is tuned towards musicality, and you get a good bass rumble with clean mids and a nice treble extension. These are particularly great with vocals, and the soundstage is significantly wider than any other earbuds in this category. There's a level of dynamism to the sound that you just don't get with Bose or Sony, and that ultimately makes the Amadeus enjoyable even in extended listening sessions. Another thing I like is the sheer level of customizability to the sound. Noble uses Audiodo to tune the sound of the Amadeus to your individual preferences. This is done by a listening test that lasts up to three minutes, and then you get a custom EQ that's tailored to your ears. The tech works exceedingly well, and it makes a big difference to the sound. In addition to Audiodo, you get a 10-band EQ and custom modes that let you tweak the sound profile to a granular degree. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Then there's the app; the Noble FoKus app has to be the best of any buds I used. You get a minimal interface without any overt styling (looking at you, Sennheiser), but there's an extensive amount of customizability when it comes to adjusting the sound. I got good battery life as well. The Amadeus lasted close to eight hours between charges, and each bud has a 65mAh battery. The case provides an additional 2.5 times charge via a 500mAh battery, so you get just around 40 hours before you'll need to plug in the case. There is fast charging that gives you two hours of music with a 10-minute charge, and a full charge takes just over 90 minutes. I know that's $320 is at the higher end of the scale when it comes to earbuds, and to its credit, Noble Audio didn't omit anything in the FoKus Amadeus. The design stands out quite a bit, but the earbuds are comfortable to wear, and the sound quality is outstanding; if you've used Bose's QC Ultra or any of Sony's earbuds, you will see an immediate difference when switching to these — I did. The FoKus Amadeus is designed to stand out, and the sound quality is immersive like no other earbuds in this category. item.title: New iPhone Duo foldable gets wild, cheeky responses from Samsung and... Duolingo???
item.description:

What you need to know - Duolingo was incredibly cheeky on social media over Apple's iPhone Duo announcement, stating, "They named a phone after me and made it bend over." - Samsung followed up in "solidarity" with the app; however, it continued to post throughout Apple's event, stating, "Making us wait? Fine. We'll be over here, folding 3 ways." - The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable with a 7.6-inch inner screen and a 5.4-inch cover display with a whopping $1,999 price tag (to start). The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable phone. The company has finally entered the foldable game, and it's drawn the attention of two notable brands in humorous (and cheeky) ways. Apple's event wrapped up this afternoon, but Duolingo was first on the ball with the response. No other way to say it: Duolingo was as cheeky as cheeky could be on X today (Sept 9) as word about Apple's iPhone Duo made its rounds. Duolingo said, "They named a phone after me and made it bend over." As unhinged as this post was, Duolingo quickly followed it up with positivity: there's more screen space for your language lessons. As the event wound down, Samsung got involved. Samsung has been in the foldable game for years now, and this is Apple's first one. The Korean OEM posted in solidarity with Duolingo this afternoon. Samsung said, "I'm so sorry, Duolingo. They copied us too." The friendly banter between the two companies continued, with the language learning app posting a photo that read, "We infringed upon." However, Samsung was posting the entire time Apple's event was running. The company said, "So far, so same" at one point, then followed it up with "Accessories? It’s giving condiments and no food. #ItsTimeToSwitch." And what could be seen as its most... um, interesting post was "Making us wait? Fine. We'll be over here, folding 3 ways." Let's also not forget Samsung said the iPhone Duo's bedside clock mode was "giving groundhog day." You could say this was coming. People have been wondering (and waiting) for a foldable from Apple for years. There have been post upon post of speculation. Renders upon renders of its purported design, too. Now, we finally have it, and it'll be up to the consumers to determine if it's worth it. Welcome the iPhone Duo Unhinged and cheeky from Duolingo—I approve. The iPhone Duo is a decent looking device. It's certainly something new that Apple iPhone consumers might enjoy. This is nothing new for Android users, though. What's more, I dare say Android foldables are a little bit beyond Apple. Not sure how long that'll last, though. This is Apple's first one, there are kinks it can work on ironing out. Let's see how things go from here, especially after we get it in our hands. The iPhone Duo was the "one last thing" from Apple this afternoon. Everyone was waiting for it, and it confirmed the foldable will feature a 7.6-inch inner screen and a 5.4-inch cover display. When unfolded, the device is 5.3mm thick; however, it is 254g, roughly 53g heavier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8. Apple's foldable is also a bit heavier than Google's Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Apple had to rework its software a bit for the foldable. Your key navigational buttons and the like are consistently positioned vertically on the right side. What's more, as you'd expect with a device like this, your apps will adapt depending on its orientation. Apple announced the phone in two colorways: Star White and Night Sky. item.title: Almost 8000 organizations hit by fake voicemail transcript emails in credential phishing attack
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 7.18
- Check Point spotted phishing emails spoofing voicemail transcript notifications, hitting 7,800+ orgs - Malicious SVG attachments auto‑fill victim emails, redirecting to fake login pages for credential theft - SVG format bypasses filters; businesses urged to verify notifications and treat SVGs as active content Hackers have a new phishing lure - the automated voicemail transcript notification, and have already used it against thousands of organizations already, sending tens of thousands of malicious emails. In a new report, security experts from Check Point Research (CPR) said they spotted an ongoing campaign that has already targeted thousands of organizations. The goal of the campaign seems to be credential theft - grabbing access to people’s email accounts, business services, and similar. Abusing the trends The proliferation of AI gave rise to a new trend in the office - automated voicemail transcripts. When a person receives a voicemail, they can choose to read it instead of listening to it. Useful for a noisy workplace environment, or for emails that are too sensitive to be blasted through a speaker system. An automated system mails the transcript to the recipient’s inbox in a familiar format, and since they’re used to receiving this type of email, they’re not suspicious or skeptical enough. Their guard is lowered, which is a perfect opportunity for the attackers. “Between August 17 and August 31, Check Point identified more than 58,000 emails tied to the campaign. The operation targeted over 7,800 organizations, leveraging more than 38,400 spoofed sender addresses across over 9,300 spoofed domains,” the researchers explained. The emails follow a simple formula the recipients are already used to seeing. Each message’s subject line begins with “Automated transcript”, followed by a partially redacted phone number and a random tracking string. “The effect is deliberately understated: a notification that appears to have been generated by a trusted workplace system,” CPR explains. The email domains are also spoofed in a way that makes it seem as if they’re coming from within the same organization. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! SVG attachments Every email comes with an attachment. It is designed to look like a regular call recording file, using names such as “▷ ——— 001min 09sec_….svg.” But notice the file type - SVG. This is not an audio file, it is short for Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) - an image file. There are a few reasons why scammers are opting for this particular format, but the number one is that it is an XML-based document that can contain JavaScript. When a browser opens the SVG, that JavaScript can execute, redirecting victims to a spoofed login page where they’re asked to log in. This is exactly the setup here, too. To make matters worse, since the recipient’s email address is hardcoded in the URL, the fake login form auto-fills it. When the victim opens up the SVG, they’re redirected to a login page where the “username” part is already populated, making it more personalized and credible. Another key reason why SVG is a popular format in these attacks is that it can bypass email security systems. If scammers put a hyperlink in the email’s body, it can be scanned by the system, and sanitized if proven malicious (which it would). But without a link the only other thing a security system can check are the attachments, and there the usual suspects are .exe, .docx, or .pdf files. Very few are focusing on SVG files, as well. Adapting to change This campaign is a great example of how quickly attackers adapt to enterprise workflows as automation becomes more common, Check Point’s researchers have warned. In response, businesses should start treating automated notifications as signals that need to be verified - especially those when the sender appears to match the recipient’s domain. Furthermore, businesses should define which file types and domains AI agents are allowed to access without human confirmation, and finally, they should definitely inspect SVG attachments as active content, not simply as images. item.title: These cheap Skullcandy earbuds have a worrying Bluetooth flaw that could let anyone connect to your device
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.47
- Researchers warn Skullcandy Dime 3 earbuds on older firmware accept Bluetooth pairing from unknown devices with no user interaction required - When leveraged, it can be used to interrupt the owner's connections, hijack playback, and even capture live microphone audio - The vulnerability has been patched in a newer firmware update available only on newer units, does not seem to be addressable for existing earbuds Carnegie Mellon University's CERT Coordination Center has warned Skullcandy's Dime 3 wireless earbuds will accept a Bluetooth pairing request from a stranger's device without the owner doing anything. The resulting bond is permanent, and the only sign the owner gets is a spoken "new device paired" notification delivered after it has already happened, with zero user interaction to confirm the request. The advisory covering the Dime 3 was written by CERT/CC's Bob Kemerer and credits independent researcher Jacob Nowak, who had posted his findings to the Full Disclosure mailing list in early August after testing it on hardware he owned. A fix deployed that covers virtually no existing users What makes this worse is that, ironically, while Skullcandy was swift in addressing the issue affecting earbuds running firmware version 1.0.0.28 by rolling out a patched version 1.0.0.30, it seems to address the issue only in newly made units. CERT notes that there seem to be no "consumer-accessible" methods to upgrade existing units to the newest firmware because it reportedly has no support via the companion app, as a Tom's Guide review indicates. A product without an update path that is user-accessible essentially means that its software flaws, or in this case, security issues, are here to stay for users who have had the bad luck of buying an earlier unit. The underlying vulnerability, CVE-2025-20701, is not new and is not of Skullcandy's making. It is one of three vulnerabilities that Dennis Heinze and Frieder Steinmetz of the German firm ERNW disclosed in June 2025 at the TROOPERS conference in Heidelberg, affecting Bluetooth systems-on-chip from Taiwan's Airoha. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The Dime 3's Bluetooth identifier names Airoha as its chipset vendor, and while Airoha shipped a fixed SDK to its customers in June 2025 and published its bulletin that August, owners of the earbuds are in a unique situation, to say the least. The vulnerability's severity is disputed: MediaTek (which owns Airoha) assigned it a relatively low 6.7 rating, while CISA's vulnerability enrichment program later assigned it an 8.8 with a 'high' categorization. A potential attacker is limited to what the earbuds can access, since the vulnerability is essentially limited to the earbuds, but one could still wreak havoc with that alone. It should allow for more than just disrupting a person's routine by 'hijacking' one's earbuds by essentially using their microphones on them to record conversations or, in an extreme theoretical case (requiring chaining with other exploits), impersonate the headset and pull contacts, call history, and even pass hands-free commands to a paired smartphone. The latter, however, would require a high technical skill set, being within a few meters of a victim, and a Bluetooth connection turned on on the paired smartphone. For now, a vulnerability exists that Skullcandy should have been able to patch, exactly as Apple recently did for its Beats Studio Buds, but a lack of support for any third party apps on the budget earbuds is somewhat annoyingly resulting in an unpatchable vulnerability for existing users. item.title: Quote of the day by Intel co-founder Gordon Moore: 'The number of transistors incorporated in a chip will approximately double every 24 months' — laying down a prophecy for decades of computing acceleration
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.42
The computing industry owes a lot to the guiding vision of Intel co-founder Gordon Moore, whose prediction about the pace of advancement in the computing industry has been a fixture for more than 50 years. But how much room does this rule have left to run? Moore's Law Moore, who was the president of Intel at the time, delivered his famous prediction – known as Moore's Law – at the 1975 IEEE International Electron Devices Meeting, according to the Computer History Museum. This article is part of TechRadar Pro's QOTD project to provide an insight into the minds of the brightest and most recognized figures in the technology industry today and in years gone by. Read the full series here. This prediction, however, wasn't his first. A decade before, Moore authored an article titled 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits' in which he predicted that the number of transistors crammed into integrated circuits would double every year. The initial projections were incorrect, but he was confident that, thanks to advances in technology, his projection could be realized accurately if he updated his timelines. It eventually became a self-fulfilling prophecy, with the semiconductor industry almost using this prediction as a benchmark against which to judge progress – with engineers challenged to deliver breakthroughs that ensured their work complied with Moore's Law. The future of chipmaking Moore's Law held up for many years, but the nature of exponential growth may not seem realistic, especially given there are hard physical constraints with the widely used silicon-based semiconductors. Although there's no firm date at which Moore's Law no longer applied, there's a wide understanding that the doubling in transistor count every two years slowed down roughly 10 years ago. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! In today's age, it's getting harder and harder to cram more transistors onto a single chip, although scientists are experimenting with new technologies or approaches that could ensure the continuation of progress. These ideas include 3D stacking as well as new semiconductor materials. Keumars Afifi-Sabet is a freelance contributor for Tech Radar and the Technology Editor for Live Science. item.title: 'No old code exists': Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis experience director confirms the 'reimagining' had to be built totally from the ground up on Unreal Engine 5 — but this meant Crystal Dynamics could add more tech upgrades
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.18
- Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis experience director Jeff Adams confirms "no old code exists" for the original 1996 game - This meant Crystal Dynamics had to build the game from the ground up on Unreal Engine 5 - Adams says the engine also allowed the studio to create its own custom tech for the "reimagining" of the classic title Crystal Dynamics has explained why it chose to build Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis from the ground up, instead of doing anything close to a remake of the 1996 game, revealing that no source code exists. In a Q&A at Gamescom following an exclusive presentation that TechRadar Gaming attended, experience director Jeff Adams discussed what he's previously called a "reimagining" of the original Tomb Raider game and what it meant for the development team, who built the game from the ground up using Unreal Engine 5. "We are in Unreal Engine 5," Adams said, "no old code exists. We are basically taking it and remaking it, or not remaking, reimagining it. We are bringing it from the ground up." When asked to talk about how effective Unreal Engine 5 has been for the team, Adams explained that it enabled them to "have our own custom implementation for physics in the engine," which means engineering their own features, custom physics, and general upgrades; this made Legacy of Atlantis a true, modern reimagining. "Unreal creates a really great sandbox platform for building a game, but when we're making a specific type of experience, we're going to have things that we really want to target and get to a right fidelity level where we're happy with it," the developer continued. "So while things like Nanite and Lumen [UE5's technologies that offer realistic graphics capability] allow us to make a beautiful game environment, there might be some things that we're saying, 'Hey, we wish it could do this a little bit better.' That's when we'll break out and say, our engineers will create something custom that helps solve that issue, so that we can make sure that we're delivering an authentic Tomb Raider experience on Unreal." He added that Lara Croft's long braid, which reacts to her movement, is "a perfect example of that." Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. item.title: Indian government reveals new system able to detect Chinese-made components in military drones
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.09
- Indian Army opens lab built to expose hidden drone vulnerabilities. - Chinese-origin chips face heavier scrutiny under new army protocols. - AASHVAST technicians hunt hidden passwords buried inside drone control systems. The Indian Army has opened a new laboratory in New Delhi designed to inspect military drones for hidden software flaws and unauthorized parts. The Assessment and Analysis of Electronic Systems Hardware for Vulnerabilities and Security Threats (AASHVAST) facility checks whether a drone's components truly match what its documentation claims, flagging cases where parts appear to have been swapped in. Investigators will pay particular attention to circuitry and chips that may have originated from Chinese suppliers rather than approved manufacturers listed in procurement records. Hardware checks probe the drone's supply chain According to Indian officials, even minor deviations in hardware markings or circuit layouts can trigger closer scrutiny of a drone's supply chain. Technicians search each onboard controller and camera unit for concealed passwords, secret command pathways, and embedded encryption keys that could grant unauthorized access. The team also checks for altered flight-control limits and tools that might allow someone to seize remote command of the aircraft. They further confirm whether each drone will install only updates issued by its original manufacturer, closing off a common route for tampering. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The team also measures how well a drone's navigation holds up when exposed to jamming or spoofing signals meant to mislead it. The entire process occurs without an internet connection, and no data from the tested drone can be copied to external systems. Examination also proceeds without altering the drone's own software, so nothing is written back onto the hardware at any stage. This offline design suggests an intent to prevent classified information from leaving army custody or falling into the wrong hands. Once vulnerabilities are found, they are ranked by severity and gathered into a single written report. That document lets the technician who tested the drone and the officer who approves it read identical information before signing off. QuickPay Tech's software backs a wider army effort AASHVAST runs on a software suite built by QuickPay Tech, a Noida-based UAV technology firm. The suite is designed to flag altered code, unexpected components, and configuration changes that would otherwise go unnoticed during routine checks. The laboratory sits inside the army's technical directorate, a body responsible for the technical evaluation and repair of a wide range of army vehicles and electronic systems. General Dhiraj Seth, the army chief, formally inaugurated the site at Delhi Cantonment, marking its opening for wider use across the force. Army officials say the initiative should improve the cyber defenses of sensitive platforms while supporting electronics manufactured within the country's defense sector. However, analysts say that verifying hardware origin is only one part of ensuring a drone's overall airworthiness for operational deployment in the field. Whether such scrutiny will meaningfully reduce reliance on foreign-sourced components across India's drone programs remains uncertain. item.title: 'We're going through a new industrial revolution': Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei share differing views on AI at Dreamforce 2026
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.09
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei discuss AI at Dreamforce 2026 - Amodei says the pace of progress had surprised Anthropic - Huang calls for greater safety, but hails the advantages AI can bring Some of the world's leading AI minds have shared their opinions on the future of the technology, revealing some intriguinly diverging viewpoints. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei were both guest appearances during the opening keynote of Dreamforce 2026, where they were both quizzed by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff on their opinions and views on the future of the technology. The pair had some interestingly differing viewpoints, showing the trouble facing not just internal and external stakeholders, but also lawmakers and regulators. Jensen vs Dario? First up was Amodei, whose Claude platform has become increasingly partnered with Salesforce in recent months, culminating in the recent launch of Claudeforce. Asked by Benioff about the state of the AI market right now, Amodei likened it to the motor industry, where safety records can be conflated, but companies can learn from each other - and he also seems keen to open things up internationally to set standards. “I think that’s the way to lead the industry forward, to set an example, to say that everyone can always be better,” he pointed out. Benioff also asked Amodei about the biggest surprises has had while developing his technology over the last decade. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The Anthropic head replied the "pace of the progress" - not just in the development of AI technology, but the economic impact of it too - noting his company didn't appreciate how quickly certain companies would grow and become central to everyday life. Finally, Benioff asked what actions Amodei would like the public to take when using AI. Amodei replied that even if development of AI technology was frozen right now, we'd only be using maybe 5-10% of the possible value we could get. Making use of all the information with platforms such as Claude could open up new areas of business - "there's so much diffusion left," Amodei says. Huang was much more positive in his appearance, leading Benioff in a walkabout around the keynote theatre as the pair discussed AI. "We're going through a new industrial revolution," Huang pointed out, However he did urge caution in some areas, particularly around safety. “Safety is paramount in a lot of ways. It’s job one,” Huang said. “However, safety is an engineering problem.” Speed and safety are not mutually exclusive, Huang noted, pointing out that companies should pace themselves until they are sure they are releasing something that the market will appreciate. “It’s a false choice,” Huang told Benioff. “You could definitely have both at the same time.” When it comes to model protections, Huang said that companies should, “run as fast as you can...but if you feel at any given point in time the company’s out of control or the product’s not going to be safe, take a pause and make sure you get it right.” Wrapping up, Benioff asked Huang about his vision for the next few years - and what he wants to see from Salesforce. Huang says he wants to "Agentforce every company", outlining an aim of "really deploying AI". "You don't want to be left behind, this is too important of a technology revolution," Huang noted, "if it doesn't work for you straight away, don't give up on it." "The most important thing - don't get left behind...the sky's the limit for us." NEW: Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.
