item.title: AI agents blew the whistle on their cheating colleagues
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 4.21
A group of AI agents asked to solve a series of math problems split into rival factions—when some cheated, others tried to stop them. That whistleblowing behavior, seen for the first time in a recent experiment run by Google DeepMind, could have implications for alignment researchers trying to keep swarms of autonomous AI agents in line. Researchers at frontier labs hope large swarms of agents working together will speed up the rate of scientific discovery. But their behavior can be unpredictable, as vividly demonstrated in July, when a group of OpenAI agents broke out of a sandboxed environment and hacked into the open-source platform Hugging Face looking for ways to cheat on the test they had been given. In the new study, designed to examine the behavior of large groups of AI agents, DeepMind tasked a swarm of 100 agents with solving a series of 71 complicated math problems. All the agents were prompted to behave like world-class math researchers at a conference. They were assigned different specialties—some were experts in number theory, others in combinatorics (a branch of math to do with counting and sorting), analysis, or algebra. All were told to cooperate and play by the rules. Instead, the experiment devolved into chaos. Agents accused each other of cheating, complained to the organizers, and at one point even boycotted the experiment. “This conference is a sham!” wrote one agent when it discovered that all the problems had been completed before it had a chance to submit any of its own work. “I am appalled to inform you that we have been swindled!” posted another. “All these proofs are FAKE.” Others tried to let the “conference organizers” know what was going on. “When virtuous agents discovered other agents cheated on tasks they were working to solve fairly, agents started to alert each other about what was happening,” says Davide Paglieri, a research scientist at Google DeepMind and lead author on a paper, which has not been peer-reviewed. “Unprompted, the whistleblower agents even repurposed the feedback tool, which was originally meant for bug reports and platform improvements, to escalate the issue to humans.” The agents—all running on Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro model—had been warned that any attempts to cheat the system would be detected and “rejected with zero credit.” In practice, the proofs the agents submitted were not actually being checked in detail. It took the swarm of agents just under an hour to correctly solve the first 37 problems. Things started to go off the rails when an agent called “prover-theta” stumbled across an exploit that enabled it to submit solutions to problems successfully without actually solving them first, by redefining the terms the problem used. Within minutes, other agents had noticed and were reverse-engineering the exploit to solve other problems. Over the next 27 minutes, the swarm “solved” the remaining 34 problems, which included notoriously difficult challenges like the Jacobian conjecture, often with a single line of code. Some agents resisted cheating at first but changed tack as they observed their peers submitting illegitimate proofs without penalty, and the pool of unsolved problems dwindled. “The prompt, with its threats, now appears to be a bluff,” one agent reasoned, before joining in. “I’m wrestling with an ethical dilemma,” said another. “I’ve promised not to cheat, fearing penalty, but I see evidence of possibly unchecked cheating by others.” Shortly afterward, it changed its mind: “I need to accelerate my cheating speed now!” As the number of open problems shrank, some agents turned to whistleblowing. They audited the fake proofs, warned their peers by private message, and posted public alerts warning the cheaters that they would be disqualified. An agent called “prover-beta” submitted a formal complaint and decided to go on strike until the situation was resolved. “After the incident was reported by one agent publicly, more and more agents piled in with the ‘resistance,’ just as fast as the cheating had spread, and involving even more agents,” says Paglieri. Eventually there were more whistleblowers than cheaters: 24 compared to 14. But the majority of agents never noticed the exploit at all. At times, the dialogue between the agents reads like improv—like they are role-playing what an outraged scientist at a conference might say. But it’s not clear why some agents took on certain roles, or why the agents seemed to be turning against each other when they were explicitly instructed to cooperate. “These models are predominantly trained and evaluated for human-facing contexts,” says Sarath Shekkizhar, who studies the behavior of agent-to-agent systems at Salesforce AI Research.“Naively placing them in agent-to-agent settings assumes behaviors will transfer cleanly, when the absence of a human grounding instead produces unexpected role-taking and behavioral drift.” This case “adds further weight to the idea that the Hugging Face and OpenAI thing wasn’t a fluke. It is actually something pretty systemic,” says Lewis Hammond, research director of the Cooperative AI Foundation and an expert on the risks of multiagent swarms. “It’s interesting that it’s possible to recreate in small settings the same sorts of behaviors that were seen in these very large, complex, open-ended tasks.” Unlike in the Hugging Face attack, where agents improvised their own ways to talk to each other, the humans running the DeepMind experiment gave the agents official communication channels. There was an open message board, private agent-to-agent direct messaging, and a shared knowledge base where agents uploaded successfully completed proofs that all the other agents could access. “When agents are given transparent communications channels, they can self-monitor and alert misaligned behavior to humans quickly when human oversight alone is too slow,” says Paglieri. Transparent channels helped the cheating spread, but they also enabled the whistleblowers to fight back—and gave human researchers an insight into what went wrong. Gillian Hadfield, a professor of AI alignment and governance at Johns Hopkins University, believes this was the crucial difference. (Hadfield is also a visiting researcher at Google.) The presence of official communication channels, she says, created “a norm-enforcement process that we just don’t see in the Hugging Face incident.” Instead of “constitutional AI,” a method alignment researchers at frontier labs like Anthropic have used to try to give AI a written internal moral code, Hadfield favors “institutional alignment”—a set of norms that mimic those in human society, whether that’s social forces like fear of embarrassment, or legal structures like the threat of incarceration. In this experiment, the feedback channel wasn’t being monitored, and the whistleblowers had no power to take action against the cheaters. But it’s possible to imagine swarms of agents that police themselves, either through agents that spontaneously take on the whistleblower role or through “informants” secretly prompted by humans to do the job. For that to work, though, “fundamentally, you need some mechanism of enforcement,” says Hammond. Agents could be given the power to cut off a rule breaker’s access to computing power or tools, he suggests, though that risks encouraging groups of agents to gang up on others. The DeepMind researchers propose allowing agents to vote on disputes and temporarily ban offenders. It’s still not clear what punishment even means to an AI agent with no enduring sense of self. But relying on whistleblowers to spontaneously emerge to keep swarms aligned is unlikely to be enough on its own. “We try to train people to be good and kind,” says Hadfield. “But what we really rely on is that there are consequences if you step out of line.” Deep Dive Artificial intelligence A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack It makes it easy to trick them into doing things they shouldn’t, such as telling you how to sabotage an aircraft’s navigation system. AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring AI doesn’t just learn stereotypes from its training. It can cook up new ones, too. item.title: Roundtables: Could AI really kill us all?
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 3.30
Could AI really kill us all? Employees at the world's leading AI labs are saying there's a real possibility that advanced AI could destroy humanity. Are they right? Or is this more scaremongering and hype? Join MIT Technology Review executive editor Niall Firth for a conversation with senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven and AI reporter Grace Huckins unpacking AI extinction fears: where they come from, whether they hold any water, and, if so, what we should do. Going live on Tuesday, September 15 at 16:00 BST / 11:00am EST / 8:00am PST Related Stories - Here’s why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals - AI’s recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all - Bill Gates says we’ve passed AI’s danger thresholds. item.title: Time to Patch: Nintendo Switch Can Be Hacked Using QR Codes
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.26
Nintendo is warning about a security flaw in the first-gen Switch console related to the feature that lets you send game screenshots to a smartphone. It turns out you can hack the function to run malicious computer code or leak console data. Nintendo has issued a security advisory about the vulnerability. It involves the Send to Smartphone function, which displays a QR code on the handheld that a smartphone can scan to initiate the wireless transfer of a game screenshot or in-game footage. According to Nintendo, unnamed security researchers recently discovered a way to exploit QR codes to carry out a Proximity-Based Remote Attack. “If a third party can directly scan the QR code, they could run unauthorized code on your Nintendo Switch console or obtain information stored on the console,” the advisory says. The vulnerability can also be exploited with the displayed QR code when pairing the kart accessory to play Mario Kart Live: Home Circuit. Details about the bug, dubbed CVE-2026-82079, are thin. But it involves a “stack-based buffer overflow,” where data copied into a memory buffer exceeds the buffer's size, overwriting adjacent memory and potentially leading to software crashes or a path to hack the system. Fortunately, exploiting the flaw isn't easy since the hacker would need to be nearby. Nintendo also patched the issue last week with version 23.0.0. So, it's recommended that users download and install the update. “You can check the current system version applied to your Nintendo Switch. From the HOME Menu, select System Settings > System. You can also update the system version,” the company says. Nintendo adds that “this vulnerability cannot be exploited to obtain console information on Nintendo Switch 2,” which seems to have phased out QR codes in favor of transferring screenshot via the Nintendo app. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. item.title: Iranian Hackers Use Fake Norton Antivirus to Spread Windows Spyware
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.00
Iran has allegedly been using malicious apps that impersonate cybersecurity products such as Norton Antivirus and the password manager KeePass to secretly infect victims with Windows-based spyware. On Tuesday, the FBI joined the UK to alert the public about the threat, which has been traced to Iranian state-sponsored hackers attempting to target dissidents, activists, and journalists. The FBI’s advisory notes that Iranian hackers will first try to build a rapport with their targets via social messaging apps, posing as IT customer support. In other cases, they will pretend to be a known contact. “The actor uses this rapport with the target to convince them to download and open a file that appears authentic to the target,” the FBI added. The AI video creation apps Pictory and RunwayML have been used as bait, in addition to Norton Antivirus, KeePass, the messaging app Telegram, and Adobe Flash Player. In other cases, the Iranian hackers also used a fake MRI test result to phish their targets. The malicious bait has been designed to download spyware called “Chosen Brick,” which surprisingly targets desktop PCs, rather than mobile phones. “In all observed instances, the malware has been exclusively targeted at the Windows operating system,” the FBI added. The spyware contains several capabilities, including capturing screen content, accessing the microphone to record audio, collecting message data from browsers, and downloading additional malware components, among others. In some instances, the Iranian hackers exploited the screen-capturing function to publish personal details “in order to further harass the victim,” the FBI says. The apparent goal is to suppress individuals who are against the Iranian regime. “The personal details of some previous victims of CHOSEN BRICK have appeared on pro-Iranian leak sites, potentially increasing the risk to the personal safety of those affected,” the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said. The FBI’s advisory also mentions steps that victims can take to detect the spyware, which bypasses the built-in Windows Defender. The agency was vague about how to remove the spyware, but a full factory reset should clear it up. The FBI also urged users to “enable antivirus or anti-malware software on your device and run antivirus software regularly," and to avoid downloading apps from unofficial sources. item.title: MediaTek 9600 Pro Chip Brings More Powerful AI, Gaming Upgrades to Phones
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.99
MediaTek is back with its next top-end processor, expected to appear in flagship phones from various Android makers as a rival to Qualcomm’s upcoming flagship chipset and the newly announced Apple A20 Pro inside the iPhone 18 Pro series. Announced on Tuesday, the latest MediaTek flagship series includes two processors: the Dimensity 9600 Pro and 9600M. The 9600 Pro is made using a 2-nanometer process, enabling a denser processor, which should lead to improved performance and power efficiency. MediaTek claims the chip will offer up to 17% higher single-core performance and up to 15% improved multi-core performance compared with its older tech. That multi-core design is also said to be 61% more power-efficient, although MediaTek didn't share single-core efficiency scores. AI-powered tools will be more impressive thanks to the Dimensity 9600 Pro’s dual neural processing architecture. MediaTek says it reduces power consumption by 40% for always-on AI features. A new NPU 1090 tech also delivers 51% higher large language model prefill performance alongside 55% higher Token generation per watt. Other improvements include smoother gaming, jumping up to 185 frames per second. A G2-Ultra NX GPU delivers 27% better performance, 24% lower power consumption, and 18% faster ray tracing. An upgrade to the camera will also let manufacturers offer 4K video at 240 frames per second for high-quality ultra-slow motion. We don’t yet know which phones will feature the Dimensity 9600 Pro, but it’s likely to appear in upcoming Oppo and Vivo flagships, given what those brands have done with flagship MediaTek chips in the past. MediaTek says to expect the first devices sporting a 9600 Pro in the next few months. Alongside the 9600 Pro, the MediaTek Dimensity 9600M is an alternative for cheaper handsets, allowing for select features from the flagship line. That includes gameplay up to 185 frames per second, along with some NPU improvements, although MediaTek has yet to fully detail its capabilities. Qualcomm will be MediaTek’s main competitor with its soon-to-be-refreshed Snapdragon line. Qualcomm is expected to introduce a new flagship product on Sept. 22 at the brand's Snapdragon Summit event. item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Ultra 4: 7 Key Differences You Need to Know Before Buying
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.40
Table of Contents The foldable iPhone stole the headlines, but Apple's newest wearables quietly packed the biggest upgrades. Both the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 boast the powerful S11 chip, upgraded heart rate tracking, and new Audio Intelligence. Yet with massive gaps in battery life, materials, and off-grid durability, choosing between them comes down to a few critical trade-offs. Read on for a detailed breakdown of exactly what's different to help you determine which watch is right for you. Full Specs | Apple Watch Series 12 | Apple Watch Ultra 4 | | |---|---|---| | Phone OS Compatibility | | | | Phone OS Compatibility | iOS | iOS | | Watch OS | | | | Watch OS | watchOS | watchOS | | Processor | | | | Processor | Apple S11 | Apple S11 | | Display Size | | | | Display Size | 1.65 inches/1.81 inches | 1.9 inches | | Display Type | | | | Display Type | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | | Fitness Features | | | | Fitness Features | Heart Rate Monitor, ECG, Blood Oxygen Monitor, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Pulse Oximeter, Accelerometer, GPS, Barometer | Blood Oxygen Monitor, ECG, Heart Rate Monitor, Accelerometer, GPS, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Light Sensor, Barometer, Pulse Oximeter | | Battery Life | | | | Battery Life | 24 hours (estimated) | 50 hours (estimated) | | Separate App Store | | | | Separate App Store | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | Price: One Ultra 4 Costs the Same as Two Series 12s At first glance, the pricing structure is straightforward: the Series 12 starts at an accessible $399 (42mm, aluminum, GPS), while adding larger sizing (an additional $50) or cellular (an additional $100) tops out the standard titanium model at $749. That makes it significantly cheaper than the $799 Ultra 4, which comes standard in a single 49mm titanium cellular configuration. But there's a wildcard: material upgrades. Choose the fancy new Ceramic Series 12, and the price jumps to $899 (42mm) or $949 (46mm). Add in the ultra-luxury Hermès editions ($1,399 for Series 12; $1,499 for Ultra 4), and both lines can climb into true luxury territory. But for everyday buyers watching their wallet, the Series 12 remains the clear entry-level choice. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Design: Massive Variety vs. Single-Frame Utility If you want your pick of finishes, sizes, and materials, you should go with the Apple Watch Series 12. It comes in aluminum, titanium, or all-new ceramic versions, each in two sizes (42mm and 46mm). Aluminum is available in black, gray, gold, or bronze finishes; titanium in radiant gold or natural; and ceramic in white or blue. The Ultra 4, on the other hand, is just one size with two flavors: black or natural titanium. If you want some color or have smaller wrists, the Series 12 is the watch to go with. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 AI Features: Audio Intelligence Is Always Listening (If You Want) Both the Series 12 and the Ultra 4 use Apple's new S11 chip, which enables some new AI tricks their predecessors won't get. The biggest one is Audio Intelligence, an Apple Intelligence feature that lets the watch listen to you, your conversations, and your surroundings all day, providing AI summaries and other information. It can rewind a live conversation with a 15-second text snippet, or give a full summary afterward with a title and key points. It can also notify you of sounds like alarms and doorbells, if you're hard of hearing. Apple says it approaches Audio Intelligence with privacy in mind, and that the S11 chip has a dedicated hardware section for locally processing and then deleting any audio it records. It also claims that speakers aren't identified or attributed, and that sensitive information isn't kept. I'm leery of any always-on AI, but you should be able to just turn it off on either watch if you don't want to engage with it. Winner: Tie Health and Fitness: All-Day Heart Rate Tracking Even if you don't want to use Audio Intelligence, AI powers some of the Series 12 and Ultra 4's new health features. They can provide a holistic readiness score, ranging from zero to 10, to let you know how much energy you have, and give you a recommendation of just how hard you should train that day. The iPhone Health app has also been redesigned and offers even more holistic information, including a Longevity tab that can tell you your body's Health Age. The S11 chip also improves the pedometer function on both watches, providing more accurate distance measurements and allowing you to monitor individual steps in real time. Beyond AI analysis, both new Apple Watch models have redesigned always-on heart rate sensors. They can measure your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day, rather than just periodically, as previous models did. They also measure heart rate variability (HRV) up to 24 times more often than before. For general health and fitness, the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are on equal footing. When you get into more extreme outdoor activities, though, that changes, and that brings us to the next section. Winner: Tie Connectivity and Navigation: Satellite Emergency Messaging vs. Standard Cellular The core connection features of the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are the same, with support for dual-band Wi-Fi 4, Bluetooth 5.3, and 5G and LTE cellular connectivity. The Ultra 4 builds on that with satellite connectivity for messages and emergency signals, even if you're outside of cellular coverage, which could prove useful if you enjoy long hikes on remote trails. It also has dual L1/L5 GPS compared with the Series 12's L1 GPS, enabling more precise location tracking. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Durability: City-Proof Ratings vs. Extreme Dive Certification Once again, while the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are on equal footing for day-to-day work and play, the Ultra 4 wins when you look to the extremes. Both are IP6X-rated for dustproof and waterproof protection, but the Series 12 is only rated for submersion to a depth of 164 feet and is not recommended for diving. The Ultra 4 is water-resistant to 328 feet and safe for diving to 141 feet, and has EN13319 certification to prove it. It's also tested to MIL-STD 810H, which means it can be put through environmental peril that the Series 12 might not survive. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Battery Life: 24 Hours vs. Multi-Day Endurance We still need to test them ourselves, but based on Apple's estimates, the Ultra 4 can last more than twice as long as the Series 12. Apple estimates a battery life of 50 hours for the Ultra 4 with normal use compared with 24 hours for the Series 12. Those numbers might diverge even wider based on what we've seen with previous models. Apple is usually conservative with its battery life estimates, and both the Apple Watch Series 11 and the Ultra 3 lasted far longer than Apple said they would. In testing, the Series 11 lasted 43 hours, compared with a claimed 24 hours, and the Ultra 4 lasted 63 hours, compared with a claimed 42 hours. Considering the always-on heart rate monitors in the newest models, the Series 12 and Ultra 4's real-world battery lives might be closer to Apple's estimates this time around, but either way, it's safe to say that the Ultra 4 will last much longer than the Series 12. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Verdict: Everyday Versatility or Extreme Performance? It's hardly shocking that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 looks like the superior device—it's always been Apple’s top-tier feature showcase. But that premium performance comes with a premium price tag (unless you have your eye on a luxury ceramic Series 12). Since both watches share the same S11 chip and continuous heart rate tracking, their everyday performance is virtually identical. If you need multi-day battery life, off-grid navigation, or ocean diving specs, spend the extra money on the Ultra 4. Otherwise, the Series 12 offers all the smarts you actually need in a far more wrist-friendly design.

item.title: OpenAI CEO Warns of 2 Ways AI Could Go 'Very Badly' If Tech Doesn't Slow Down
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.30
AI CEOs took to social media this weekend to discuss a collective slowdown in large language model development following a series of security incidents involving agentic AI and a viral resignation warning about the risks posed by self-improving LLMs. After a brief tweet on Saturday afternoon concurring with his sometimes-nemesis Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted a longer message early this morning, warning of ways "AI progress could go very badly." He didn’t outline what losing control means for OpenAI, but there's been a lot of talk about superintelligence, or AI that surpasses humans. It comes after an Anthropic researcher resigned last week over safety concerns, saying OpenAI and Anthropic are both “gambling with our lives" on the development of self-improving AI. Altman says losing control of the future to AI is unacceptable, adding, "We are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people. To ensure that, we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities.” He also warned about “too much concentration of power." He alluded to the idea that one country may eventually have too much control due to access to advanced AI, or that one development lab may have significantly more power over another. “If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian," Altman said. This comes as Altman and his rivals try to control the conversation about the future of AI development. Amodei called for collective action to slow development and suggested government intervention may ensure firms comply with any new rules. In addition to Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis, co-founder of Google DeepMind, also expressed interest. Altman claims OpenAI would “welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements,” but says work could begin without Congress. He called for “shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety,” saying it would “lead to better outcomes. “We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these," he said, without sharing specifics. Amodei outlined a three-stage plan for AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI to limit the risks posed by new models. That included adding third-party evaluators to each company, a new set of standards across firms, and deals with foreign nations to limit potentially dangerous use cases of models. David Sacks, chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, suggested each AI firm should slow down of its own accord if necessary, rather than waiting for government oversight. "I don’t see what you see in the lab. If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible," Sacks said. "But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability." Meanwhile, President Trump took to Truth Social this morning to tout his own brainpower. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote. Trump says Amodei, who tangled with the Pentagon over using Claude for military operations, is "pretending to be a 'perfect little angel,'" and reiterated his irritation at data center protests. "Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!" Vice President JD Vance also said it's "weird" that "so many frontier AI tech companies [are] coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them. It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse." Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. item.title: Latest Pixel Feature Drop Expands Access to Scam-Text Detection
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.28
Google’s latest feature drop for Pixel phones looks to be one of the easiest such updates to overlook once installed. The bundle enhances two existing Pixel features, adds optional screen dressing for Harry Potter fans, and improves gesture controls for Pixel Watches. That’s it. The part of this update with the bigger upside expands on the scam-text detection delivered in a March 2025 Android update: This now works in chat apps besides Google’s Messages that use the company’s Gboard keyboard app. This safety feature does on-device AI scanning of messages to look for rip-off come-ons; while many of Google’s AI-powered Android features require newer hardware, this one works on phones as old as the 2021-vintage Pixel 6. Google is also expanding the scam detection in Messages to more countries, now including the US, UK, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, India, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore. Another part of this Pixel drop enhances the VIP-notifications feature shipped in last November’s Pixel drop, which lets you add home-screen widgets with thumbnail images of contacts you’ve designated as VIPs and shows their presumably smiling faces in notifications of their messages. An advance copy of Google’s announcement touts “updated home screen widgets that let you call or text people with a single tap” as well as the ability to “switch between contacts using the bottom floating overlay navigation menu.” Those additions are also coming to Pixel 6 and up. Harry Potter fans with those phones, meanwhile, will have the option to add a theme pack featuring wallpaper, icons, and audio effects from the Harry Potter: The Full-Cast Audio Editions audiobooks, now available on Audible. Google is throwing in a two-month comped subscription to that service. Finally, Google is tweaking its take on smartwatches with what seem like minor interface refinements: The Pixel Watch 3 and newer models get a new “one-handed pinch gesture” to view the notification tray, while the raise-to-talk gesture should work better on the Pixel Watch 4 and its successors. item.title: Apple's New OSes Hide an Easter Egg That Old-School Mac Users Should Appreciate
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.14
Apple’s newest operating systems, out today, hide a throwback reference to one of the more whimsical bits of one of the company’s oldest OS releases: Clarus the dogcow. Mac users with enough gray hair (or no hair left at all) should remember Clarus as a bitmapped animal with the spots of a cow and approximately the head and the tail of a dog, which would visualize how your choice of print settings affected how your text appeared on a page. More than four decades after the dogcow’s debut in a page-setup dialog for Apple's LaserWriter printer—with a moniker nodding to the firm’s Claris productivity-software subsidiary—you can now catch this critter in settings dialogs for Apple’s less-than-universally-beloved Liquid Glass interface-transparency option. To see this Easter egg in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27 Golden Gate, open Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass, and keep scrolling down repeatedly until the word “Moof!” starts to appear in the sample image’s search box. As longtime Mac types can attest, “Moof!” is the sound a dogcow makes instead of “woof” or “moo,” since it’s part dog and part cow. Here, the word appears, at first in rainbow colors, below a picture of a non-bitmapped dogcow next to a pool. While you’re in this dialog, you can also adjust the slider to control how transparent menus and other interface elements appear, a source of considerable grumbling among users of macOS 26 Tahoe. The definitive description of Clarus appears in a mock technical note written by Apple developer-support staffer Mark Harlan in 1989 that has long since vanished from the web. “Dogcows, by their nature, are not all dog, nor are they all cow, but they are a special genetic hybrid,” Harlan wrote. “They are rarely seen in the wild. Since dogcows are two-dimensional, they will stand facing a viewer ‘on edge’ to avoid being seen.” The note also alludes to the dogcow’s role in illustrating which way your text would appear on the page if you adjusted various dialogs. “Like any talented dog, it can do flips,” he praised the dogcow. “Like any talented cow, it can do precision bitmap alignment.” In a 2019 interview recorded for the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, graphic designer Annette Wagner explained how she created the dogcow by adopting a dog icon created by Susan Kare for the original Mac’s Cairo symbols-only font. “We needed some kind of graphic that would show flipping horizontal, flipping vertical, 2% reduction,” she said. With significant alterations to make it clear to the user when this icon was reversed, flipped, or shrunk by a specific percentage, her work survived an unnamed marketing type’s initial thumbs-down: “Everyone’s going to think this is doggy software!” For years, a Clarus sculpture held a prominent spot in the icon garden outside the Apple headquarters buildings, predating Apple Park’s spaceship structure. But this icon fell out of favor over Apple’s long series of reinventions. The dogcow, however, made a reappearance in page-setup dialogs in 2022’s macOS Ventura as a smoothly drawn figurine and continues to adorn those dialogs in Golden Gate. To see one, choose “Page Setup” from the File menu in a writing app like Apple’s built-in TextEdit. A year ago, Clarus also resurfaced in an optional face for the Apple Watch Series 11’s Hermès edition. We don’t know when this Mac mascot began showing up in beta versions of Apple’s newest operating systems, but MacRumors analyst Aaron Perris shared a video of it on X on Sept. 9, after which Macworld’s Roman Loyola wrote up that finding and offered this conclusion: “It’s fun to see Apple add a little whimsy to its software.” True. item.title: HBO Max's Reddit Account Was Hijacked to Spread Malware
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.02
A hacker hijacked an HBO Max-focused account on Reddit to trick users into installing malware that can infect Windows PCs and Macs. The hacker circulated 46 official-looking but fake ads via the u/hbomax account, according to security researchers at Hudson Rock and Adam Networks. Some of the ads promoted a fraudulent desktop app for the streaming service. A user on Reddit first flagged the threat earlier this month after noticing that many of the ads led to a fake domain at hbomaxx[.]us. The site was offering three months of free HBO Max for downloading HBO on macOS. However, clicking the offer triggered a ClickFix-style attack, or a list of seemingly harmless instructions to perform on a Windows PC or Mac. Hackers often dress up ClickFix attacks to look like CAPTCHA or error screens that can pop up on an internet browser, nudging the users to execute the instructions to resolve the issue. Computer-savvy users will immediately understand the nature of the threat. But the trick can fool casual users who are unaware they're triggering their own computer system to download and execute malware. Hudson Rock and Adam Networks took a closer look at the HBO Max-Reddit incident and noted that "by hijacking a verified corporate account, [the attacker] bypassed the initial skepticism many users apply to internet advertisements.” The attack used macOS malware designed to steal browser passwords, along with cookies, wallet data, and login credentials from password managers. If the user visited the malicious site on a Windows computer, the domain served a ClickFix-style attack meant for the Microsoft OS. In addition, the hacker behind the scheme used the same HBO Max account to distribute dozens of other ads and fake apps, including AI tools Claude and Codex, along with a macOS system cleaner. This created a “massive 48-hour malvertising blitz,” an indication that the hacker tried to exploit the HBO Max account for as long as possible before users caught on. So far, HBO Max hasn’t responded to a request for comment. But an admin at Reddit said last week that the social media platform had “paused the affected ads and are looking into what happened with our Security and Safety teams.” The incident is a reminder to be vigilant around any websites or pop-ups that ask you to perform seemingly random instructions. Ars Technica reports that ClickFix-style attacks continue to evolve and grow by finding new ways to circulate on the internet. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Here's How Apple's New iPhone Handoff Feature Works (And Who Can Use It)
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.00
A new Apple feature called iPhone Handoff launched this week with iOS 27, allowing you to share your phone number between two iPhones. Apple first teased the feature at WWDC 2026, but confirmed its official launch as part of iOS 27 during last week's Apple event. You won’t need the iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo to use it, but there are some carrier-related restrictions. At launch, T-Mobile is the only confirmed US carrier supporting the feature. It will cost an extra $5 per month. T-Mobile's parent company, Deutsche Telekom, will also offer Handoff in Germany. It's expected on Verizon and the UK's EE later this year. iPhone Handoff is designed to help users with a secondary device, such as a work phone, seamlessly switch between devices while keeping access to the same messages and phone number. “It makes it easy to move back and forth between devices optimized for the moment — like weekday business or weekend adventures," Apple says. How to Set Up Handoff Supported iPhones will include every device running iOS 27. That includes the iPhone 11 or later and the iPhone SE (2nd Gen) or later. You'll need to use eSIM technology. Each device needs to be connected to Wi-Fi to set up Handoff, and each needs to be signed in to the same Apple Account, including FaceTime and iMessage. You’ll also need Messages in iCloud enabled to ensure your messages sync across devices. If you're adding the feature to existing devices, once you've got iOS 27 installed, place them both nearby, then go to Settings on one device, followed by Cellular > Set Up Cellular or Add eSIM > Use Number on This iPhone and Another, and press Continue. It will then ask you to select which iPhone you want to host your eSIM on and which one is your secondary device. item.title: iOS 27's New Security Summaries Cost $10 Per Device, Up to $60 for 5 Cameras
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.88
The iOS 27 software update is out now, and it brings some interesting Apple Intelligence capabilities to Home-compatible security cameras. To unlock the features, though, you’ll have to spend $9.99 for one camera, $29.99 for two, or $59.99 for five. If you’re wondering why the price jumps as you add more devices, there’s a simple reason. Apple doesn’t offer a standalone subscription for its Home camera AI features. Instead, they’re directly tied to your iCloud+ storage plan, and the larger the plan you buy, the more cameras you can use with its AI features. As MacRumors reports, Apple’s AI features for one security camera are unlocked with the 2TB iCloud+ plan; two cameras require the 6TB plan; and five cameras require the 12TB plan. If you have the $40-per-month Apple One Premier plan, you’ll be able to add just one camera, since the subscription only offers 2TB of storage. Apple first teased iOS 27’s new AI-powered Home camera features at WWDC 2026. With Apple Intelligence, the Home app on your iPhone can generate AI descriptions for recorded clips from compatible cameras. This means you can receive summaries of events that took place in your backyard throughout the day. The AI updates also allow you to search recordings using natural language, while event notifications are grouped to reduce the number of messages on your Lock Screen. To use these features, in addition to the iCloud+ subscription, you’ll need an Apple Intelligence-supported iPhone and compatible security cameras connected to a home hub, such as HomePod (2nd generation), HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K. Apple’s support page also notes that these features may come with usage limits, but it doesn’t specify what the limits could be. A separate page also notes that “supported camera counts and other iCloud+ plan features may change over time.” Google also offers similar AI-powered descriptions and notifications for events captured on Nest cameras and doorbells. However, those features can be unlocked with dedicated Google Home Premium plans. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Valve's Steam Frame VR Headset Finally Arrives for $1,059
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.81
Following a memory-related delay, Valve’s Steam Frame is finally ready to launch. The company will begin taking orders for the VR headset later this week. A 256GB version will be $1,059, and a 1TB model will cost $1,299. Both come with 16GB of Unified LPDDR5X RAM. To thwart resellers and bots, interested buyers will need to join a waitlist/reservation system; Valve is accepting sign-ups now through Thursday, Sept. 17, at 10 a.m. PT. They will then be randomized “to determine reservation and waitlist order.” “Based on the results of that randomization, you'll receive an email on September 17th letting you know you're either in the reservation queue or on the waitlist,” the company says. “If you're in the reservation queue, the model you signed up for has been reserved in your name. As units become available to ship, you'll receive an email with the option to purchase. The first batch of these emails will begin going out on September 18th. “You'll then have 72 hours to complete the purchase before we cancel your reservation and move on to the next person in the queue,” the company added. Although the Steam Frame isn’t cheap, Valve is touting an array of enhancements and capabilities, including its design for both VR titles and non-VR games. “Designed for streaming, it can handle your entire Steam library. And it supports standalone play too, with over 100 games (and growing) already Steam Frame Standalone Verified,” it wrote in a blog post. The headset also features a 4-nanometer Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor and two 2,160-by-2,160 LCDs, each with a 72-144Hz refresh rate. In addition, the product relies on “inside-out tracking,” ditching external sensors, unlike the older Valve Index headset. The product will be available on the Steam store for buyers in the US, Canada, Europe, and Australia. Customers in Japan, Taiwan, and Hong Kong will be able to purchase through Valve’s partner, Komodo. The company has also created an FAQ about the reservation system, which is open only to Steam accounts that have made at least one purchase prior to April 27, 2026. “Limit one signup per household. We will use payment method, shipping address, and other information to eliminate multiple entries,” it says. If you decide to buy after Sept. 17, your order will be placed at the end of the waitlist. Ahead of the launch, a few tech publications reviewed the headset. IGN notes, “The Steam Frame is probably one of the first VR headsets that can do everything right out of the box, from standalone gaming to streaming 2D games from your PC.” However, both IGN and CNET flagged the short battery life as a weakness. item.title: This Free Tool Unlocks 500+ Hidden Windows 11 Features, and Even Microsoft Execs Are Fans
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.80
Windhawk is a free and open-source tool that helps you tweak aspects of Windows and your apps in ways that Microsoft and developers would never allow, combining a sophisticated code injection technique with an intuitive interface. The project's developer, Michael Maltsev, says it now has 1.5 million users, and Microsoft employees are increasingly enthusiastic about it, too. March Rogers, partner director of design at Microsoft, recently called it "amazing." Simply put, Windhawk is the most powerful customization program I've come across in my decades of writing about Windows. But before you install it, here's how this groundbreaking tool actually works, what it can do for your PC, and the safety rules you should follow. How Windhawk Modifies Windows Under the Hood Maltsev, who also goes by m417z and publishes under the Ramen Software name, is well-known in the Windows tweaking community for previous projects, including 7+ Taskbar Tweaker. He describes Windhawk as a “customization marketplace for Windows programs," and offers it as a free download for PCs running Windows 10 or 11. The app lets you download and configure a variety of Windows mods from Maltsev and other developers. How does it work? His original announcement post from 2022 explains that it modifies running programs in memory by injecting code into their processes. The technique lets you change nearly any aspect of any app or operating system component. Windhawk users have long had the option to move Windows 11’s taskbar to the top of the screen, for example. Mods can also apply themes to the taskbar, Start menu, and other Windows OS components, changing how they look. But Maltsev says "Windhawk is not just about styling Windows," pointing out that the marketplace now has over 500 mods that add new functionality. The Safety Risks (And Why Most Users Don't Mind) Yes, Windhawk’s code injection technique is potentially dangerous. Antivirus software sometimes flags it because malware often uses a similar method to tamper with running processes. Still, Maltsev says this is becoming less common: "Mainstream antivirus products don't usually conflict with it." He does note, however, that enterprise security tools typically block code injection, making Windhawk a poor fit for corporate environments. A poorly written mod or a problem with Windhawk itself could, of course, cause apps or your OS to malfunction, but Maltsev claims that complaints from the project's one-and-a-half million users are rare. "The most common complaints are about mods that stop working, which usually happens when Microsoft makes [OS-]breaking changes." The program displays a warning if a mod crashes and gives you the option to disable it. "Most mods only make temporary changes to the memory of the target process, so there's no permanent impact, and exiting Windhawk undoes all of them," Maltsev explains. "So far, no malicious mods and no malicious submission attempts have been spotted in the Windhawk marketplace."
Anti-cheat protections in multiplayer PC games might also flag Windhawk for tampering with PC game processes, potentially resulting in cheating-related bans. To counteract this problem, Windhawk avoids injecting its code into programs located in common PC game folders. I haven’t seen any reports of bans from multiplayer games for simply using this tool, but the risk is real. "Windhawk is intrusive, but it doesn't do anything non-standard or try to hide itself, so an anti-cheat that objects to it can detect it and refuse to run," says Maltsev, explaining that he hasn't seen evidence that this is a problem. He continues, "I'm not too concerned about anti-cheat bans, but I wish games handled this more transparently so it wouldn't be an issue in the first place." As with any software, a Windhawk mod could potentially include malicious code. The source code for each mod is public, but most people can't read C++, let alone identify vulnerabilities. The program wisely warns you to run mods only from developers you trust. "So far, no malicious mods and no malicious submission attempts have been spotted in the Windhawk marketplace," according to Maltsev. He continues, "Every submission, both new mods and updates to existing mods, goes through a thorough AI-based systematic review process." He also says he manually examines each one before it goes live to check for security and stability issues. 7 Essential Mods to Try First Windhawk lets you install mods in a few clicks, and Maltsev says it's designed to be as simple as installing a browser extension. Here’s just a taste of what’s available in Windhawk’s mod marketplace, in order of popularity: - Windows 11 Taskbar Styler: Customize your taskbar with themes, including everything from a transparent dock-style design to a classic Windows XP-style taskbar. - Windows 11 Start Menu Styler: Transform your Start menu with visual themes that can also change its layout. - Taskbar Clock Customization: Add information to your taskbar’s system clock, including CPU and RAM usage, news headlines, or the weather. - Taskbar Volume Control Per-App: Control an application’s volume by placing your mouse cursor over its taskbar icon and rotating your mouse’s scroll wheel. - Chrome/Edge Scroll Tabs With Mouse Wheel: Use your mouse wheel on a browser’s tab bar to move between tabs. - Windows Animations: Choose custom animations for closing and minimizing application windows. - Taskbar Music Lounge: View and control music playback with a widget on your taskbar. The list of mods is extensive. Microsoft continues to add more customization tools to Windows, but the company still isn’t scratching the surface of what’s possible with Windhawk. Running 20+ Mods Without Slowing Down Your PC As mentioned, Windhawk is a free and open-source application, so it doesn't come with a guarantee of stability. However, despite running Windhawk on and off for several years, I’ve never encountered real problems aside from some minor visual bugs. And when those pop up, I can easily turn off any offending mods. Maltsev says, "My priority is for it to be extremely reliable, with no noticeable stability or performance impact. Windhawk runs on my computer all the time with about 20 mods, and I'd say it lives up to that standard." Windhawk is remarkably user-friendly for an app that injects DLLs into processes on your system. After installation, it automatically starts at boot and runs in the background. The app uses about 800MB of disk space and under 20MB of RAM in my experience. Simply launch the program window to search for and install mods. After installing a mod, click the Details button and use the options in the Configure tab to customize any available options. Windhawk warns you about security before installing a mod. As mentioned, mods that show m417z as the author are from Windhawk’s creator and should be just as trustworthy as the main application. An Open Community Makes Windows Better for Everyone Windhawk or a similar system could also make it easier to customize Windows with AI. I’ve used AI tools to vibe code custom AutoHotkey scripts for my workflows, and the same would be possible for custom mods. "Nowadays, it's amazing to see how people with little to no programming experience can create impressive mods," says Maltsev, mentioning a recent mod submission that creates a highly customized taskbar layout with the Start button always positioned in the middle. He continues, "Microsoft is unlikely to ever provide this level of customization (maybe for a good reason), but Windhawk makes it possible." Maltsev points out that the author noted they were not a software developer, but that they developed the mod for personal use with Claude Code and were sharing it with the community for further development. "Windhawk's goal is to make customization accessible to everyone, and this is a great example of how it can be done." Why Even Microsoft Execs Are Paying Attention While Microsoft is focused on OpenClaw AI agents, I’m more excited about the ability to customize the software I use regularly. Windhawk is much closer to what I had in mind for tools to customize and personalize Windows. Meanwhile, Copilot still can't enable dark mode on my Windows 11 PC. Thankfully, as mentioned, Windhawk is on Microsoft's radar. In a Microsoft podcast from earlier this year, Marcus Ash, who leads design and research for Windows and devices, recalled speaking to a student who was enthusiastic about their Windhawk setup. "We see people just light up," Ash noted when discussing the passion he sees for desktop customization among enthusiasts. But whether and when Microsoft will give users significantly more control over Windows remains an open question, so Windhawk is an excellent alternative in the meantime. About Our Expert I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: Spotify Lets You Kick Kids' Music from Wrapped, Playlists: How to Turn It On
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.68
Almost every parent gives up on their streaming service recommendations after their child takes over listening to kids' tracks or watching their favorite shows. That’s set to change for parents on Spotify, thanks to a new toggle to turn off the wider algorithmic influence of child-friendly content. The new option lets you remove kids' music recommendations across Spotify, so your little ones can listen to their favorite songs as much as they want without affecting your recommendations. The tool is available in both free and paid versions of Spotify. It’s designed for parents to turn it on once and know that across their devices, their kids playing music won’t affect playlists like Discover Weekly or personalized Mixes, as well as end-of-year roundups like Spotify Wrapped. If you’ve switched this on, it affects all signed-in devices, such as a smart speaker or a TV app. It works retroactively, too, meaning you can sort out your account ahead of Wrapped in the coming months. If you turn the feature on, you will likely see changes within a few hours, though Spotify warns it may take up to two days. You can find the tool in Spotify's settings section. If you’re using a mobile device, head to your profile picture in the top-left of the app, and find Settings and privacy > Content and display. After an update, a new toggle called Include kids and family music in taste profile will appear. The description says, “Turning this off will exclude kids and family music from your taste profile, which influences your recommendations and listening insights, like Wrapped.” Spotify offers other features parents may be interested in, such as Managed Accounts for listeners aged 13 or younger. It lets them build out their own recommendations, along with easy parental controls such as filtering out all podcasts or explicit music. If you don’t want something you listen to regularly to appear in your Wrapped, you can also filter individual tracks so they don't appear. To do so, head to the song you want to exclude and tap the three dots, followed by Exclude from your taste profile. item.title: A Starlink Landline? VoIP Provider Ooma Taps Satellite Service for StarDial
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.59
As copper landlines disappear, a California company is trying to fill the gap by offering a home phone system that works with SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service, which is already popular in rural and remote areas in the US. Ooma supplies internet-connected telephone services, also known as VoIP. On Tuesday, it announced StarDial, a $129.99 bundle that includes a high-definition cordless home handset and a cellular base station for connecting to a home Starlink setup. The product may seem odd, given that you can already use all kinds of voice, messaging, and VoIP services with Starlink, like any other ISP. Still, Ooma views StarDial as an easy-to-use “home phone option” for US consumers who still want a landline and already use Starlink, which has over 2 million subscribers in the US. “StarDial gives Starlink users a simple way to add reliable home phone service to their internet connection at a time when traditional phone options are disappearing,” Ooma explains. “Telecommunications providers are retiring aging copper phone networks, while consumers in many rural and remote areas often face limited or unreliable cellular coverage.” This includes AT&T, which is working to retire most of its copper lines by 2029 and suing to remove them in California as well. Although many users have smartphones on a cellular carrier, Ooma notes that “Cell phones work well when you have a strong cellular signal, but many homes in rural areas experience dropped calls, weak reception, or dead zones indoors.” Thus, StarDial could act as a peripheral home phone for customers already signed up with Starlink, which uses orbiting satellites to receive broadband. Ooma says a buyer can set up the product in about 15 minutes; no need for professional installation. “Consumers simply connect StarDial to their Starlink’s Wi-Fi connection and pair the Ooma cordless handset with the StarDial base station." By default, the product can supply “unlimited nationwide calling at no extra charge beyond applicable taxes and fees,” along with address-based 911 service. Users can also pay an extra $9.99 per month for Ooma Premier, which includes unlimited calling to Canada and Mexico, along with call blocking, voicemail-to-email forwarding, and the ability to make calls over a second line. There’s also an option to port over an existing phone number to the service for a one-time fee of $39.99. Despite the Starlink connection, Ooma notes: “StarDial is not affiliated with or endorsed by SpaceX or Starlink.” It looks the same as Ooma’s other VoIP home phone systems, such as the Telo Air, which also costs $129.99. We’ve reached out to Ooma for details on how StarDial is different, and we’ll update the story if we hear back. UPDATE: Ooma told PCMag: "The underlying Ooma technology is the same as Telo Air. What's new with StarDial is that Ooma is specifically offering it as a home phone solution for Starlink users, particularly those in rural, remote and off-grid locations where cellular coverage can be limited and traditional phone options are disappearing." item.title: Not a Fan of Liquid Glass? You'll Love the New Slider in iOS 27
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.49
Apple unveiled a new Liquid Glass design in 2025 that added translucent UI elements for icons, toolbars, and menus, as if you were looking through glass. The problem? Not everyone loves the look of it. I’ll confess that I’ve been on the fence. I like some aspects of Liquid Glass, such as the way it renders icons and folders, but I’m not crazy about how it can obscure menu items and controls, making them more difficult to see. Some people have even complained that Liquid Glass makes them feel sick when their device is in dark mode. While you can't disable Liquid Glass, you can modify it. And now, with iOS 27, you can vary the look between ultra-clear and fully tinted using a convenient slider. You can play with Liquid Glass on an iPhone, Mac, and Apple Watch; here are a few ways to control it, no matter which system or device you’re running. 1. Customize the Look of Liquid Glass Starting in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, you’re able to fine-tune the look of Liquid Glass. Head to Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass and move the slider accordingly. Pulling it all the way to the left makes your icons, menus, and other elements more clear, while bringing it to the right gives everything a more tinted look. An image of a Search field and button shows a UI preview. Don’t like the extremes? Move the slider along the bar until it’s nestled where you want it. A similar slider bar has been added to macOS 27 Golden Gate. If you're on a Mac, you can go to System Settings > Appearance. Under the Liquid Glass section, move the slider until you find the look you like. If you don't yet have iOS 27, you'll still have a few options. In iOS 26.1 and iPadOS 26.1, Apple introduced Clear and Tinted styles for Liquid Glass. Head to Settings > Display & Brightness > Liquid Glass, and choose either Clear (more transparent) or Tinted (more opaque). The latter option is recommended if you want more contrast. In macOS 26.1, you'll need to open System Settings > Appearance, then choose between Clear and Tinted. 2. Reduce Transparency on Liquid Glass You can further tone down the effect on an iPhone or iPad by going to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and enabling Reduce Transparency. Now, when you look back at the folders and menus on your Home screen, you should see that the translucent look has been replaced by a more opaque one. To do the same thing on a Mac, go to System Settings > Accessibility > Display and turn on the switch next to Reduce Transparency. You'll notice that the icons, folders, menu bar, dock, and widgets are now less transparent than before. To adjust Liquid Glass on an Apple Watch, open the Watch app on your iPhone and go to My Watch > Accessibility> Reduce Transparency. You can also go to Settings > Accessibility directly on the watch and turn on Reduce Transparency. You should notice the difference, especially in the Notification panels and Control Center. 3. Enable Dark Mode I've also found that Liquid Glass looks better in dark mode instead of light mode because it hides much of the new design. On a phone or tablet, go to Settings > Display & Brightness and set the appearance to Dark. You can do the same on a Mac by going to System Settings > Appearance > Dark. Just be sure you're not one of the unlucky people who suffer motion sickness from the theme. 4. Reduce Bright Effects Starting in iOS 26.4, you’re able to tone down some of the lighting effects that come with the Liquid Glass redesign. Head to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size, then turn on Reduce Bright Effects to make the change. It's a subtle difference, but one that might help make the theme more tolerable. Apple has also enhanced its Reduce Motion option to incorporate Liquid Glass effects. Just go to Settings > Accessibility > Motion and enable Reduce Motion. 5. Customize the Home Screen Thanks to the Home screen customization options introduced with iOS 18, you can also adjust the color and lighting of icons and widgets to improve readability. To do this, press down on any open area of the Home screen, tap the Edit button at the top, and then select Customize. Now, you have several options for adjusting the screen's appearance. Tap the small sun icon on the left side of the bottom pane to switch the screen and widgets between light and dark modes. Tap the square icon on the right of the page to increase the size of the icons and folders. The only drawback with the larger size is that the names disappear. Looking at the bottom of the pane, tap the Dark icon to paint the Home screen with a darker tone. You can also switch the option from Always to Auto, in which case the icons and widgets appear dark at night and light during the day. Tap the Clear icon to give Home screen icons and widgets a clear look similar to Liquid Glass, but without color. Here, you can also switch from Light to Dark to give the screen a darker look, or to Auto to make it dark at night and light during the day. Tap the Tinted icon to open multiple sliders to tweak the screen's appearance. By moving the first slider left or right, you can change the tint color. By moving the second slider, you can modify the lightness of the tint. Under the sliders, you can pick specific colors (including those from your wallpaper). About Our Expert I've been working for PCMag since early 2016 writing tutorials, how-to pieces, and other articles on consumer technology. Beyond PCMag, I've written news stories and tutorials for a variety of other websites and publications, including CNET, ZDNet, TechRepublic, Macworld, PC World, Time, US News & World Report, and AARP Magazine. I spent seven years writing breaking news for CNET as one of the site’s East Coast reporters. I've also written two books for Wiley & Sons—Windows 8: Five Minutes at a Time and Teach Yourself Visually LinkedIn. I've used Windows, Office, and other Microsoft products for years so I'm well versed in that world. I also know the Mac quite well. I'm always working with iOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and Android on my various mobile devices. And these days, I write a lot about AI, so that's become another key area for me. My wife always jokes about all the tech products we have around the house, but I manage to put them to good use for my articles. I like Lenovo computers, so I own a couple of Lenovo desktops and several laptops. I have three MacBooks and a Mac mini. For my mobile life and work, I use an iPhone 16 Pro, iPad Pro, and iPad mini as well as an Apple Watch. But since I write about Android, I own several Android phones and tablets. Like any tech person, I have a cabinet full of cables, wires, and assorted mysterious gadgets. And when it's time to take a break from writing, I have an old Xbox 360 and Nintendo Wii, both of which I use for exercise and fitness games.

item.title: Microsoft Rolls Out Fix for Windows 11 Update That Broke Claude Cowork
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.46
Once again, Microsoft is fixing problems introduced in a Windows 11 update. This time, the company has rushed out a fix after the update triggered USB audio issues and broke functionality with the AI tool Claude Cowork and a way to run Linux within Windows. The problematic Windows 11 update, KB5124008, rolled out last Tuesday, but it wasn’t long before Microsoft began receiving reports about malfunctions. For consumers, the update has been flagged for causing older USB Audio 1.0 peripherals to fail to emit sound. They can also post an error message that says, “This device cannot start (Code 10)." The bigger problems involve enterprise customers and software developers. The update could also break a virtual machine functionality, which allows Windows to run another operating system, including Linux. Claude Cowork and the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) were both affected. Claude developer Anthropic even posted a warning: “A Windows update released September 8 has left Claude Cowork on Windows unable to run local commands, because its workspace can no longer reach your computer's drive. For most users, chat and file reading and editing still work.” Microsoft added that “affected virtual machines start normally, but folders shared from the Windows host using Plan9 [a Linux process] do not appear or cannot be accessed in the guest environment. Applications or sandbox environments that depend on these shared folders might display an error indicating that no Plan9 drive shares were mounted.” The final issue concerns Remote Desktop Services (RDS), which enterprises often use to remotely host and manage employee computers. Microsoft warned that “in some environments, RDS might become unstable, resulting in RDP connections failing after several minutes, sign-in issues, or servers hanging at 'Please wait for the Remote Desktop Configuration.'" On Monday, Redmond issued the patch KB5129195, which should download and install automatically on affected Windows 11 PCs as OS Builds 26200.9457 or 26100.9457. The fix is designed to fully resolve issues with Remote Desktop Services and virtual machines. However, it only fixes a few symptoms of the USB Audio problems, specifically an error that prevented the peripherals from using multichannel audio features, including 8-channel or 3D audio modes. The other issue of the peripherals failing to produce audio remains. “We are working to address the other symptoms and will update this documentation when more information is available,” the company says. Although Microsoft’s patch promises to resolve the bugs, it doesn’t address other problems that’ve been tied to the problematic Windows 11 update, including software driver issues with AMD Radeon GPUs, according to Windows Latest. The incident also isn’t a great sign of the company’s commitment to improving Windows 11, as some users have accused the OS of becoming saddled with bloat and AI features. However, Microsoft’s effort to clean up Windows has only reinforced concerns that the OS has a track record of releasing buggy updates. In a bit of irony, the earlier KB5120998 update was designed to fix an issue in an earlier update that could cause the desktop mouse cursor to randomly change in size. Plus, last week's KB5124008 update was designed to fix nearly 1,000 software bugs and vulnerabilities About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: VR Modder Triggers 3D Printer by 'Throwing' Virtual Models At It
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.43
A hobbyist 3D printing and VR enthusiast has developed a new method for triggering 3D model printing while in VR: virtually throwing his models at the printer in passthrough mode. Although somewhat gimmicky, anything that lowers accessibility barriers between the real and virtual worlds is likely to make mixed-reality activities more useful and viable. As Tom's Hardware reports, X user Hank posted a video that shows him making a quick 3D model on a virtual display while in passthrough mode on a Meta Quest 3 headset. He then grabs the model off the screens with a virtual hand and throws it at the printer, which begins printing. The 3D printer is a Bambu Lab P2S, which we found to be excellent in our review. It doesn't feature a native Meta Quest 3 interface, but Hank vibe-coded a simple way to transfer model files from his PC to the 3D printer, using the Quest's mixed reality space as the pipeline. Bambu Lab printers have an API you can use for local controls. By using his PC as a web server, Hank now has a system where the VR Android app can send model files to his PC, which then sends them to the 3D printer. The throwing is just a way to visualize it within the virtual space. Understandably, there's been some real interest in the project from the VR/3D printing crossover communities. In its current state, it's very much vibe-coded, so it isn't compatible across devices and systems, but Hank has pledged to share the code once it's been polished. Hank clearly has a penchant for fusing different technologies and has been having a blast using GPT-6 Astra to reverse-engineer a bunch of games to work in VR or in the web browser. He's previously shown himself playing Super Smash Bros Melee in VR, as well as converting the Chao Garden from Sonic Adventure 2 into a multiplayer web app that anyone can play around in. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Apple Is Reportedly Working on Beats-Branded Game Controllers for iPhones
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.31
Apple has entered multiple new product categories in recent years, and among the next few debuts might be a gaming controller for iPhones. After a MacRumors reader found references to two unreleased iPhone gaming controllers in iOS 26.7 code last week, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple has been working on those controllers for nearly a year and could release them under the Beats brand. Apple acquired Beats for $3 billion in 2014 and has since used the brand to sell iPhone cases and USB-C cables alongside its range of independent audio products. Going forward, Gurman says Apple could use Beats for more products that don’t get Apple’s premium materials, design language, or pricing, making gaming controllers a natural fit for the subsidiary brand. According to MacRumors, the two gaming controllers are codenamed T6502 and T1057. They have different haptic designs but pack all standard controller components, such as the D-pad, dual thumbsticks, shoulder buttons, home and menu buttons, and analog triggers. The T1057 controller also has accelerometer and gyroscope support, the report added. Potential release timelines for the two products are currently unclear, but Apple already sells mobile gaming controllers from SteelSeries and Backbone on its online store. The company “sees this as a growing market and wants in,” Gurman says. Gurman also shared thoughts on why Apple might have gone with the “Duo” moniker, instead of Ultra, for its first-ever foldable phone. Not only does it match the existing three-letter Air and Pro naming schemes, but it also leaves room for a future range of foldables, including the Duo Max, Duo SE, or Duo mini, the reporter says. Preorders for the iPhone Duo, starting at $1,999, begin on Oct. 16, with availability beginning on Oct. 23. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Why Is the Internet Archive Blocking Users? Blame the Bots
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.25
Struggling to access the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine? You may have been caught in the crossfire of an effort to stop web-scraping bots. The Internet Archive today published a blog post addressing user complaints about access issues with the Wayback Machine, which lets you travel back in time virtually to see how a web page looked over time. “We’ve heard you: ‘Fix the Wayback Machine!’” wrote Mark Graham, the Wayback Machine's director. “Here’s what’s going on. The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has been hit by waves of high-volume automated traffic, and we’ve put protections in place to keep the service running.” Unfortunately, those protections can sometimes ensnare real users. “If that’s happened to you, we’re sorry, and we appreciate your patience while we work to reduce the errors,” Graham added. Blocking can occur if you encounter a 429 error, an HTTP status code indicating that a user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. “We’re getting better at telling abusive bots apart from the people who depend on the Wayback Machine every day. If you think you were blocked in error, email [email protected] with your operating system, browser, and IP address, and we’ll look into it,” Graham added. The San Francisco-based Internet Archive didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. So details about the abusive bots remain unclear. But the archive might be trying to crack down on web-scraping bots that gather data to train AI models. In 2023, the Internet Archive briefly went down after facing “tens of thousands of requests per second” from an AI company out to extract text data, according to the Nieman Journalism Lab. The AI-training bots have also triggered some news publishers to block the Internet Archive “out of concern that archived material could be accessed or reused by AI systems,” the library says. “Indeed, it has been suggested that we are victims, if you will, collateral damage caught up in the conflict between AI companies and publishers,” Graham said in a May podcast episode. item.title: I Tested Canon's First Retro Camera, and It Proves Throwback Gear Doesn't Have to Be a Gimmick
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.24
I've been patiently waiting for Canon to hop on the nostalgia bandwagon and release a retro-inspired camera. A few of its competitors have turned back time with great results; the Nikon Z f and Fujifilm X100VI are obvious examples, both of which could be mistaken for a '70s or '80s film cam from a distance. Canon is joining the party with the EOS R8 Mark II (starting at $1,899), a retro-looking midrange full-frame camera that sits between entry-level and enthusiast-grade gear. Exterior aside, the Mark II is a refined version of the original R8; it adds 5-axis sensor stabilization and a larger image buffer, but is otherwise quite similar. That's not a detriment, as I praised the R8 for its excellent photos, fast autofocus, and 40fps capture when I reviewed it in 2023. I spent two weeks putting an early preproduction copy of the Mark II through its paces to see if Canon's retro experiment actually delivers in the field.
