Subtle Retro Style That Doesn't Overdo It In typical Canon fashion, its retro design approach is a little more conservative than that of other brands. The first thing I noticed is that the EOS R8 Mark II is an all-black body, while most mirrorless cameras with throwback designs are made in both a two-tone silver-and-black and a black finish. The silver bodies read a little more "old school" than all-black, but the R8 Mark II's textured leatherette does some heavy lifting in the visual department, covering the grip and rear thumb rest in contrast to the rest of the camera's matte black finish. Canon tells me that it looked back to the EOS T80, its first-ever autofocus SLR, when sketching up the R8 Mark II. It's not the obvious choice. I know I'm not alone in wanting to Canon to make a digital camera that looks like the AE-1, a '70s manual focus SLR with distinctly angled lines and a buzzsaw-style shutter speed dial, but the T80 has its charms. Its lines are more angular, a significant departure from Canon's typically rounded edges, but despite that change, the R8 Mark II still feels like a modern Canon. It fits comfortably in my hands, and the company's hallmark angled shutter release and vertical forward exposure dial are in line with other models in the R mirrorless series. Ditching Frustrating Vintage Dials for Modern Usability Some cameras that look to the past for design inspiration go all the way with film-camera controls like manual shutter and aperture dials. Discrete shutter and aperture controls can be intimidating to new users (for years, they were only available in bougie digital rangefinders from Leica), but they have made their way down to entry-level throwbacks like the Fujifilm X-T30 III. Canon opted to stick with a PASM Mode dial and two flexible exposure dials for the R8 Mark II, a scheme that's far more approachable for advanced amateurs who want to make the jump to full-frame and beginners stepping up from a smartphone. Set the Mode to Auto or Program (P) if you want the camera to do most of the work, Aperture (Av) if you want to adjust the f-stop to blur or sharpen backgrounds, and Shutter (Tv) to freeze or blur motion. It also has Flexible (Fv) control, an exposure mode that Canon's been pushing since it launched the basic EOS RP. It lets you switch between aperture and shutter priority with the press of a button, so you aren't locked into either. I've found it more confusing than helpful, but there's room for disagreement. The R8 Mark II also includes Scene (SCN) modes that adapt settings to different real-world scenarios, a real benefit for beginners. The controls are largely the same as those on the EOS RP and R8, though not identical. The On/Off/Video toggle switch is now on the right side, nestled alongside the rear exposure dial. The R8 Mark II also adds an eight-way thumbstick that doubles as a joystick, letting you move the active focus area and navigate menus. It makes the camera more versatile for wildlife, sports, and action photography, as you can more easily manually focus on what you want. The thumbstick is more responsive and comfortable to use versus the R8's four-way d-pad (which continues on in the Mark II as well). It also includes a beginner-friendly menu system called Creative Assist. Available exclusively in the Auto mode, it replaces the usual array of numerical ISO, f-stops, and shutter speeds with a touch menu that's written in layman's terms. It lets you select a color tone from a list of presets, take photos with a defocused background using a slider that goes from Blur to Sharp, and adjust scene brightness with another slider. It also lets you adjust color saturation, tint images (blue/orange and green/magenta sliders are included), or switch to monochrome with or without a color tint (blue, green, purple, or sepia). And for experts, all other modes use standard photo nomenclature—f-stops, shutter speeds, exposure values, and so on. The Lightest Full-Frame With Sensor Stabilization Ease of use is one thing, but the R8 Mark II is easy to carry, too. It weighs just about 1.2 pounds without a lens, and is available in a starter kit with the compact RF 24-50mm F4.5-6.3 IS STM if you want a zoom to match. Together, the two weigh just shy of 1.7 pounds. I didn't get a chance to try the kit lens, so I grabbed the 4.2-ounce RF 28mm F2.8 STM ($349.99) and took it on a few photo walks around town. It felt like carrying almost nothing. It's worth noting that the R8 Mark II's nearest direct competitor, the Nikon Z5II, is heavier at around 1.5 pounds. The EOS R8 Mark II earns a superlative as the lightest full-frame camera with a stabilized image sensor, a feature that's missing from both the RP and the original R8. Sensor stabilization is handy; I used it to take some long-exposure images without lugging a tripod around, and it also makes it easier to get posed portraits in dim light. The biggest challenge will be getting your subject to stay still for a photo. The slim, lightweight build doesn't come without drawbacks. The R8 Mark II keeps the same relatively small (0.70x), 2.4-million-dot EVF as the older R8. If you want a viewfinder upgrade, consider stepping up to the EOS R6 Mark II, the next model up in Canon's line. Its EVF shows a larger image (0.76x), is sharper (3.7 million dots), and, since the R6 Mark II uses the same 24.5MP image sensor and processor, its picture quality is indistinguishable. The chips aren't perfectly identical, however. Canon's Shogo Yamaguchi explains that the company always "fine-tunes the sensor to optimize for each camera," but it is clear that the R8 Mark II's photos are "effectively" the same as the R8 and R6 Mark II. Smart Subject Tracking That Keeps Up With the Action Canon is more bullish on its improvements to the R8 Mark II's autofocus system. It's tweaked the algorithms to deliver stickier subject tracking versus the original, and extended the buffer to hold 30% more Raw and 58% more JPGs in a burst, too. I'm not yet able to perform technical testing as I've only tried a pre-production version of the R8 Mark II, but those figures are in line with up to around 100 compressed Raw (C Raw), 50 Raw, or 140 JPGs when using the fastest 40fps continuous drive setting. Dialing the drive all the way to 40fps is serious overkill for non-professional sports and most wildlife scenarios; you're better off using the High (20fps) setting for those situations. The focus system has all of the same tricks you'll find in Canon's pricier cameras. It can identify and track different subject types and jump to focus on eyes and faces for people, pets, and wildlife. I tried the focus with my cat and the ultra-bright RF 50mm F1.2 lens, and the R8 Mark II reliably put the focus box on her eye. It also has precapture, a mode that continuously saves images to memory when the camera is focusing, and only starts writing photos to your card when you press the shutter all the way in. Precapture snags a half-second of action before you press the shutter, compensating for slow reaction times and making it easier to catch fleeting moments without filling up your memory card. Smooth 4K60 and Creator-Friendly Video Extras More and more creators are turning to mirrorless cameras for video and vlogs, and while the R8 Mark II isn't purpose-built for video like its EOS R6 V, it's still a heck of a good camera for movies. It records up to 4K60 at a 16:9 aspect ratio using the full width of the sensor, and the stabilized sensor avoids the jumpy, jittery look when recording handheld. The IBIS system is bolstered by a digital system that crops into the frame to deliver steady video even when handholding telephoto lenses. In my experience, the digital IS works very well. I recorded handheld video with an 800mm lens using the EOS R6 V and was astounded by the results. The R8 Mark II also includes a swing-out screen, so you can monitor the frame if you're using it to vlog from the studio or for self-recording, and it has both headphone and microphone connections. I think content creators will be happy with its feature set. Speaking of which, Canon is adding one cool video option—the R8 Mark II can "blur out" during a shot. With the press of a button, the R8 Mark II shifts the lens's focus from the subject to its nearest point. It's a good way to end a video, one with more visual interest than a basic fade to black. The feature, called Video Defocus, isn't mapped by default, but is easy enough to assign to a button in the camera menu. Preorders, Pricing, and How It Stacks Up Against Rivals The R8 Mark II looks like another excellent camera from Canon, and a solid choice for photographers and content creators who want the full-frame look and prefer a stylish, lightweight build. I've only had a chance to use a preproduction copy, but if Canon hadn't told me it was an early sample, I never would have guessed it. I didn't run into any noticeable bugs or quirks while I was trying it out; it feels fully baked to me. Canon is pricing the camera at $1,899 as a body-only unit, or $2,099 as a kit with the RF 24-50mm F4.5-6.3 IS STM lens. It's also selling an Extension Grip, an $89.99 baseplate that adds a little height to the body for photographers who want just a bit more camera to hold onto. Preorders are open today, and Canon expects to start shipping in late October. The price is competitive. After all, the Nikon Z5II goes for $1,849.95 as a body, while the slim Sony a7C II costs far more at $2,499.99. The R8 Mark II beats the Z5II on speed and is noticeably lighter and smaller, but the Z5II's larger, sharper viewfinder may be enough to pull some creators to its side of the fence. The Sony a7C II is as tiny as the R8 Mark II, and its 33MP sensor packs more pixels than the R8's 24MP chip, but like many Sony cameras, it is on the pricey side. Among the Canon line, the original R8 is still available for $1,649; it's very similar but doesn't have a stabilized sensor. Creators who want a larger camera and better viewfinder may want to step up to the R6 Mark II for $2,299. All are good tools for imaging and video, so pick the one that appeals to your sensibilities and best fits your budget when you're ready to make the jump to full-frame. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: iOS 27 Trick Increases Size of iPhone Duo Bezel to Accommodate Cases
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.17
Putting a case on a smartphone is usually as easy as pushing it into place, but it's more difficult with a foldable phone. Apple has introduced a software setting to help you adapt if an accessory doesn't perfectly align with its new iPhone Duo design. A new feature called Shift Left Edge was spotted in iOS 27 by blogger Nicolas Lellouche during last week's iPhone event, and MacRumors later reported on it. A video from Apple's event shows the feature turning on and off through a toggle within its settings. The iOS 27 description reads, “Moves content when you are using a case that partially covers the left edge of the outer display of your iPhone.” Turning it on then makes the left-hand border roughly twice as thick as it normally would be, although the bezel remains slim overall. The idea is to add more black space to the left-hand edge of your phone, so you won’t lose any of the picture to an encroaching accessory. Without any further time with the iPhone Duo, no one appears to know whether the cases sold by Apple would require this feature to be enabled. It may be that this option is designed for third-party accessories rather than Apple's official case and folio with a kickstand. The iPhone Duo is set to come with its own version of iOS 27, featuring various new ways to interact with the phone across its two displays. For example, the apps you regularly use in your iPhone's dock will now appear on the right-hand edge, bringing them closer to your thumb. Duo preorders start on Oct. 16 and the phone launches on Oct. 23. The handset starts at $1,999, rising to $3,199 for a top-end 2TB edition. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Acer Swift Go 16 AI Review: This Big-Screen Workhorse Runs at Just a Trot
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.81
Want to go big without spending too much money? The Acer Swift Go 16 AI (starts at $1,099.99; $1,149.99 as tested) is a large-screen productivity laptop with a sturdy chassis, a comfortable keyboard, and a decent array of ports. However, it offers lower performance than comparable laptops in the same price range, while its screen brightness, battery life, and titular AI features come up just "good enough." For everyday word processing, web browsing, and video streaming, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI gets the job done, and you can even push the laptop to do light gaming and graphic design. However, the Asus Zenbook A16 ($1,699.99 as tested), our Editors' Choice winner for lightweight 16-inchers, is a better option for people willing to spend a little extra for an incredible 3K OLED panel and longer battery life. At the time I wrote this, Acer offered three Acer Swift Go 16 AI configurations: one with an Intel chip, and two with AMD chips. In an odd inverse, the entry-level model comes with an OLED screen, while the two pricier options have IPS LCDs. Otherwise, you'll see a range of storage and memory options, though even the most powerful model remains a straightforward productivity machine. The entry-level model is the SFG16-I71T-51LC, which retails for $1,099.99. It features an Intel Core Ultra 5 Series 3 CPU, integrated Intel Graphics, 16GB of LPDDR5X memory, a 512GB SSD, and a 16:10, 1,920-by-1,200-pixel OLED touch screen. If you want the fanciest version of the Acer Swift Go 16 AI, look for the SFG16-A71T-R87F. This configuration typically costs $1,599.99, but you can find it as low as $1,149 at some retailers. This model comes with an AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 CPU, AMD Radeon 880M integrated graphics, 32GB of LPDDR5X memory, a 1TB SSD, and a 16:10, 1,920-by-1,200-pixel IPS touch screen. In the middle is the model I tested: the SFG16-A71T-R5UY. This PC retails for $1,249.99, but you can find it for $749.99 at certain retailers. It comes with an AMD Ryzen AI 7 445 CPU, AMD Radeon 840M integrated graphics, 16GB LPDDR5X memory, a 1TB SSD, and a 16:10, 1,920-by-1,200-pixel IPS touch panel. Choosing the Acer Swift Go 16 AI configuration you need is relatively easy. If you want an OLED touch screen and don't mind a smaller SSD, go for the Intel model. If you want more powerful components, choose an AMD build. Still, no matter which version you select, you won't spend an exorbitant amount of money. Just be aware that you'll find similar systems under the Acer Swift 16 AI (no "Go") and Acer Swift Go 16 (no "AI") brands, so make sure you have the right name and model number before you hit the buy button. The Acer Swift Go 16 AI has its shortcomings (which I'll touch upon later), but its physical design isn't one of them. The laptop features an all-metal chassis (0.63 by 14 by 9.9 inches) with an intriguing, laser-etched triangle design on the lid. The metal build makes the machine feel solid and sturdy, but at 3.53 pounds, it's not too heavy for its size. For comparison, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI is heftier than the 2.87-pound Asus Zenbook A16, but lighter than the 4.12-pound Dell 16 Plus (DB16250). I brought the laptop everywhere with me for about a week and worked wherever I could find Wi-Fi. It fit in my backpack's laptop compartment (just barely), and while I noticed its weight, it wasn't uncomfortable to carry. As large-display productivity laptops go, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI is practical and a little stylish. The Swift Go 16 AI has more than enough ports for getting things done. On its left side are HDMI, USB Type-A, and two USB4 Type-C ports; either of the latter can power the machine. On the right side, there's a Kensington lock notch, another USB-A port, a 3.5mm audio jack, and a microSD card slot. In terms of usability, I was able to connect a mouse, a keyboard, a headset, and an external display while the computer was plugged into an outlet. That said, I wasn't left with any spare USB ports after I made those connections. You may need to invest in a USB hub if you have more gear. Everything about the Acer Swift Go 16 AI feels big. The 16-inch display is one of the laptop's major selling points, since it makes it easy to work in text documents and spreadsheets, browse the internet, watch videos, or play non-demanding games with that much screen real estate. The IPS panel display is decent, with a 1,920-by-1,200-pixel resolution and touch-screen functionality. The screen isn't very bright, and the colors are a little muddy, but it's good enough for both work and play. The Acer Swift Go 16 AI has a respectably large touchpad at 5.9 by 3.9 inches. It never got in the way, even when my hands rested on it while typing. In addition, the keyboard has a smart layout, with sleek, rectangular keycaps and a full number pad on the right. Some 15- and 16-inch laptops have number pads off to the right of the main key layout, useful if you routinely crunch numbers, but that's a personal preference, and some designs can be cramped. The keyboard also has white backlighting, an essential if you're working in the dark. Although the Acer Swift Go 16 AI's speakers feature DTS:X audio technology, the sound quality is similar to that of most other laptops in this price range. The bass isn't particularly strong, but the treble is clear (and you can crank the volume up fairly high). I listened to classical music while working, rock music while cooking, and children's music while playing with my daughter, and the sound quality neither truly impressed nor disappointed me. Likewise, the webcam and microphone were mixed bags. On the upside, the 5-megapixel IR webcam has a physical shutter, which provides an extra layer of privacy. On the downside, the camera produces dull, washed-out images with highly inconsistent lighting levels. The microphone made me sound tinny and robotic during testing, as if I were speaking from the middle of a cavernous room instead of less than a foot away. A good headset can address the mic issue, but the image quality may be a problem if your work requires frequent video calls. In that case, you may want to buy a dedicated webcam. Since "AI" is in the Acer Swift Go 16 AI's name, I expected artificial intelligence to play a big role in the laptop's operations. After all, the machine has the Acer Intelligence Space app, which lets you launch eight AI tools, including a digital assistant and an image generator. Upon closer inspection, though, none of the AI apps work that well. The AI agent runs on outdated, open-source Llama technology and struggles with simple queries. (When I asked it what LLM it ran on, it replied that it didn't know what "LLM" meant.) I also tinkered with Acer Qubi and Acer AI Workspace, very similar assistant tools. (The former features a cutesy robot interface and the latter has a more professional design.) On top of that, it took a few tries to download the AI image generators, and the OLED optimization tools didn't offer improvements for the IPS display. AI aficionados have probably used better programs online, while AI neophytes may wonder why they need these tools at all. The Swift Go 16 AI is also a Microsoft Copilot+ machine, which means it has access to sophisticated AI features built directly into Windows 11. As with other Copilot+ machines, the enhanced Windows search and live translation features occasionally come in handy. Otherwise, you can get most of the same functionality through the standard Copilot app on other systems. In terms of performance, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI runs the gamut from unremarkable to decent. In most of our benchmarks, this laptop scored either right in the middle or toward the lower end of the pack, with consistently average performance across productivity, graphics, and screen quality tests. On the positive side, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI didn't perform badly in any category, holding its own among similarly priced competitors. This laptop can handle productivity and light content creation, though its competitors can handle the same tasks just as well, if not better. For comparison machines, I've chosen a handful of like-priced 15- and 16-inchers: the 2025 Apple MacBook Air 15-Inch ($1,299 as tested), the Asus Zenbook A16 ($1,699.99 as tested), the Dell 16 Plus ($1,149.99 as tested), and the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3 Gen 11 ($1,299.99 as tested). While the CPUs and graphics systems vary by model, most of these machines are standard productivity laptops with similar performance levels. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess using a variety of automated operations in the popular image editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The Acer Swift Go 16 AI did somewhat better in our productivity and content creation tests than in our other benchmarks. In the standard PCMark 10 test, the laptop came in a relatively close second, with its only first-place ranking in the PCMark 10 storage test. It also ranked second and third in the PugetBench and HandBrake tests, respectively. Overall, the system didn't distinguish itself much from the pack, placing toward the middle or bottom of our rendering and CPU tests. While the numbers themselves aren't impressive, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI's real-world performance is fine. For about a week, the laptop was my go-to machine for word processing, managing spreadsheets, browsing the internet, listening to music, and streaming online videos. I didn't encounter much lag or slowdown, even with many applications or tabs open, and the system didn't run extremely hot. Based on our benchmarks, though, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI doesn't offer the best performance for the price. We challenge all systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), stress the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development, like Metal and DirectX 12, to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Lastly, Solar Bay measures ray-tracing performance in a synthetic environment. In our graphics testing, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI didn't impress. Although it only came in last place once (the standard Steel Nomad test), the PC didn't earn any first-place spots. Otherwise, this laptop remained near the middle of the rankings, generally losing out to the Apple MacBook Air 15-Inch (2025, M4) and the Dell 16 Plus (DB16250). Granted, the graphics tests are not make-or-break benchmarks for the Acer Swift Go 16 AI. It's not a content creation or gaming laptop, and it doesn't need powerful 3D rendering performance. Still, it's another area where this laptop's performance is "good enough" rather than "good." We test each laptop's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with the display brightness set to 50% and the audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. In addition, to gauge display performance, we use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its Windows software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). Battery life is one area where the Acer Swift Go 16 AI performs well. While 17 hours and 12 minutes puts it right in the center of our tests, it's not that far behind the Apple MacBook Air 15-Inch (2025, M4) and Asus Zenbook A16, which clocked 18:31. In practical terms, the Acer Swift Go 16 AI has more than enough battery to last through a workday and into the evening. The Acer Swift Go 16 AI's screen color and brightness rank right back to the middle of the pack. It can display 99% of the sRGB color gamut, which is good, although its competitors all reach 100%. However, the Acer laptop can only display 81% of the Adobe RGB gamut and 82% of the DCI-P3 gamut, whereas many competitors match or exceed those numbers. With 99 nits at 50% brightness and 353 nits at 100%, the Swift Go 16 AI is neither the brightest nor the dullest screen among its competitors. Final Thoughts Acer Swift Go 16 AI - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Acer Swift 16 Go AI is a productivity laptop that doesn't live up to its full potential. Despite a solid design, decent components, and a reasonable price, nothing about the machine stands out from rival laptops. Some of its competitors are thinner, lighter, and cheaper, and most of them offer better performance. For example, if you need an even lighter laptop with a crisp 3K OLED, the Asus Zenbook A16 is the way to go. And if the display size and numpad are non-negotiable, the Dell 16 Plus (DB16250) is a stronger overall machine. Still, the Acer Swift 16 Go AI may be a worthwhile purchase for anyone needing a no-frills productivity laptop in a sturdy metal chassis—though you should wait until a sale knocks a few hundred dollars off the price. About Our Expert I've covered science and technology for the past 15 years, with a special focus on gaming hardware. During my career, I've reviewed hundreds of mice, keyboards, headsets, monitors, smartphones, laptops, desktops, and various other gadgets that defy easy categorization. I've also covered some of the industry's biggest trade shows, including the Consumer Electronics Show, E3, IFA, SXSW, and PAX East/West. After starting at The Escapist, my work has appeared in Tom's Guide, Tom's Hardware, Laptop Magazine, LiveScience, Space.com, Scientific American, and Worth Magazine.

item.title: PSA: Don't Bring a Gun in Your Waymo
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.74
Waymo employees pulled over one of its driverless cars to facilitate a "high-risk vehicle stop" for the San Francisco Police. Two juveniles were later arrested for illegal possession of a firearm. The incident occurred on Sept. 3 around 4 a.m. in San Francisco’s Outer Richmond neighborhood. Waymo tells the Los Angeles Times that it stopped the robotaxi due to a “violation of our terms of service involving a firearm." Officers detained the two passengers after seizing a “loaded, AR-styled assault rifle also known as a ghost gun,” from the driverless vehicle, as well as suspected marijuana and mace spray, the department said on Facebook. It's unclear whether Waymo alerted the police or the SFPD asked the company to intervene, but the company has called the police on passengers before. Waymo vehicles include cameras inside the car to monitor rides. "Among other things, we may use cameras to...check that in-car rules are being followed [and] promote safety and security," according to a Waymo FAQ. "Our Support team may review video under certain circumstances, including after an issue is brought to our attention. Occasionally, in more urgent circumstances, Support may access live video during a trip." This comes as Waymo expands its robotaxis to Las Vegas, making it the 15th city and Nevada the seventh state with Waymo services. The expansion is initially limited to a 24-mile area around the Vegas Strip, with further coverage of Clark County to come. Waymo joins Zoox in offering driverless car services in Las Vegas. About Our Expert I’m a New York-based writer currently serving as PCMag’s Editorial Intern. I cover the impact of technology and internet culture on our daily lives, with a specialization in video games and cultural criticism. I have written for Kotaku, The A.V. Club, Unwinnable, Aftermath, and more. In addition, I have a formal background in video game development and visual design. You can find all of my work on my website.

item.title: The Secret VPN Trick to Keep Your Speeds Fast Without Losing Protection
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.67
Some websites and apps—like certain banking platforms or streaming services—don't always work smoothly with the encryption a VPN provides. That's where split tunneling becomes incredibly useful. This feature lets you control which apps or websites use the VPN connection and which ones connect directly to the internet through your regular network. For example, you can keep your browser protected by the VPN while letting your online game or banking app bypass it for faster speeds or fewer identity verification issues. You no longer have to turn off your VPN entirely just to access specific services. In this guide, I’ll explain how split tunneling works, when it makes sense to use it, and what privacy and security trade-offs you should consider before enabling it. What Is Split Tunneling (And How Does It Save Your Speeds)? Connecting to a VPN encrypts all of your outgoing network data. Applications, games, and browsers will all route through that encrypted tunnel by default. Split tunneling allows you to route specific programs through your regular network instead, thus forgoing any encryption. Why would you want to do this? Encryption increases your latency, even with the fastest VPNs. If you're playing competitive games, every millisecond counts. Without split tunneling, you would have to decide between privacy and performance. Routing your game outside your VPN's encrypted tunnel lets you play without sacrificing privacy. You'll still be broadcasting your gaming activity to any onlookers, like your ISP, but your more sensitive data across other applications and websites will be protected as usual. App-based split tunneling allows you to route specific apps through your VPN while keeping others on your local connection. Browser-based split tunneling usually comes in the form of a browser extension that functions as a lightweight version of your VPN, protecting your general browsing rather than your entire device. The Best VPNs I've Tested A good VPN combines app and browser split tunneling into a single feature by allowing you to configure both apps and URLs in the main client. In the full app, you can filter apps on your device. The browser version lets you allowlist websites that will bypass the VPN, but you won’t be able to modify any programs without using the full client. Some services offer what's called "inverse" split tunneling. This feature lets you route most of your traffic through your regular network, then choose which applications are protected by your VPN. It's useful if you have just one or two apps you want protected, such as a torrent client or a streaming browser. While both versions of this tool are convenient, it is best to use each one carefully. Your data will be visible when using apps or sites that are not encrypted. Why and When to Enable Split Tunneling It may not be obvious why you would want to exclude certain services from your VPN's protective encryption. After all, you're likely using a VPN to protect all your data. However, there are a handful of reasons you should consider using split tunneling. Most come down to performance, accessibility, and preference. Here are some of the biggest reasons you may want to use split tunneling, and when not to: - Improve performance: Routing an app outside your VPN tunnel will allow it to use your base internet speeds. This can be critical for fast-paced tasks like gaming or data-intensive ones like downloading large files. - Access local services: Rideshare apps and local websites can malfunction on a regular VPN connection. If you can’t get a regional service to work, consider routing it out of the encrypted tunnel. - Work remotely: Your work laptop or office network is probably already protected by a business VPN. Your personal service could conflict with it and prevent you from logging in to important systems. - Stream local content: Using a VPN to access regional streaming services like Netflix can change the content you see, depending on the location of the server you connect to. You should use split tunneling and route your favorite streaming service through your local network if you want to view that region’s unique content. Alternatively, you can use your VPN to access a server in that region if you want to stay protected and watch your favorite shows. - Bank online: Banks have advanced fraud detection algorithms that can go off if you try to connect to your account with a VPN. You may end up blocked, or, even worse, your account could be flagged for fraud, resulting in your cards being locked down when you need them most. - Use devices on your home network: Sometimes VPNs will prevent your device from being visible on local networks, which can make using devices like printers impossible. Good luck casting your favorite streaming app from your phone to your TV when your phone is in the UK with access to the BBC, but your TV is here at home. Routing a specific app on your device through your regular network connection instead of the VPN can fix that problem. Is Split Tunneling Actually Safe? Carelessness and improper usage are the main risks with split tunneling. It’s easy to misconfigure a split tunnel and accidentally leak your IP address, location, and browsing details to your ISP and advertisers. You could get a threatening letter (or worse) from your ISP if you allow activity like torrenting to go through your regular network connection. The actual security risks are minimal. There’s always a chance that you could connect to a compromised public network, but those attacks have become rare with the widespread adoption of HTTPS. A reputable antivirus will do more to protect your traffic against malicious attacks than any VPN, though I recommend using both for a layered security toolkit. Add a password manager and enable two-factor authentication to further improve your privacy. About Our Expert My writing journey started in 2012 and has taken me through various niches, but my main focus has always been on tech. I contributed to several growing PC hardware and software sites, focusing on gaming, peripherals, and privacy. As the amount of information we put out on the internet has grown, so have the threats and the tools we use to combat them. With VPNs gaining traction in the late 2010s as a tool for the public instead of just an option for business security, I found myself reviewing countless options in this continuously changing landscape. This led to my role before PCMag over at WizCase, where I honed my knowledge of VPNs and privacy tools and eventually oversaw all of the content produced. I led a talented team of fellow writers and editors to evaluate VPNs, password managers, antivirus, and parental controls.

item.title: Webflow vs. WordPress.com: Which Website Builder Comes Out on Top?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.19
Table of Contents There's more to the world of website builders than just the biggest names. If you're interested in creating your own online home, but are unconvinced by Editors' Choice winners Duda and Wix, you have many alternatives to consider, such as Webflow and WordPress.com—two reliable platforms that can meet your site-builder needs. I've covered the website builder space for years and have tested both services. Here, I'll outline their pros and cons to help you decide which to choose. Full Specs | Webflow Website Builder | WordPress.com | | |---|---|---| | Free Version Offered | | | | Free Version Offered | | | | Unlimited Monthly Data Transfers With All Plans | | | | Unlimited Monthly Data Transfers With All Plans | | | | Unlimited Storage With All Plans | | | | Unlimited Storage With All Plans | | | | Web Store | | | | Web Store | | | | Blogging Tool | | | | Blogging Tool | | | | Download Selling | | | | Download Selling | | | | Basic Image Editing | | | | Basic Image Editing | | | | Site Portability | | | | Site Portability | | | | Site Membership | | | | Site Membership | | | Plans and Prices Webflow and WordPress.com both offer free tiers that let you sample limited versions of the services before making a potentially pricey commitment. WordPress.com's free plan is ad-supported and features unlimited monthly data transfers with 1GB of storage. The free Webflow, on the other hand, is much more limited. You can only create two webpages, and there's a 1GB monthly data transfer limit. In addition, Webflow's unique backend functionality limits you to creating only 50 CMS items, such as blog posts and images. With either service, you must pay for the complete site-building experience. Webflow's Basic tier (starting at $25 per month or $15 per month, billed annually) comes with 10GB of monthly data transfers, 10GB of file storage, and the ability to create up to 300 webpages. The Premium plan ($39 per month or $25 per month, billed annually) keeps Basic's storage allotment but starts with 50GB of monthly data transfers (with the option to increase it up to 2.5TB) and includes 2,000 CMS items. The business-focused Team package ($2,500 per month, billed annually) includes numerous professional features, such as AEO agents, publishing workflows, and priority tech support. For full professional flexibility, contact Webflow for a custom Enterprise-tier price. WordPress.com's Personal plan ($9 per month or $4 per month, billed annually) offers 6GB of storage, several themes, plug-ins support, and e-commerce tools. Premium ($18 per month or $8 per month, billed annually) ups storage to 13GB per month, enhances analytics, adds premium themes, and unlocks video uploads. The Business tier ($40 per month or $25 per month, billed annually) has 50GB of storage and GitHub integration. Finally, the Commerce tier ($70 per month or $45 per month, billed annually) includes professional e-commerce upgrades powered by WooCommerce. WordPress.com not only offers cheaper options but also has more straightforward pricing overall. In contrast, Webflow has more hidden fees. For example, if you want extra space, you must pay $0.50 per gigabyte per month up to 100GB. Meanwhile, extra bandwidth starts at $30 per month for an extra 50GB. Even Webflow's e-commerce features are gated behind a separate tier, starting at $42 per month for 500 e-commerce items. Winner: WordPress.com Templates, Themes, Integrations, and Plug-Ins When it comes to themes and templates, Webflow's issues are once again more about pricing than functionality. It lets you build attractive websites, but not all Webflow templates are free. The best designs are premium products, priced from $29 to $129. Webflow's free templates are visually bland, so the premium templates are basically required to build an attractive site. There's another restriction, and a big one: You can't swap templates. In other words, you must rebuild the website if you want a fresh look. On the upside, Webflow lets you integrate both free and paid third-party integrations, such as CRM tools and traffic analytics tools. With WordPress.com, all paid users now have access to the many excellent third-party WordPress plug-ins and themes. Making the most of these attractive themes is annoying, given the lack of a true WYSIWYG editor for easily arranging site elements. Still, you can work around that with select plug-ins. You can also swap themes whenever you want. For both services, the number of themes and apps is in the thousands. But WordPress themes, even free ones, look better overall. Meanwhile, by relaxing the rules around third-party apps, WordPress now offers more power, flexibility, and options to expand your site's capabilities than Webflow does. Winner: WordPress.com Blogging and Image Editing WordPress.com has roots as a blogging platform, so its blogging features don't disappoint. The interface is still pleasantly simple, even after replacing the WYSIWYG editor with a block editor. I wish there were more customization options for mobile sites, though. The photo editing tools are also limited to basic actions like cropping and rotating. The nicest perk is the ability to upload photos to an online repository for later access. Webflow matches WordPress’s blogging prowess with its set of CMS tools, which gives you a system to efficiently manage content. The system is especially well-suited to blogging, as it lets you focus more on writing posts rather than on maintaining a consistent design. Just remember, your tier determines how many CMS items you can make. The builder makes it easy to switch between desktop and mobile views. Webflow also has better image editing features, letting you resize images, adjust opacity, set borders, and apply filters and transitions. Winner: Webflow AI Tools AI tools are the trendy new ways website builders help you build your site faster and with less effort. They tend to include similar features, but each builder puts its own spin on the concept. For example, WordPress.com has an AI helper. For $5 per month, you can task the JetPack AI assistant with completing simple tasks like "improving" your writing or generating suggested content. WordPress users can also add AI functionality by downloading new plug-ins. Webflow's AI features are a little more ambitious. Like WordPress.com, Webflow also offers a natural-language AI assistant to tweak text and optimize pages for SEO. However, it goes further by allowing you to enter prompts to generate entire web applications using the App Gen AI tool. Still, I don't recommend using AI website-building tools because they strip sites of essential human creativity. Winner: Webflow Customer Service When it comes to offering site-building assistance, Webflow and WordPress.com are pretty comparable. Both services offer 24-hour live chat and let you search for answers through company forums and knowledge bases. Both services, unfortunately, also lack phone support. Winner: Tie And The Winner Is... WordPress.com Webflow and WordPress.com are two of the most evenly matched website builders I've compared. No matter which one you pick, you'll enjoy a high-quality site-building experience, even if neither one is an Editors' Choice winner like Duda or Wix. However, WordPress.com pulls ahead thanks to its less restrictive pricing and integration into the broader, powerful WordPress ecosystem.

item.title: macOS Golden Gate Review: Apple Intelligence Finally Delivers
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.15
After a rocky start with Tahoe, Apple gets it right with macOS Golden Gate. The new desktop OS turns Apple Intelligence from a marketing buzzword into a suite of powerful, everyday tools while smoothing out Liquid Glass's most annoying design quirks. In addition, it brings system-wide performance boosts, improved child safety features, a more flexible menu bar, and resizable apps via iPhone mirroring. Golden Gate stands alongside Microsoft's Windows 11 as an Editors' Choice winner for modern desktop operating systems. With Golden Gate, Apple is looking firmly toward the future. The OS supports all Apple silicon-based Macs, as well as the MacBook Neo, which uses a different hardware architecture. Golden Gate is the first macOS version to not support any Intel-based Macs. If you have an older Intel Mac, you're stuck on macOS Tahoe. You can expect Apple to release security updates for Tahoe and older Intel-compatible versions for around seven years after their initial release. Alternatively, you can repurpose your Mac in fun ways. Golden Gate still runs Intel-only apps via the Rosetta 2 framework, but next year’s macOS 28 will include only a stripped-down version of that emulation tech, intended to support just a few classic games. I hope that third-party developers like CodeWeavers find some way to keep other Intel-based apps usable going forward. Developers should note that even though macOS now focuses on newer Apple hardware, Xcode will still build apps that run on Intel and Apple silicon Macs (and the A-Series Neo), so you shouldn't expect changes on that front. If you’re running any recent version of macOS on an Apple silicon machine, your System Settings app will eventually prompt you to upgrade your system to Golden Gate. I always recommend against upgrading to a new macOS version until the first point release arrives (typically after two or three weeks), but if Tahoe’s glitzy interface gets on your nerves, you can probably update safely right now. If you don't get the upgrade nudge, simply open the System Settings app, click on Software Update, and follow the prompts. If you want to be super cautious and check out Golden Gate before risking your setup, use the Disk Utility app to create a new volume. Then, install Golden Gate on that volume by downloading the installer from the App Store. When the installer menu appears, make sure to click Show All Disks and choose the new volume instead of the default. When you boot into that new volume, the Migration Assistant will let you import your apps and data from your existing partition. When you’re ready to switch to Golden Gate as your daily driver, head back to the Disk Utility. Then, you can either delete the volume with your old OS or upgrade the old volume and delete the one you used for testing. Here are what I consider the biggest changes with macOS 27, in order of importance: - Apple Intelligence is everywhere, handling everything from minor productivity tasks to writing new apps from scratch. - The Liquid Glass user interface is far more consistent and less distracting than in Tahoe. - New interface elements and other features suggest that touch-screen Macs are getting closer to release. - Child-safety features give parents unprecedented control over their children’s buying, browsing, and messaging activity. - Speedier performance for file transfers, networking, and messaging, along with snappier searching and indexing. I cover all of these improvements in more detail below. Cupertino made big promises about Apple Intelligence with the launch of macOS Sequoia in 2024, but didn’t follow through until now. The most major change is to Siri, which now works much like other AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT and Claude, and is accessible everywhere. With it, you can conduct deep conversations over text or voice and assign it various tasks across apps; it considers your personal data in these interactions. Apple also now makes its AI features feel like seamless parts of the operating system. For example, you can click the Siri icon on the menu bar—or simply say “Siri”—and type or speak your request to get a summary of the document you’re previewing or a full description of an image in an app. You can also open the new Siri app to ask fresh questions or review previous ones. If you’ve been running the beta versions of Golden Gate, you may have noticed some dramatic improvements in Siri’s abilities over time. For example, when I was testing the first public beta, I asked Siri to write a polite thank-you note in response to an open email in the Mail app. At the time, its message was full of characterless prose and clearly sounded machine-generated. However, the current version of Siri produces text that reads convincingly human. This same level of interactivity extends across all native macOS apps. The Shortcuts app, for example, now lets you create automations simply by describing what you want it to do. You can also Cmd-click on almost anything in Calendar, Messages, and elsewhere to bring up an Ask Siri prompt. In the Calendar app, for example, I asked Siri for the best no-highways route to another city, and after a few seconds, it gave me a link that opened the route in the Maps app. Apple Intelligence in the Photos app did a beautiful job of reframing a photograph. It rotated the perspective so that the subject was looking forward rather than to the sides, filling in detail to the left and right based on the original. Moreover, it did all this from the same place where you can perform traditional tasks, such as cropping an image or changing its color balance. Still, the AI experience isn't completely free of issues. I ran into problems, for instance, when trying to create a shortcut that would tell me the current distance to my home city. When I asked Apple Intelligence to build this tool in the Shortcuts app, it complied in seconds. But, when I tried to run the app, I got an error message that it didn't have access to my location and that I might need to turn on Location Services (which was already on). Additionally, I asked Siri to create a shortcut to move the currently selected Mail message to a folder I use for storage. Siri subsequently told me that it couldn’t write shortcuts. I then asked it to write an AppleScript to perform the same task, and it said it couldn’t write AppleScripts either. But when I right-clicked a message in the Mail app, chose Ask Siri, and asked for an AppleScript tool to perform this action, it immediately followed through. Strangely, the Ask Siri option in the Mail app also said it couldn’t write a shortcut. Speaking of AI-powered coding, you can now run an AI agent directly inside Xcode. This was possible with Tahoe, but the integration is tighter under Golden Gate. I’ve always wanted a no-frills, no-cost macOS app that lets me launch an app or document simply by pressing a hotkey—a capability that has long been part of Windows but is available on macOS only in overstuffed apps like Alfred or Raycast. I selected Claude Code as my AI agent in Xcode, and a half hour later, I had an elegant app that did exactly what I needed, which I successfully published on the App Store. If you listened closely to the keynote presentation at WWDC 2026, you got the message that Apple took the many complaints it (deservedly) received about the Liquid Glass interface to heart. Golden Gate revises the design system to reduce the distractions that should never have been present in the first place. The large-diameter rounded corners are smaller, while both the distracting sidebar borders and almost all the tiny, inconsistent icons that cluttered menus are gone. The Appearance pane in the System Settings app gains a slider that lets you adjust the transparency of dialogs and menus, though you need to go to Accessibility > Display and enable the Reduce Transparency option to remove the effect altogether. This setting should be more prominent. Visual enhancements, such as a dark outline of the currently active interface element (think the search field in the Mail app), are a pleasant surprise. I’m still finding other small upgrades, including the repositioned formatting toolbar in the Mail app's message composition window (now conveniently moved from above the address fields to the top of the message text panel itself). That same toolbar is also easier to use, larger, and more visually consistent with the rest of the OS. I still feel that the Liquid Glass design system wastes space in some places. The top-line toolbars seem larger than necessary, for example. But if you never upgraded from macOS Sequoia to Tahoe because you couldn't bear to live with Liquid Glass, you don't have nearly as much of an excuse not to upgrade to Golden Gate. Ever since Steve Jobs famously set limits on his children’s screen time, Apple has led the pack in child-safety precautions. Golden Gate enhances these features by giving parents robust controls over what their children can see and buy online. In previous macOS versions, you could limit the screen time on a child's account. In Golden Gate, you can fine-tune these limits by setting different ones for entertainment, social media, and games. You can require your child to get permission to buy apps, connect with someone new via Messaging or FaceTime, and view sites. A Communication Safety option blurs nude images and blocks images of gore and violence without sending any data to Apple. With age verification laws advancing rapidly in the US, I expect Apple to continue leaning into these controls. Golden Gate also makes many other important, less splashy improvements. The expanded Spotlight search field, for example, drops down a menu that lets you narrow the search to actions (like Shortcuts), apps, files, and the clipboard. Other changes work more discreetly. To access Safari’s “Notify Me…” command, which can alert you when a web page's content changes, you need to click the three-line menu to the left of the search bar in that app. Apple also quietly adds an essential feature to the interface that should have existed years ago: When your laptop menu bar has more icons than can fit on your screen, a little arrow appears, letting you scroll the hidden icons into view. If you’ve been using third-party apps to perform the same feat, you might want to consider ditching them. The desktop OS also borrows some gestures from iOS, such as swiping down to refresh a page. These new gestures are especially intriguing because they hint at the potential for a touch-screen MacBook. If such a device ever arrives, these controls would presumably work on the screen, in addition to the touchpad. Some other new features I enjoy seeing include: - Better-organized information on the artist pages in Music. - Full-resolution images in shared albums from Photos. - Handwritten notes and sketches in the Notes app. - Improved touch support for iPhone and iPad apps via the Sidecar feature, including markup and one-finger scrolling; this is another hint in support of a touch-screen Mac. - Keynote-like slideshow creation in Photos. - More compact, informative menu bar icons (with the battery percentage inside the icon, as in iOS). - New Tapback options in Messages. - Photo albums are shareable with Android and Windows users who don’t have iCloud accounts. - Refined support for dark mode, notably in Freeform, where black text on a white background becomes white-on-black in dark mode. - Resizable apps via iPhone Mirroring, so you can view them larger than they look in the small screen on your phone; you must update these apps for iOS 27. - Sharper flyover imagery in Maps. - The hard drive icon in Finder used to be a spinning-platter disk, but now it's more accurately an SSD. - Video podcasts in the macOS Podcasts app. When Apple announced Golden Gate, it promised snappier performance throughout the OS, and the release version delivers on that promise. Access to networked Windows machines and other Macs, file transfers, and messaging all work much faster than in earlier versions. In the Golden Gate beta versions, some apps seemed to open more slowly than they did in Tahoe, but in the final release, the whole system feels more responsive than before. Final Thoughts Apple macOS Golden Gate - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. macOS Golden Gate succeeds where past releases stumbled, delivering an operating system that feels both modern and genuinely useful. Apple Intelligence is no longer just a headline—it is a deeply integrated, highly functional set of tools that leaves Microsoft's Copilot feeling disjointed by comparison. Moreover, Golden Gate lets you tone down many of the most distracting elements of the Liquid Glass experience. Factor in top-tier child safety features and noticeable performance gains, and this release becomes an essential upgrade that's well worthy of our Editors' Choice award. About Our Expert I've been writing about software and hardware for PCMag for more than 40 years, focusing on operating systems, office suites, and communication and utility apps. I've specialized in everything related to word and document processing, including format conversion, OCR, and PDF apps. In my spare time, I build apps for Macs and Windows PCs that make it easy to run legacy operating systems (such as old versions of macOS and Windows) and work with legacy documents. I've also written about technology for non-technical publications, such as The New York Review of Books. Before joining PCMag, I reviewed music and sound equipment for audio magazines. In my other career, I'm the Lionel Trilling Professor in the Humanities at Columbia University and write books about modern literature.

item.title: Windows 11 and 10 get emergency patches, but AMD GPU issues remain
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.44
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft has released emergency patches for both Windows 10 and Windows 11, addressing critical security vulnerabilities and system bugs. - The updates, KB5129236 and KB5129195, fix issues including USB audio failures, Remote Desktop Services instability, and Hyper-V folder sharing problems with Linux virtual machines. - However, AMD Radeon GPU issues remain unresolved, and users are advised to install the patches promptly as they require a system restart. Microsoft’s September Patch Tuesday fixed a record 700+ security vulnerabilities across Windows versions, but it also caused some issues—most notably the breaking of USB audio on Windows 11. Now a week later, the company has released emergency out-of-band updates for both Windows 11 and Windows 10 to address some of those issues. Windows 11’s KB5129195 update Update KB5129195 resolves some (but not all) of the issues affecting the Windows 11 audio system, plus further issues relating to Claude Cowork and Remote Desktop Services (RDS). Some PCs with AMD Radeon GPUs are also facing issues, but this update doesn’t address that yet—nor does it address issues with File Explorer and File History that were also introduced on Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is automatically rolling out the emergency KB5129195 update to all Windows 11 PCs as a mandatory, cumulative, out-of-band update. It contains fixes from previous updates, and it also addresses a newly discovered elevation of privilege (EoP) security flaw. Installation should take about 10 minutes depending on hardware and requires a restart. Windows 10’s KB5129236 update For Windows 10 versions 22H2 and 21H2, Microsoft has released a separate emergency update called KB5129236. According to the changelog, the update resolves the following issues: [Remote Desktop Services (known issue)] Fixed: This update addresses an issue affecting Remote Desktop Services (RDS) after installing the September 2026 Windows security update (KB5122878). In affected environments, RDS might become unstable, causing RDP connection and sign-in failures or servers to become unresponsive during Remote Desktop configuration. Related tools, including Microsoft Management Console (MMC), RDS Licensing Diagnoser, File Explorer, and the Windows Update page, might also stop responding. [Hyper-V (known issue)] Fixed: Some applications that use HCS-managed virtual machines experienced issues when sharing host folder with Linux VMs using Plan9. Folders shared from the Windows host using Plan9 did not appear or could not be accessed in the guest environment. [8-channel or 3D audio modes] Fixed: Some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices functioning as expected in standard stereo configurations failed when using multichannel audio features, including 8-channel or 3D audio modes. (Note: There are other audio symptoms not resolved in this OOB update. See the “Known issues in this update” section for more information.)

item.title: How to reinstall Windows and give your PC a fresh start
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.37
Once upon a time, “reinstalling Windows” was an often recommended remedy for all sorts of computer problems. Windows 95 and XP were notorious for becoming less stable over time, with “crap in the machine” in the form of settings left in the Registry, traces of uninstalled programs that had not been properly removed, and other things that lurked. Indeed, many people chose to reinstall from time to time even if the computer showed no symptoms, as part of regular maintenance. Windows 10 and 11 are much better at keeping order and cleaning up automatically. Today, frequent reinstallations are not something we at PCWorld or any other experts recommend. But sometimes it can still be appropriate. Maybe you want to make the move from Windows 10 to 11 and prefer to start over with a fresh system instead of upgrading. Maybe you have so much junk in your system that it will simply be easier to reinstall the OS and only install the programs you really need than to sit and remove everything you don’t need by hand. Whatever the reason, this is your guide to a safe and secure computer reset. Before you start Don’t start a reset without first making sure you know you can recover your computer, and more importantly your files, if something goes wrong. Samsung 1. Back up No matter how you go about reinstalling Windows, it’s a good idea to review your backups and make sure you don’t have any files on your computer that you don’t have at least one copy of elsewhere. See our roundups of the best backup software and best cloud backup services for recommendations. If you have an external hard drive you can spare that is at least as big as your computer’s internal disc (C:), you can create a clone of it in addition to your regular backups. A clone backup means that you mirror all the contents of the internal disc to the external one, and if something goes wrong, you can restore the same way in the other direction to get your computer back to the way it was before, including all installed programs. Choose a backup program, such as our favorite one, R-Drive Image that will do this. Foundry 2. Remember what you have installed today It’s also a good idea to create an inventory of what programs you have installed on your computer, and any extensions and plugins to these. The most common example of the latter is browser plugins, and it is sufficient to take a picture or write down the list of installed extensions in the browser(s) you use. For installed applications, you can use Settings or Control Panel to get a list of all installed applications. You can then use the same list after reinstalling to see which are included in Windows and which are missing. You can then find and install the missing programs you actually want to keep and ignore the rest. 3. Check your software licences If you own any expensive software whose license only allows installation on a certain number of computers, it might be a good idea to deactivate the licence on your computer before you reset it. Otherwise, the old installation will continue to count as one of your authorized installations. This was a bigger problem in the past. Today Adobe and others have features that can automatically move licenses to a new computer or system after reinstallation. But if you have a feeling that a program you’ve bought might get lost, it’s worth checking before you go any further. 4. Windows license key Speaking of licenses, it’s also a good idea to check that you have the Windows license key to activate your computer after reinstallation. Depending on how you acquired the system and have activated it, this may work slightly differently. Foundry Open Settings > System > Activation and click on Activation Status. If it says that Windows has been activated with a digital license linked to your Microsoft account, you don’t need to do anything special. As long as you don’t make any hardware changes, the system should activate automatically when you log in to the same Microsoft account after the reinstallation. It may also say that the system is activated with a digital license, but without mentioning anything about your Microsoft account. In this case, you should choose to add an account, otherwise Microsoft may not be able to find the digital license after reinstallation or if you make changes to the hardware. By linking the license to your account, you can activate the system using the activation troubleshooter. However, if it says that the system has been activated with a license key, open Powershell/Terminal and type the following command: wmic path softwareLicensingService get OA3xOriginalProductKey If a key is displayed, you can write it down. If no key is displayed, it is probably because Windows was included when you bought the computer and the key is embedded in the hardware. This means that the same version of Windows should be activated automatically after reinstallation. 5. Synchronize settings Microsoft If you use a Microsoft account, you can now synchronize many system settings, both between multiple computers and as a kind of settings backup when you reinstall your system. Go to Settings > Accounts > Windows Backup. Here you can activate two features: Remember my apps: The system will offer to automatically install the so-called modern Windows apps you had installed via the Microsoft store. Does not apply to regular programs that are installed with a custom installer. Remember my settings: This saves settings such as Wi-Fi, assistive technology, personalization, and language. In short, most things. When you log in to your account after the reinstallation, the system will read the synced settings and set everything up again. Zapping everything or just the system? How total do you want your reboot to be? That question determines which type of reinstallation you should choose. There are two basic methods of reinstalling, and for each method there are a few different options that affect the outcome. From Settings or through your computer’s recovery environment, you can reinstall Windows over the current installation, and either keep or delete files in the user folder. This will remove installed programs, except those that came with the computer. Creating installation media on a USB stick gives you a few more options, including the ability to reinstall the system and keep both your files and any installed programs. The table below shows the different options. | Type of reinstallation | Options for reinstallation | What happens to programmes | Files in your home folder | Files in other folders and on other discs | | In settings | Fixing problems with Windows Update | All programs and settings are preserved | Preserved | Preserved | | In Settings or via the recovery environment | Keep my files | Programmes that did not come with the computer are deleted | Preserved | Preserved | | In Settings or via the recovery environment | Delete everything | Deletes programs that did not come with the computer | Deleted | Deleted | | With installation media | Keep everything (default) | All programs and settings are preserved | Retain | Preserved | | With installation media | Keep personal data | All programmes are deleted | Retained | Retained | | With installation media | Do not retain anything | All programmes are deleted | Deleted | Deleted | | Clean install with installation media | Reformats C: or all disks and partitions. All files and programs are deleted. | | | | Caution: Warning! Keep in mind that if you choose to reformat the entire computer with installation media, disks other than C: will also be deleted. Method 1: Via settings The easiest way if the computer still boots is to restore Windows via Settings > System > Recovery. Here you have three options. If you think something is wrong with Windows itself but are not looking to clean up in other ways, you can start by trying Fixing problems with Windows Update. It will download and reinstall all system files without affecting installed programs, settings or your files. If you want to start from scratch instead, select Reset this PC. You will then be given another choice, to keep or delete your own files. Whichever you choose, installed programs will disappear and all settings will be reset. This is a good choice if you want to remove all the old junk that has accumulated over the years, but still want to keep the files in your home folder. You can also access this feature from the Windows recovery environment. Foundry With all three options, the system takes care of the rest. The computer will reboot a few times during the process, just like with some system updates. Once that’s done, you’ll have to go through the Windows Welcome Wizard, sign in to your Microsoft account again, and so on. Then you can just start installing programs you really need. You’ll also have to redo some system settings, but if you made sure to synchronize settings (see above), most of them will be restored. Method 2: With installation media These are actually two different methods, but they both start the same way: with a USB stick that turns into installation media. You can create the installation media on any Windows computer, not necessarily the computer you are reinstalling the system on. You need a USB stick of at least 8GB, which will be reformatted (i.e. all files will be deleted), and the Media Creation Tool which you can download here. When you run the program, you will have to choose the edition and language of Windows. After that, select the correct USB drive and click on it. The program will first download Windows and then create the installation media. If the computer boots properly, you can start the reinstallation by running setup.exe on the USB stick via Explorer. The program will chew for a while. Then click past user agreements and other things until you get to a dialog where you can choose what you want to keep. Select the Keep personal files and apps to upgrade in place. The options Keep only personal files and Nothing work as via Reset this computer in Settings (see above). Boot your computer from the USB stick If you have a major problem and Windows doesn’t start up as usual, you can boot your computer from the installation media and reinstall the system from there. Unfortunately, the Windows installer is not very good at handling more than one hard drive or SSD in the computer, so if you have discs other than C: it is a good idea to physically disconnect them. This avoids potential errors and means you don’t risk deleting something you don’t want to delete. You can reconnect the discs once Windows is installed and the computer boots properly. Boot your computer from the USB stick by plugging it in, starting your computer and pressing the button that opens the boot menu. Foundry Once it has booted, select the language and keyboard, click next, and then Install now and the installer will start. Fill in the product key or proceed without, and select the correct edition of Windows in the next step. Accept the user agreement and you will be presented with two options: Upgrade or Custom. Upgrade works just like Keep personal files and apps and Fix problems with Windows Update above, and only works if Windows Update can install the system on top of the existing one. All files and installed applications will remain, but the reinstallation may not do any good. Custom can either reinstall Windows and move all your old files to a new folder on C: called Windows.old, or reformat (delete) C: and install a completely new system without any other files on the disc. To keep the old files, select the Windows partition from the list of available partitions and move on without doing anything more. To start from scratch, delete all partitions from your computer’s boot disc, where the current Windows resides. If you have more than one hard drive or SSD in your computer and haven’t unplugged them as I recommend above, you need to be careful here, as you can easily accidentally delete the other disks. Look for a partition that is named something with Windows and is of type Primary. Note the drive number. My Windows partition is on Drive 1. Select each partition on that drive in turn and click Delete. When the whole drive is just Unallocated space you can select it and click Next. The installer will then format the drive appropriately and begin the installation of Windows. Once everything is ready, just sign in to your Microsoft account and let the settings sync if you chose to. Then you can move your files back from the backup and install the programs you need.

item.title: Gmail’s hidden trick: One inbox, endless custom addresses
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.28
For those who read this newsletter, you’re probably aware that Gmail can do a lot more than most people think. But there’s one neat trick you may not know about and it’s called “plus addressing.” Add a plus sign and a word of your choosing after your address, and Gmail will deliver the message to your main inbox. Go ahead and give it a try: send a test email to [email protected]. It lands right where your regular mail does. So that’s cool, but what’s the point? First, you can sort your mail without lifting a finger. Gmail’s filters let you search for a specific plus address and route it straight to a label or folder. Set up a filter for “+shopping,” and every receipt and promo lands in one place, out of your main inbox. Second (this is why I use it), you can catch companies that sell your address info. If [email protected] starts getting spam from unrelated senders, you know exactly which website sold or leaked your information—not that they’d ever do such a thing, of course. There’s a catch, though. Not every website accepts a plus sign in an email address. Some sign-up forms will reject it outright or throw an error. When that happens, you can fall back to a temporary email service or just use your regular address instead. Plus, addressing is really easy to set up and you don’t have to create new accounts. Give it a try next time you sign up for something new. For more fun and helpful tips, tricks, website and app recommendations, be sure to subscribe to our PCWorld Try This newsletter.

item.title: Webcam not showing up on a call? Check these 4 things
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.06
Suddenly, it happens. You’re about to use your computer to join a video meeting and connecting goes perfectly. You can talk, chat, and see all the other participants just fine, but the problem is that no one else could see you. Does this sound familiar? Here are four common solutions. Video apps such as Teams and Google Meet have a camera mute button so you can decide for yourself when others should see you. It can also be useful if you have a poor internet connection, which causes the call to stutter. If everyone switches off their cameras, you’ll save bandwidth and get better audio quality. In some cases, the camera is switched off by default when you start the call, so you’ll need to switch it on yourself. Another common reason is that you’ve accidentally pressed the wrong key on your computer. Many computers have shortcut keys to turn off the camera, which is useful if you want to quickly prevent others from seeing you. This button is often found on the top row of keys (F1–F12) and usually features an image of a camera. As a rule, you switch the camera on and off by pressing the Fn key together with the appropriate specific F keys, such as F1. Some computers also have a slider next to the camera that physically hides it behind a small plastic cover. Slide this to the side to turn the camera on. It’s also possible that you’ve enabled the camera block in Windows. In that case, you can unlock it by opening Windows Settings (via the Start button at the bottom left). Select Bluetooth & devices, then Cameras, and make sure no camera is disabled. If it is, simply click Enable.

item.title: Windows 11’s September patch breaks USB audio, and there’s no fix yet
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.56
Microsoft recently confirmed that the September Patch Tuesday security update (KB5124008) is causing problems with USB audio on some Windows 11 systems. However, Microsoft did not disclose how many users are affected, only stating that some computers with USB Audio Class 1.0 devices are reportedly affected. On the support page for the update, Microsoft has listed this under its “Known issues in this update” section: After installing the September 8, 2026, Windows security update, some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices might fail to start or produce audio. Affected devices might experience one or more of the following symptoms: - The device displays an error in Device Manager: “This device cannot start (Code 10).” - No audio output. - Volume controls are unresponsive or remain at zero. - Sound settings are unresponsive or unavailable. - Some devices might function in standard stereo configurations but fail when using multichannel audio features, including 8-channel or 3D audio modes. Some customers have reported that they’re able to restore audio in these cases by switching to 2-channel mode. This issue is limited to USB Audio Class 1.0 devices. Unfortunately, there’s no known workaround for this problem as of this writing. The issue affects Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 24H2, as well as 26H1 via update KB5124012. Microsoft says it’s working on a resolution and will update the support page once more information is available.

item.title: Windows 11 has a secret way to skip the Microsoft account requirement
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.56
Microsoft really wants you to use a Microsoft account when setting up Windows 11, and that’s why the company has been killing the workarounds for using Windows 11 with only a local account.
